speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will remember that on Thursday during the discussion on business for the week a request was made that the Prime Minister report to the House on the results of his trip to Russia. I agreed to bring that to the Prime Minister's attention. He does very much wish to report to the House as soon as possible. As you can appreciate, he just returned yesterday and he does have his remarks together. They are being typed now.
What we would like to suggest-and there have been discussions among the parties in order to enable this to be done-is the following. I will put it forward in terms of an understanding rather than asking for a House order if I may.
The understanding would be that we go through Routine Proceedings. The first item of government business is a vote on the Ways and Means proceeding No. 8. I understand that there may be a wish to have a recorded division on that. It is also my understanding that there would be a 15-minute division bell agreed upon and that we would then revert to Statements by Ministers in order to allow the Prime Minister to report to the House at that time.
I think that if there is a general understanding in the House to proceed on that basis I would request that the House do so.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to report to the House on my visit last week to the Soviet Union where I held extensive discussions with President Gorbachev and Prime Minister Ryzhkov. I also had very useful meetings with a number of important leaders, both government and party, in Kiev and Leningrad. The Secretary of State for External Affairs also held lengthy and constructive meetings with Mr. Shevardnadze.
I want to express my personal gratitude to the leadership and the people of the Soviet Union for the warmth and kindness they extended to all members of the Canadian delegation.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
This was the first official visit to the Soviet Union by a Canadian Prime Minister in 18 years. In fact this is somewhat misleading because contact between our two nations has in recent years become quite sustained and productive. In 1983, when Mr. Gorbachev was responsible for agriculture, he made his first ever official visit to the west to Canada where he remained for some 10 days on an extensive national tour and of which he speaks with great affection and joy for the people that he met and the personal experiences that he enjoyed.
I visited Moscow less than six months after becoming Prime Minister in March 1985 for the funeral of former General Secretary Chernenko, during which I met with Mr. Gorbachev, then the new Soviet leader.
This high-level contact was followed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs' visit to the U.S.S.R. in April 1985 and Mr. Shevardnadze's return trip to Canada in 1986, and by periodic meetings between the two since, including in New York in September and in Moscow last week.
The minister responsible for the Wheat Board visited the Soviet Union in 1987 to promote the interests of Canadian grains and oilseed producers who have maintained huge sales to the Soviet Union over many years.
The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture made an important visit to the Soviet Union earlier this year where he attended the third meeting of the Mixed Agricultural Commission since 1985. Former Agriculture Minister John Wise represented Canada at the 1985 and 1987 meetings.
The contacts between the Soviet Union and Canada on an ongoing basis were productive and, as I have indicated, sustained.
My visit to the Soviet Union came at a most critical juncture, at a time of powerful change in that country and of cascading reform throughout eastern Europe. As President Gorbachev said in our meeting: "Our times are changing so fast, are so dynamic that without good personal contacts among leaders it is impossible to build a good relationship". I fully subscribe to that view.

The discussions we had were both frank and very far-reaching. We talked about the economic and political

November 27, 1989

changes now occurring in the Soviet Union and the great significance they have for that country's future.
President Gorbachev was acutely aware of the difficulties he faces in implementing perestroika and glasnost successfully. He is, above all, a realist.
But I was struck by his determination to succeed and by his confidence that success is possible. He considers the course that he has set for transforming the Soviet Union to be right and irreversible. I believe that he is correct.
I also believe, strongly, that it is in everyone's interests, including our own, that he succeed.

The changes that he is seeking to provoke within the Soviet Union are profound and pervasive. Perestroika is not simply about improving the economic performance of the Soviet Union, although that is both urgently wanted and very badly needed. An important new law dealing with economic reform is to be tabled by mid-December. I think Mr. Shevardnadze advised the Secretary of State for External Affairs that it would perhaps be on December 12.
Perestroika is about establishing a new political order based on greater individual freedom and responsibility and on more democratic institutions. Perestroika is about establishing a new political order based on greater individual freedom and responsibility and on more democratic institutions. It is about putting into place a whole new economic structure, based on a greater role for the market, on productivity growth, and on individual motivation and individual reward. It is about designing a new social system and instilling a new way of thinking into the Soviet consciousness based on fundamental attitudinal changes, on diminishing dependence on the state and on greater creativity of thought and independence of action by the individual. President Gorbachev told me that "The revolution we have embarked upon is above all a revolution of the mind, of people's mentality".
Resistance to change runs deep in the Soviet Union. In my judgment, there is no viable alternative to Mr. Gorbachev's plan or to Mr. Gorbachev himself. In politics, change often comes suddenly and with little warning. In public life, no one is indispensable. To the
Routine Proceedings
extent, however, that anyone is indispensable to the ongoing well-being of his own society, it is probably President Gorbachev because of the overwhelming extent to which the entire agenda of reform is identified personally with him, both at home and around the world.
Our discussions also covered in frank detail domestic developments in the Soviet Union that are of great interest to the Canadian people: human rights, religious freedoms, emigration, the rights of nationalities and the very nature of the Soviet federation. The Soviet Union has made very encouraging progress on all of these matters since Mr. Gorbachev came to office.
The fundamentals of the Soviet system are being questioned, often in publicly televised debates by newly-elected deputies and by ordinary citizens throughout the nation. Prominent dissidents and political prisoners have been released from detention and many have been allowed to leave the Soviet Union. For the first time, unofficial groups not connected with the Communist party are being tolerated and encouraged. Permission to emigrate from the Soviet Union, in particular by citizens of the Jewish faith, has increased greatly in recent years, so much so that there is, today, no backlog of family reunification cases between Canada and the Soviet Union.
A new emigration law is now being considered by the Supreme Soviet. Our hosts assured us that it is consistent with the standards on population movement established by the Conference on Security and Co-Operation in Europe. The Soviet authorities also intend to put into place more relaxed regulations on secrecy restrictions which, as we all know in this House, has been the root of many of the remaining "refusnik" cases. I had the opportunity in the Soviet Union to visit briefly with some Jewish refusniks who seek to emigrate to Canada and to Israel.
New regulations on emigration will soon be followed by a new law on religious rights, expected to be submitted to the Supreme Soviet in the near future. We were assured that it would provide the basis as well for a new relationship between church and state in the process of dealing with many of the concerns raised by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by myself last week over the treatment of the Pentecostal Church and the Ukrainian Catholic and Ukrainian Orthodox

November 27, 1989
Routine Proceedings
Churches and of other religious groups in the Soviet Union.

It has become very clear that the question of nationalities and of ethnic minorities is fundamental to the nature of the Soviet Federation and, ultimately, fundamental to the future of the Soviet Union itself. Problems elsewhere, in other nations, pale in comparison with the tremendous challenge facing President Gorbachev in governing a country of such enormous diversity and profound divisions. We see evidence of those problems every day on television: in Armenia, in Georgia, in Moldavia and elsewhere. The strains in the fabric of the Soviet Federation are serious and no one appears to be more conscious of them than President Gorbachev himself. He indicated to me that he is determined to respond to those strains positively and with imagination before they degenerate further into greater instability.

His resolve to seek greater equity and fairness for nationalities and minorities is equalled by his determination that this new level of social and political justice be found within the federation, a federation that will allow the various republics greater autonomy, particularly in culture, language and the economy.
In our discussions with President Gorbachev and with Foreign Minister Shevardnadze, we also focused on today's often tumultuous international agenda. In the political declaration President Gorbachev and I signed in Moscow six days ago, which Foreign Minister Shevardnadze has subsequently characterized as a "milestone" and as "an intellectual breakthrough" for both nations, the Soviet Union recognized the benefits of change and endorsed the right of countries to make their own way in the world without outside interference by anybody.
The regional conflicts in Central America, southern Africa, Indochina, the Middle East and Afghanistan were covered quite comprehensively, particularly in extensive meetings between Mr. Shevardnadze and the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
President Gorbachev and I discussed the rapidly evolving situation in eastern and central Europe very frankly. We reviewed these areas not only in terms of developments unfolding in that part of the world but, equally important, in terms of their impact upon the over-all relationship between East and West.
Change has come to eastern Europe rapidly, unevenly and unpredictably. Every day seems to bring more dramatic news and more unforgettable images: former Czech Prime Minister Alexander Dubcek making a triumphal speech before hundreds of thousands of people in Wenceslaus Square; breaches, at last, in the Berlin Wall as millions stream through to satisfy themselves first hand about western values and western institutions; non-communist political parties exercising power in Poland and the Prime Minister of Poland being received two days ago with warmth and encouragement by President Gorbachev in Moscow; the privatization of economic activity on a growing basis in Hungary; and exciting new freedoms of speech and protest and movement for peoples throughout the east which, for 40 years, has known little of freedom and less of its benefits. The pace of change has become torrential, overwhelming in some ways our capacity to assess the transformation that we are in the process of witnessing.
A revealing insight in this regard appeared yesterday, I thought, in The New York Times where Harvard professor Michael Sandel commented that "the most appropriate response now is not caution or boldness-we are beyond all that-but attentiveness and appreciation because, when history turns this fast, what we want from statesmen are not vain attempts to control events that have a momentum of their own, but that they be alive to the possibilities that these events will leave in their wake."
I think that is important advice from Professor Sandel, and it is advice that the government and the Parliament of Canada, I suspect, will follow.

The world is now clearly departing from a sterile period of East-West confrontation and embarking on one of immensely more fruitful relations, a course that ultimately promises genuine democracy in Eastern Europe, more liberalized trade and investment opportunities across that vast region, more predictable relations with the Soviet Union and profound reductions in the emphasis on defence in all capitals of the world. Eventually, as governments continue to emerge in Eastern
November 27, 1989

Europe that have the freely given support of their people, European stability will be put on a durable basis.
But the transition period will have to be managed carefully. And, in fact, the people of Eastern Europe and the leadership of the U.S.S.R. are handling the changing situation very prudently.
In these swiftly changing circumstances, NATO retains its great importance because it is the locus for discussion of the Western response to political change in the East and for coordinating positions in the crucial conventional arms reduction discussions in Vienna and on the superpower negotiations on strategic weapons in Geneva.
Distinctions need to be made between intentions and military capacity. It should be remembered that the Soviet Union retains enormous conventional and strategic forces. Everyone's security objective is served by a balance in military capacity at progressively lower levels of arms. Both sides want lower levels of arms.
NATO is a political, as well as military, organization and is an indispensable part of the western diplomatic infrastructure. It was clear from my discussions with President Gorbachev that neither sides thinks it is time to abandon any alliances. In fact, President Gorbachev signalled very clearly that it would be imprudent to change alliances or institutions in a manner that could destabilize east-west relations, as eastern Europe goes through a period of such convulsive change.
I proposed to President Gorbachev that we seek to establish a closer relationship between himself and the leaders of the major industrialized western countries. In response to President Gorbachev's interest in integrating the Soviet economy over time more closely into the world trade and payment system, I told him I would propose to my G-7 colleagues that each year's chairman be mandated to discuss with him the ideas and strategies that emerge from the Economic Summit. This would provide him with a regular opportunity to obtain a first-hand report on the preoccupations and interests of the leaders of the principal western governments whose co-ordinated policy approaches have produced in recent years an era of remarkable economic growth and a series
Routine Proceedings
of initiatives that both intrigue and challenge President Gorbachev and about which he asked many questions and some of which he would seek to apply, given the new circumstances he chooses to develop in his own nation.
President Gorbachev warmly welcomed this proposal. [Translation]
Agreement was also reached on developing a closer bilateral consultation process on a range of international issues of mutual concern.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and Mr. Shevardnadze, as well as their officials, will meet more frequently for that purpose.
In Moscow, I also raised with Mr. Gorbachev the Arctic arms control proposals he had set forth in his Murmansk speech several years ago.
I pointed out to him that Mr. Clark had responded to those proposals on several occasions but that we were quite prepared to discuss with the Soviets any refinements they might have to make to their original ideas.
I pointed out, as well, that I continued to believe that current ongoing arms control negotiations between the two superpowers and the two alliances had proven successful and were the best avenues for making progress on these issues.
He understands fully our position and agreed that further review of this issue should be pursued by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and Mr. Shevardnadze.
In terms of bilateral co-operation, last week's visit marked a watershed in our relations.

We signed 14 bilateral agreements-more than had been signed in the previous 20 years-on subjects ranging from international affairs to Arctic co-operation to the environment to military and cultural co-operation to investment protection. Foreign Minister Shevardnadze told Izvestia at the end of last week that the Soviets attach particular significance to the environment agreement because "Canada-was one of the first to place environmental protection on the international agenda and Canada has achieved remarkable success in this area."
Routine Proceedings

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
The Soviets intend to open a new office in Toronto and discussions will start shortly on our respective plans for those offices. We hope to put our office into operation before long.
I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that the establishment of a new office in Kiev will, I think, go a long way in responding to an increasingly obvious need for Canada to be represented in the capital of the Ukraine.
Nearly one million Canadians trace their roots back to the Ukraine. Many of them still have family there. At present, 35 per cent of the visa applicants at our embassy in Moscow come from the Ukraine. With more relaxed travel restrictions in the Soviet Union, we can expect a substantial increase in human contacts between Canada and the Ukraine.
Moreover, an office of this dimension in Kiev will allow us to tap the commercial and trade potential of the Ukraine, a market of some 52 million people whose economic needs can be responded to by the transfer of Canadian technology, joint venture initiatives and direct equity participation, to say nothing of the transfer of skills, knowledge, and know-how in the area of agriculture where, as the leaders of the Ukraine have pointed out to us, the need and their need is greatest and Canadian expertise is acknowledged to be world class.
The Canadian private sector is also taking an unprecedented interest in the Soviet economy. The Canadian government has been strongly supportive of the private sector as it seeks new economic opportunities in the Soviet Union and new trade and investment niches for Canada.
Our two-way trade has for too long lacked diversification and dynamism and I was delighted to see the enthusiasm and resolve of Canadian business people in Moscow surveying new opportunities and anticipating new challenges, none more enthusiastically than distinguished businessmen like Frank Stronach , Albert Reich-mann, representatives from Lavalin, and other leading firms from British Columbia to Newfoundland which was represented by Vic Young of Fishery Products International.
A broad commercial relationship with the Soviet Union will help us not only to diversify our exports, now largely dominated by grain sales, but also to provide the products and services and technology that will help to support the goals of perestroika by satisfying some of the rising expectations this policy has triggered among the Soviet people.
That is the greatest challenge, I believe, confronting Mr. Gorbachev today, the problem of the rising expectations generated by the enthusiasm with which his reforms were introduced and received by the people. A lot of progress is expected the next day and yesterday in the Soviet Union and he is incapable of delivering as rapidly as he would like on all of these expectations.
That is why it is so important for countries like Canada to come forward in tangible ways with trade missions that sign deals that create new wealth and new opportunities in order to provide him with the support.
I mention, parenthetically, Mr. Speaker, George Co-hon, the chief executive officer of McDonald's who has been working to open the largest McDonald's in the world in the Soviet Union. He placed an ad in the Moscow newspapers for 500 people he wanted to have work in his new restaurant which the Soviet Union believes and hopes can expand to 15 or 20 across the country in short order. However, in the Soviet Union, he put an ad in the newspaper asking for 500 young men and women to seek employment. When we left he had had
14.000	applicants, and they were coming in at the rate of
1.000	a day. I told him that if it did not work out there, he might consider putting it in my riding.
This is the kind of enthusiasm with which the Soviet people are responding to Canadian business people. I think that this kind of attitude is a good, friendly, productive and a very creative one. This is a constructive

and welcome response to the daring and innovative reforms being implemented by the Soviet leadership.
Last Wednesday, in Moscow, I attended with Prime Minister Ryzhkov the inauguration of an organization, the Canada-U.S.S.R. Business Council, that will do much to underpin our new political relationship and to bolster our bilateral commercial ties.
The council includes almost all of the principal Canadian firms with significant current or prospective commercial interests in the Soviet Union and is co-chaired by Albert Reichman, President of Olympia and York, and Alexei Malkevitch, head of the Soviet Chamber of Commerce.

The Canadian business delegation that was in the Soviet Union during my visit numbered about 240 people. A good number of them signed agreements for direct investment, joint ventures or equity participation arrangements.
These agreements, worth one billion dollars, plus, are an extremely important part of building a new relationship between Canada and the Soviet Union.
President Gorbachev made very clear that the U.S.S.R. was not looking for direct aid from the West.
What the Soviet Union wished to have with Canada was a cooperative, mutually beneficial, political, economic and technological relationship because of the many similarities between our two countries, and because of the experience we have in coping with many categories of problems that the U.S.S.R. is now dealing with in a serious way.

For our part, Mr. Speaker, we went to the Soviet Union with the objectives of establishing a broadly-based relationship of confidence with President Gorbachev and his colleagues, of seeking on behalf of all Canadians to respond constructively to the historic changes that the Soviet leader is seeking to make and of bringing about a new beginning in Soviet-Canadian relations.
I believe that we have achieved these objectives. I also hope that, together, we have made a contribution to the building of a more durable international peace, which is
Routine Proceedings
the most important legacy our generation can pass on to our children.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Thrner (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is happening in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe today is the most important and cataclysmic change in human affairs since the last world war and indeed perhaps since the Soviet revolution itself.
Millions upon millions of Poles, Czechs, Hungarians, Russians, East Germans, Bulgarians, Latvians, Estonians, Ukrainians, Lithuanians are demanding freedom, demanding democracy, and they are getting it.
The urge for freedom is unpredictable and finally irresistible. Totalitarian regimes are falling at a staggering rate. They are being shunted aside in the sweep of history. The most remarkable feature about the drama surrounding us that we see every night on television is that so far this popular evolution is being done without violence.
Diplomats are becoming irrelevant, the pundits and experts are at a loss to explain what has happened. Very few of them predicted it. Foreign policy analysts, so used to seeing the world only in terms of the superpowers, have been confounded by what is happening. Leaders and the elites are being toppled. The people are rolling over them all. The tearing down of the Berlin Wall is only the most visible symbol of this demand for freedom.
What this government of ours has failed to grasp so far is that the urge for freedom is exploding; it is bursting out, not only in Berlin, but at almost every level in the East Bloc countries. Yet while the whole of Europe is alive with discussion, as Hungarians and Poles and Czechs are on the streets debating these issues and calling for freedom, we in this Parliament have had no discussion of what our approach should be to these massive, compulsive and unprecedented changes in the world.
The Prime Minister has signed an agreement which he claims will usher in a new era in Canadian-Soviet relations. Yet, it was this Prime Minister whose major foreign policy plank in the last election was to spend billions upon billions of dollars on building a fleet of nuclear powered submarines to protect us from the Soviets.

November 27, 1989
Routine Proceedings
The Minister of Defence still claims that the White Paper on defence is government policy, and that the submarines were cancelled only for economic reasons.
The Prime Minister has made it clear both in the Soviet Union and here that the view of this government is that the cold war is not yet over. Which is it? Are we into a new relationship, or are we still in the cold war? We cannot have two policies on this issue.

Before his official visit, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) failed to consult Canadians. He did not ask the opinion of the Standing Comittee on External Affairs. He did not consult academics, former diplomats or non-governmental organizations. The government behaved much the same as it did regarding Canada's membership in the Organization of American States. But going off course is dangerous, Mr. Speaker. The government is changing the direction of this country's external policy without first consulting Canadians. And it is not just the absence of debate. The fact is, this government has failed to produce a single official document on external affairs policy since it was sworn in.
The Prime Minister would do well to follow Mr. Gorbachev's example by injecting a little glasnost, a little openness into its external affairs policy.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

Since this is only the second speech of the Prime Minister of our country on foreign policy in the House of Commons in the last five years, he should not be surprised if Canadians are not at all sure what the policy of this government is with regard to the unprecedented changes taking place in eastern Europe.
What are the implications for NATO? What are the implications for Canada's position in this alliance? What direction do we want NATO to take? What are the implications for the movement toward 1992 and the so-called economic union of Europe? What about the possible reunification of the two Germanies? These are questions that need to be addressed. These are questions that need to be discussed in this Parliament, not in the Langevin Block, if they are ever discussed at all.
We are happy to see the Soviets' willingness to allow more autonomy in the Baltic States and the Ukraine, and we welcome the opening of the Canadian consulate in Kiev in the Ukraine. We hope that such a move will facilitate the reunification of families of Ukrainian descent in Canada. We hope also that our government policy will be to continue to encourage more autonomy within the Ukraine and the Baltic States.
Many of the agreements signed by the Prime Minister in Moscow were renewals of agreements signed by previous governments, including the 1984 Arctic Scientific Co-operation Agreement. The difference is that previous governments took a leadership role. Mr. Pearson's visit in 1955 as Secretary of State for External Affairs was the first time a major western political figure visited the Soviet Union since the great war.
A 1971 visit by Mr. Trudeau was followed by major cultural, academic and sports exchange agreements, as well as agreements on trade and scientific co-operation.

We welcome the creation of a Canada-U.S.S.R. Business Council and the desire to invest shown by business circles. Businessmen, however, are very realistic. Will they be able to make a profit and bring those profits back to Canada? Will the ruble remain a non-convertible currency? Will the Canadian government provide guarantees for Canadian investments in Soviet Union?
What we find very disturbing, however, is that the government did not offer economic assistance. Because there is a risk. If there is no economic progress, the reform process may abort, not only in the Soviet Union but also in Eastern Europe.
The joint statement by the two governments contains many generalities but no proposals, no initiatives, no studies or any indication of interest in developing Canadian perspectives on arms limitation. Joint approaches to Arctic security shone by their absence. There was no response to Mr. Gorbachev's proposal regarding a peace zone in the Arctic.
In fact, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) insisted on reminding Canadians that Soviet submarines had navigated in Canadian waters, instead of stressing a statement by Mr. Edward Shevardnadze that
November 27, 1989

Soviet submarines would respect Canadian sovereignty in the North.

These are issues that should have been addressed. There are more. The Prime Minister should have put forward serious proposals in several areas. First, Arctic security. In February, 1988,1 called for the creation of a new international regime in the Arctic, in particular the promotion of arms control alternatives. This government has refused to consider any such initiative.
The second area is Arctic sovereignty. We need a joint declaration with the Soviet Union in which they explicitly recognize our sovereignty over Canadian-claimed Arctic waters. The Soviet foreign minister's statement on Soviet submarines hinted at their willingness to support such a declaration.
The third area is Arctic environment. We are pleased to see that Canada will be hosting an Arctic environment conference next year. We are concerned that we do not have in this a clearly developed and co-ordinated policy approach to Arctic issues. Therefore, I call on the government to implement a recent recommendation that an ambassador for circumpolar affairs be named to co-ordinate Canada's Arctic policy.
We need to increase Canada's diplomatic presence in eastern Europe. We have no diplomatic presence in eastern Germany or in Bulgaria at the moment. We should, particularly now in eastern Germany.
Every effort should be made to involve Canadians more frequently and systematically in government policy discussions on important international issues with significant ramifications for them. The government needs to be more open, and that openness should begin right here in the Parliament of Canada where we have had no foreign policy debates. None of the recent initiatives of this government have been taken to the Standing Committee on External Affairs.
Another area is economic assistance to eastern Europe. Most western leaders have recognized the critical importance of a successful reform process in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe. They have given generously of their funds to help Poland and Hungary, and it will be forthcoming, no doubt, for other eastern European states undergoing economic and political reform. An unfortunate exception has been Canada, where a paltry
Routine Proceedings
$42 million was offered to Poland and Hungary while other countries were offering hundreds of millions of dollars. Why are we Canadians satisfied to give, as Lech Walesa put it, "a beautiful tie to a corpse"?
When I had the honour with my colleague from Parkdale-High Park to meet Lech Walesa in Toronto, Mr. Walesa said to us that it was important that Canada invest in eastern Europe and in Poland because we had to give the people of Poland-and he was speaking for them at this instance-a clear message of hope. We have to give some sign that Canadians have confidence in the future of the democratic movement in Poland, that there are signs of Canadian enterprise, visible signs of Canadian business, because they want to see their economies reconstructed on the basis of democracy. But time runs out and they need an urgent Canadian and western response to their problems. We must show them that as Canadians we are willing to participate with the Polish, Hungarian, Soviet and East German peoples in their reconstruction and we have to do it in a concrete way.
We did not anticipate or require that the Prime Minister's visit would solve or even address all of the major problems of the world. However, what does stand out in his public declaration so far, including his statement this morning, is that in the hours of discussions and visits not one word was spoken about the events in the world's most populace nation, the other communist superpower, the People's Republic of China. Surely this was a public opportunity for the Prime Minister to elicit support from the Soviets for the movement towards democracy in China.
I would hope that the Prime Minister impressed upon President Gorbachev that the movement toward greater freedom and democracy is not reversible. There can be no return to totalitarian methods either in the Soviet Union or in eastern Europe. I do hope that when he sees President Bush this week he will also impress upon him that the convulsions and transformations in the world demand that the United States encourage economic development and reform in the eastern bloc countries.
Both President Gorbachev and President Bush must understand that when they meet at Malta it must not be merely a replay of Yalta. It is not their world to divide again as they wish. Europeans are determining their own future. People in every part of the globe are demanding a reversal of the arms race and a commitment toward co-operation and peace. I believe that as in the move

November 27, 1989
Routine Proceedings
toward democracy in eastern Europe, the demands of the people will not be denied.
These are tremendously exciting changes occurring in the world. As a middle power with immense goodwill and respect around the globe, Canada has a single opportunity to push for even more freedom, more democracy and more peace throughout the globe. I urge our government not to let us miss that opportunity. We should be leaders in this movement and not merely followers as we have been to date.
All the men, women and children alive on the face of the globe today have spent their entire lives living in the shadow of the threat of war and the spectre of the arms race. We have poverty and suffering because for generations we have spent trillions of dollars on armaments instead of on promoting freedom. We have spent countless decades fighting one another rather than working together. There is no guarantee that this fantastic push for freedom will succeed. But Canadians expect our government to do absolutely everything possible to encourage it and to join in the movement in a very constructive way.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by thanking the Prime Minister for making this report to the House on his historic visit. It is something we would like to see more often.
I think the comments of the Leader of the Official Opposition about the need to involve Parliament more in making foreign policy in Canada is a suggestion that the Prime Minister should listen to, not only with respect to foreign policy but also with respect to other areas as well. There has been a trailing away, if you like, in prime ministerial interest in the House of Commons and we hope that this is the beginning of a new interest in the Chamber.
I would like also to say in the same vein that many of us were distressed at the way in which the decision to join the Organization of American States was arrived at without consultation with the external affairs committee of this House, or with the non-governmental organizations, churches and other groups that have an interest in Central and Latin America.
We hope that with respect to east-west relations, the Prime Minister will take Parliament into its confidence and involve the whole of the Canadian people through Parliament and other organizations in the making of foreign policy. If he did, and if he had done that earlier, I think he would have found that there was a lot of support for the kinds of things that the Prime Minister himself now seems to be considering. In that sense I think the Prime Minister is not only playing catch-up in terms of international relations with other countries but also playing catch-up with the Canadian people who have been ready for a more enlightened approach to east-west relations for some time now.
As was said this morning in a newspaper column regarding the visit, better late than never, and we are happy that the Prime Minister has now grasped what is going on in the world and particularly what is going on in the Soviet Union.
I want to compliment him on elements of the statement. What I have in mind is the relative lack of gloating in the statement, of ideological gloating. I believe it veiy important for those of us in the west not to be seen to be gloating over what has happened in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. This was a point made not so long ago by none other than Zbigniew Breczinski and many others. I say this because I have noticed in speeches made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs a certain amount of what I would call unwarranted ideological gloating.
I think it is important that in this new east-west relationship that the west retain a certain amount of humility. We should keep in mind that our system, whatever its merits, has also been responsible for incredible poverty within our own midst and in the Third World, thanks to a relationship in which wealth is still being transferred in a net way from the poorest countries to the wealthiest countries. We must remember that we too have severe environmental problems and that our society is besieged with meaninglessness and drugs and many of the other things with which other societies are also plagued. We ought to remain humble, if you like, in
November 27, 1989

Routine Proceedings
our approach while, at the same time, welcoming what is going on in other parts of the world.
I also welcome the Prime Minister's proposal with respect to developing a relationship between Mr. Gorbachev and the G-7 group. I think anything which increases personal contact between Mr. Gorbachev and the leaders of the western countries is a good thing and I hope that the Prime Minister can be instrumental in setting up more of those kinds of contacts.
I welcome the fact that when the Prime Minister was there he brought up the issue of the Ukrainian Catholic Church which is of great concern to many people in my riding, in Winnipeg, and in the country in general. I hope that the new consulate which is being set up in Kiev will be instrumental in bringing new opportunities for Canadians of Ukrainian origin to visit the Ukraine, to do business in the Ukraine, and vice versa, and that the new law upcoming in the Soviet Union with respect to relationships between church and state will see a legalization of the Ukrainian Catholic Church, something which many people have hoped for for a long time.
With respect to the Murmansk proposal, I notice in the statement that the Prime Minister says, with respect to the proposal of Mr. Gorbachev for a zone of peace in the Arctic: "Mr. Clark responded to these proposals on several occasions, but the Canadian government is quite prepared to discuss any refinements the Soviet might have to make to their original ideas".
Many people who have paid attention to the Murmansk proposal and to the period thereafter are not aware that this government has made any response except to make what constitutes no response at all.
We do not just want to know what the refinements are that the Soviets might have to their own ideas, we want to know what the Canadian ideas are with respect to peace in the Arctic. We do not have that yet. The statement says that progress on these issues is best left to negotiations between the two superpowers. This is the Yalta mentality that we are trying to overcome, that the world is trying to overcome with respect to seeking international peace and stability.
It is a profound mistake on the part of the government to leave matters pertaining to the Arctic to the context of superpower negotiations or inter-alliance negotiations because there are many things that Canada has a unique responsibility to concern itself with given our unique geo-political situation between the superpowers in the Arctic. This is something that the government does not
yet seem to have appreciated in its full measure. So what are the government's views?
I hope that perhaps today we might hear from the government as to what the Prime Minister thinks of many of the good suggestions that have been made in recent years and, most recently, at a conference sponsored by the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament on peace and security in the Arctic. There is the whole question of naval arms control and the proliferation of submarine-launched cruise missiles. There was not a mention of it in the statement by the Prime Minister. This area of growing proliferation of nuclear weapons is of increasing concern.
The Prime Minister and the government still seem locked into the view that the only things that are significant in terms of arms control are happening in Europe. What is happening in the Arctic and what is happening in the northern Pacific are things that ought to concern the Canadian government every bit as much as what is happening in Europe.
What is the response of the government to the proposal that there be an Arctic open skies policy? What is the response of the government to the suggestion that we seek-and this is a suggestion that has been made not only by the Soviet Union, but by various Canadian groups and political parties-a demilitarized zone in the Arctic or a nuclear free zone in the Arctic? Has the government got an argument why this would be a bad thing or why this is not something that the Canadian government could be showing some initiative on?
There is the proposal for an Arctic ambassador, or a circumpolar ambassador, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition called it, someone who would concern him or herself directly with Arctic matters. As well, there is the proposal for a conference on security and co-operation in the Arctic, similar to the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe.
I noticed in one of the press reports of the Prime Minister's visit that the language "common search for security" was used in a statement put out by the Prime Minister and Mr. Gorbachev. What is needed now is a bridge from the language of "common search for security" to the language of "common security". It is the concept of common security, which goes back to the Palme Commission report in 1982, that we find the conceptual framework that I think is most appropriate to Canada's situation in the Arctic, sitting as we do between the two superpowers. I would recommend a reading of

November 27, 1989
Routine Proceedings
that document and many others which have followed it, to the Prime Minister.
As I said before, we have a unique responsibility, being between the superpowers, to pursue a common security regime in the Arctic. It is not enough to leave it up to the superpowers, because it is in the context of the relationship between the superpowers that the greatest threat to our sovereignty comes. I think our sovereignty in the Arctic is not any more respected by the United States, perhaps even less so, than is by the Soviet Union. If we are concerned about sovereignty in the Arctic, we have to also be concerned about what the United States might be doing in our north and not just the Soviet Union.
The Prime Minister has made much of the fact that Mr. Gorbachev indicated to him that he would like to see the alliances continue. That may well be the case. That may well may be the view of Mr. Gorbachev. We know it is the view of the Prime Minister. I am sure that Mr. Gorbachev also believes, as we do, that there are a range of issues outside the NATO-Warsaw Pact negotiations with which Canada and the U.S.S.R. should be concerning themselves. Those are the issues which pertain to the Arctic.
As we have said many times before, it is in this context that we urge the Prime Minister and the government to seek a replacement for our relationship with the United States now constituted in NORAD which would give us more independence and more ability to respond to initiatives that are made by the Soviet Union with respect to peace and security in the Arctic.
Within the context of NATO, it seems to me that the Prime Minister should have said something this morning about his statement that the White Paper is outdated. We asked the question of the Minister of National Defence in the House the other day when the Prime Minister was away. Now is the opportunity for the Prime Minister to say what he meant when he said that the White Paper was outdated. What is going to be the follow-up of the government to that fact, a fact which I might say was perceived by many long before the Prime Minister said it was so. But the fact of the matter is the
Prime Minister has said the White Paper is outdated. What will happen now? What will be the process for reviewing Canadian defence and security policy in the follow-up to the Prime Minister's statement?
The Prime Minister is going to Brussels soon. I would recommend to him, on behalf of our party, that in view of the changing world circumstances, in view of the outdatedness of the White Paper, that a couple of things be done now.
We recommend that the Prime Minister commit himself and his government to trying to eliminate the first use policy of nuclear weapons within NATO; that the Prime Minister and his government commit itself to putting at least a moratorium on Canada's participation in the FOFA strategy of NATO, the one which has caused so much trouble for Canadians, and in particular, the Innu people in Labrador; and that the Prime Minister indicate to Canadians that Canada will put an end to cruise testing in Canada and take a different position than it did with respect to the modernization of nuclear weapons in Europe.
Finally, we recommend that Canada should seek, within the context of the mutual balance force reduction negotiations to bring Canadian troops home from Europe, something which I see the Prime Minister has already talked about. Certainly if that can be done in the context of negotiated reductions, that is the way to do it.
If NATO is to become an agent of the transition to a new relationship between east and western Europe, as many believe it can now become, given the changes in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, then I think Canada should become vigorously involved in that change.
We are looking at an entirely new situation in Europe. We are looking at a Europe which is no longer post-war Europe, not only in economic and political terms but also psychologically. I had an opportunity to be there recently and it is clear that there is an entirely new collective self-consciousness in Europe. This is something that I do not think has been fully appreciated in Canada. It means

that the United States will have less influence in Europe, not more.
It means there will be an opening for real Canadian participation of the kind that we have not seen before in shaping the future of Europe. Whether it turns out to be still an east-west relationship with a common security arrangement or whether it turns out to be a larger western Europe with the border between east and west pushed further east, or whether it turns out to be Mr. Gorbachev's common European home from the Atlantic to the Urals, whatever the case may be, it will be an entirely new Europe. The opportunity exists now for Canada to be involved in that in a way that we previously have not. Too often up until now we have simply taken the American view, whatever that happens to be, in NATO.
In the larger context, still, we would like to see Canada be much more active and principled in pushing for a comprehensive ban on all testing of all nuclear weapons and on all chemical weapons. We live in a different world in which many of the things for which there have been arguably reasons for pursuing, various courses of action have disappeared. It seems to me that the Canadian government must now take a different and bolder course.
I notice that the Prime Minister used a quote in which boldness was downplayed and attentiveness and appreciation were regarded positively. I think that is a good quote. I think there are many cases in foreign policy where attentiveness and appreciation is an appropriate first course of action. But there does come a time when boldness is required. Boldness is required in the international scene on the whole question of nuclear arms control. Boldness is also required when the Prime Minister goes to see Mr. Bush in the days ahead, to tell Mr. Bush that it is about time that the United States of America showed the same tolerance in its backyard as the Soviets are now showing in eastern Europe, and to tell Mr. Bush to change American policy in El Salvador and Central America. That seems to be an opportunity for the Prime Minister to be bold and appropriate, all at the same time.
With respect to what is happening in eastern Europe, I think the time has come for bold action to make sure
Routine Proceedings
that the democratic experiments which are happening in eastern Europe now succeed. This is our time to show that the west was not simply crying crocodile tears for the last 40 years, that our statements about the suffering and the oppression of people in Poland and East Germany, Hungary and Czechoslovakia were not just strategic statements but that they were sincere statements. When the time comes for us to put our money where our mouth is, we must show that we will put our money where our mouth is, that there will be Canadian action on eastern Europe to make sure that those new governments succeed. That is not something that the Canadian government has done so far to the satisfaction of anyone. I might add, in that respect, that what is important in all of this is that the principle of additionality be respected, i.e. that whatever aid that we may give to eastern Europe not come at the expense of the traditional aid that we have given to Third World countries. There is a very real danger that the south will be left out of this new era in the north vis-a-vis east-west relations.
Finally, because I realize that my time has run out, I think again where boldness is required is on the question of the environment. The time has come to be bold on the environment. I think it is on the environment that finally the differences between east and west, between the Soviet Union and the U.S., and between Canada and the U.S.S.R., will be trivialized in what will come to be the need for planetary solidarity, not alliances, NATO and the Warsaw Pact, but planetary solidarity.
In order to survive and in order for there to be a truly human future, all these differences will have to be trivialized. It is in our common concern about the environment that we get glimpses of what we ought to really mean when we talk about security. What is security, after all, if you cannot breathe the air, drink the water or grow food? The navies, the armies and the air forces of the world are paltry in comparison to the danger which the environmental crisis provides and I hope that soon we will see real boldness and not just attentiveness on the part of the Prime Minister to the environmental crisis.

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-36, an act to amend the Advance payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, as reported (with an amendment) from a legislative committee.

I have certain motions which I must rule on.

There are eleven motions in amendment standing on the Notice Paper for the report stage of Bill C-36, An Act to amend the Advance Payments Acts.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Motions Nos. 1, 2, 8, 9 and 11, in the name of the hon. member for Mackenzie, cause the Chair considerable procedural difficulty. These motions are attempting to remove the notion of the producer organization paying interest on money that is attributable to advance payments. It would appear that one of the principles of this present bill is to change the law related to the payment of interest. As hon. members are aware, it is not within our established practices to permit amendments that are contrary to the principle of a bill as agreed to by the House of Commons at second reading.
Consequently, in accordance with Beauchesne's fifth Edition, subsection 1 of CITATION 773, I must rule Motions Nos. 1, 2, 8, 9 and 11 out of order.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion numbered 5 standing in the name of the Hon. the Minister of agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski)is in a situation that is basically similar to those motions I have just ruled upon. However, motion numbered 5 is rendered acceptable by the fact that it is accompagnied by a recommandation of Her Excellency, the Governor General. Motion No. 6, standing in the name of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, is attempting to amend the original act. Hon. members know that it is not procedurally acceptable to amend sections of the original act that are not included in an amending bill. Therefore, in accordance with Beauchesne, paragraph 8(b), citation 773, I must rule this motion out of order.

speechtext:
It depends on how you want to put it, Mr. Speaker.
We believe that with this amendment we are changing and improving the bill. The Advance Payments for Crops Act has always been a shared risk program with the producer organizations and historically producer organizations have been responsible for 10 per cent of each advance that has been defaulted to a total of 2 per cent of the total amount advanced.
This amendment will leave producer organizations responsible for only 2 per cent of any advance defaulted, and that is covering both the principal and interest.
Proposed changes to the Bank Act alter reserve requirements for banks and this will make federal guaranteed loans less expensive. In order to be in a position for producer organizations to take full advantage of this provision the guaranteed level will be increased to 98 per cent. The reduced risk to producer organizations from the lower liability limit will allow producers to reduce administration costs.
Smaller producer organizations that do not have financial ability to assume the risk of granting high value advances will now be able to participate on the same basis as the larger and more financially strong producer organizations. This will be particularly important to the horticulture sector where the producer organizations tend to be small and newly formed organizations dealing in specialty crops such as forage seed are also small. We believe that this amendment would greatly increase the benefits to producers.

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
For producer organizations that withhold an amount of the advance to cover their liability, this amendment will increase significantly the amount of cash received by the individual producers.
I would just like to share with the House the names of some of the organizations that this legislation change will help. They include the B.C. Okanagan Fruit Producers' and Shippers Association, the Interior Vegetable Marketing Agency, Vancouver Island Produce Limited, the Alberta Beekeepers' Association, the Alberta Fresh Vegetable Marketing Board, the Peace River Seed Coop Limited, the Saskatchewan Beekeepers' Association, the Saskatchewan Vegetable Growers' Association, the Keystone Vegetable Producers, the Manitoba Com Growers' Association, the St. Lawrence Valley Fruit Growers, Blue Water Storage Limited, Georgian Triangle Apples, the Ontario Beekeepers' Association, Temiskaming Grain Growers, the Association des jardini-ers maraichers, the Co-op Federee de Quebec, the Valley Grain Pool, the New Brunswick Fruit Growers Association, the New Brunswick Potato Agency, the Nova Scotia Potato Marketing Board, the Nova Scotia Fruit Growers Association, the Nova Scotia Grain Marketing Board, the P.E.I. Vegetable Growers' Co-Operative Association and the P.E.I. Grain Growers' Co-operative.
As you can see, this change will improve the operation and viability of many of these producers of crops that are not as large as some of our producers of major commodities of grain and com but it also assists the producers of those commodities greatly and gives those people much less exposure to the sponsoring organization and allows for a greater amount of advance to be made to individual producers. Going to 2 per cent from 10 per cent and withholding 10 per cent for default of the principal makes quite a difference, but when you reduce that to 2 per cent it is considerable and that is a great benefit to the producer. I know we can count on all members of the House to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak at report stage of Bill C-36.1 must say this has been one of most cobbled up bills I have ever seen the government introduce. I recall that originally it introduced this bill under Bill C-32 in which it forgot to provide for the loan guarantee to cover the interest
owing to producers under the act. When the government brought the bill back under its present numbering, Bill C-36, it had corrected that mistake but obviously did not make provision for raising the loan guarantee from 90 per cent to 98 per cent so we have before us today a new royal recommendation because it is increasing the obligation of the Government of Canada. We have that amendment before the House and again, under Motion No. 6, we have the government trying to further amend the bill and that, of course, has been ruled out of order by yourself so we really have a cobbling together of a lot of amendments which were not foreseen in the original bill.
We could put it down to the usual screw-ups in which the government is involved, but in this case I think it just boils down to the fact that the government has not thought through what it is doing. Obviously this whole legislation came out of the government's cost-cutting exercise in which it was chopping everything in sight to the extent of some $500 million. This bill, we are told, will save the government some $54 million but it is going to cost the producers a lot more than that. It will cost some producers in this country their farms, their livelihood, their whole situation in Canadian agriculture.
We are not talking about just $27 million of interest available to farmers. We are probably talking about $400 or $500 million worth of cash flow. This provides farmers with cash flow where the interest is paid by the government, so there is no question about the lending institutions providing that to cash flow, especially at market time. We are, however, talking about the losses of hundreds of millions of dollars in the price of commodities because this legislation has the impact of reducing the value of commodities.
For instance, the Ontario Corn Growers' Association estimates that the value to Ontario corn producers is on the ratio of 15 to 1. In other words, if the government provides $1 million worth of loan guarantee or interest free loans, the benefit to producers in being able to market that corn in the winter or spring months actually turns a benefit some 15 times over.
So if there is a million dollars worth of interest-free loan money provided under the crop advance payment system, that results in $15 million worth of benefit. That is just from one little sector, the corn sector.
November 27, 1989

If we look at fruit and vegetables, if we look at soybeans, if we look at the honey producers and the major advantages to the major crops of wheat and barley in the west, then you are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars in improved price of crops.
We are extremely disappointed that the government refused to hear from farm groups right across the country which wanted to come before the agriculture committee. We are sure that they will have their hearing before the Senate Committee. The number of farm groups that are opposing this bill is outlined very clearly in an urgent message that was sent to the Prime Minister on October 2 from some 19 or 20 farm organizations including the soybean producers, la Federation des pro-ducteurs agricoles du Quebec, the Western Canadian Wheat Growers' Association, the Keystone Agriculture Producers, the United Grain Growers, the Flax Council of Canada, the Corn Producers, the Western Canadian Pulse Growers and a whole list of other farm groups.
It has been an incredible mix-up all the way along for these producers. The government effectively is killing the program by charging interest. Most groups, like the com producers, estimate that the amount of saving for those with good credit ratings probably amounts to nothing. So who is going to put themselves through all the red tape of this program if they can borrow the money at 1 or 2 per cent above prime on a regular basis?
This amendment provides some improvement to the legislation. It means that a com producer who was getting $30,000 before and had to put up security of $3,000, 10 percent, will have to put up security of only $600 under this amendment. So it improves the bill. I wonder why the government did not put it in the original bill. Clearly, this amendment is a minor improvement to a bill that in general destroys the whole advance payment program because the farmer has to pay the interest. The losses are not only in cash flow at cropping time, the losses, in fact, occur to the value of the crop. The value of crops will be reduced because many producers will have to sell immediately.
We think that the disadvantages to these producer groups are veiy seriously affected and we wonder why the government is unilaterally cutting programs. We have entered into a free trade deal with the United States. The government said that over the seven years it
Government Orders
would negotiate a reduction in subsidies on an equal, equitable and balanced basis. Here we have a major program that provides $400 million or $500 million in assistance to farmers that is being chopped unilaterally. The Americans are not chopping their similar program. Here we have a government destroying a program that, if it were to be reduced at some stage, surely should have been reduced in a negotiation under the subsidy code program that is provided for in the free trade deal in order to have the Americans scale down their support programs.
It is not only in the prairie grain advance payments or the crops advance payments program that the government is unilaterally chopping programs, it is chopping a whole raft of programs, some $500 million dollars this year. If you count the Western Grain Stabilization payments not being made, if you count the special grains program payments not being made this year, you are looking at $2.5 billion in the budget and in the estimates that are cut from previous years.
What the government is doing, essentially, is kind of a scorched earth program, reducing and destroying programs. It does not come right out and say it in this program but that is the end result of this bill. This amendment that is being proposed today will help in some ways, but the over all program is going to be drastically cut because farmers now have to pay the interest on these advance payments whereas in the past they have not had to pay it. Therefore, there was no question about them getting the support. Under this program there is a big question whether they will be able to qualify for this support because they will have to be personally responsible for repaying that loan.
This amendment will help, but the over all program is being destroyed by this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak for a few moments on Motion No. 5, the change to the percentage required by the producer groups.
The resentment on this particular change in the advance payments by the government would have been much less if the government did not seem to be deliberately moving in a direction which is being felt negatively in rural Canada. The government has deliberately made

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
a decision to abandon some traditional support programs without replacing them with effective alternatives.
This particular bill just happens to be one of the dozens of attacks that rural Canada is feeling from the government and from the situation in which the government has placed rural Canada in the last few years. The elimination of interest-free cash advances is just one of the items upon which the government is moving that is being felt by the rural communities particularly, and in this case the farmers.
The program was in place for a specific purpose and in the case of the Wheat Board grains it was there to allow the orderly marketing of those grains and to assist in the movement of the grain from the farm through the system. In the case of the other alternate crops, the cash advances were an attempt on the part of the farm groups, with the assistance of the government, to take advantage of the best possible price when putting the product on the market. It worked particularly well in the second case.
But now we are asking the farmer to pay interest on this advance loan and in the process of doing that we have almost eliminated that second reason for the advance payments being in place. Whether they become responsible for 2 per cent or not does not make much difference because many farmers are telling me right now that there is no way that they can pay the prime rate plus 2 per cent or prime rate plus 1 per cent, or whatever the government ends up charging for these particular loans. They cannot afford to get a 10 per cent loan in the hope that maybe the price of com or soybeans, or whatever product they are putting on the market, is going to go up by that amount or by a great amount.
If you are getting $6 for your canola right now and you borrow so that you do not have to ship it and it only goes up to $6.50, you are going to be losing money on getting a loan.
As I said before, the government is just adding this to a number of other methods that it is using to attack rural Canada. It has done it by the quota-breaking in the free trade agreement whereby it has allowed more of the products to be imported into Canada, consequently pushing down the price of the product and the ability of the farmer to compete.
Second, the government has put in place a reduction of the industrial milk prices, again an attack on the farmer and his ability to survive.
We have had the commercialization of the Farm Credit Corporation. It does not matter whether you leave 2 per cent liability for the producer in this particular case if you are eliminating the total reason for having the loan at all. So the commercialization of the Farm Credit Corporation is also an attack on rural Canada and the farm group.
The GATT is being used by the United States to attack the development of trade in farm products. There is a great concern out there that by putting the free trade agreement in place we gave the United States another method of attacking the trade in farm products with the United States.
There is a great concern out there as well that the GATT negotiations are going in the wrong direction, that our government is giving in to the definition of subsidies which is going to further harm the production of farm products in Canada.
We have a continuing situation of high interest rates in Canada and those high interest rates are harming the farm community considerably.
The crop insurance program is supposedly being reformed but what is actually happening is that the federal government is withdrawing from crop insurance and is going to make, over a period of time, the farmer himself, the producer himself, responsible for crop insurance, another attack on rural Canada and the farm community-
Over the last four years we have had a number of what the government likes to call user-pay changes in the inspection of meats, grains and other products where the cost of inspection has gone onto the farmer, indirectly in some cases, but in many cases directly, so that the farmer is picking up a larger portion of the cost of getting those products on the market.
In the last few days we had the White Paper presented by the Minister of Agriculture. This White Paper calls into question the very basis of the support programs which have been put in place over the years to make sure that we have orderly marketing and that the farmers can survive in particular parts of the agricultural industry.
November 27, 1989

We have other attacks which are indirect but are just as badly felt. We have the closing of 1,500 rural post offices. Many farmers are now finding themselves driving many more miles, sometimes 30, 40 or even 50 miles to pick up their mail.
We have the shutting down of VIA Rail, also an attack on the farmers of rural Canada. We have an increase in freight rates and we have a definite bias in regional development toward industrialization and against development of farm products and farm processing.
We have, finally, but maybe not least, an attack on the survival of farms because of the goods and services tax. The goods and services tax is going to increase input costs by 9 per cent and that 9 per cent is quite often the margin of profitability in producing a particular crop.
We have all of these attacks, so it does not make much difference whether or not you leave the producers' liability at 2 per cent. If you do all these other things, you are attacking the survival of the farmer and the survival of the farm community.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak very briefly on this amendment. As members of the House can see, the amendment put forward by the Minister of Agriculture is virtually the same as amendments put forward by the member for Algoma and myself. I want to explain to the farm organizations, which noted that there was a discrepancy between the two acts that this bill amends and a certain amount of discrimination, why there is still a 2 per cent form of discrimination against certain commodity groups and certain users of the Advance Payments for Crops Act.
On our part, it is not because we did not think that they should be treated equally. In fact, we think that the Advance Payments for Crops Act should have the same coverage against liabilities as the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. For your information, Mr. Speaker, the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, which is the elder of the two, sets out that the Government of Canada will back the lender, in this case the Canadian Wheat Board, to 100 per cent of its losses. But under the Advance Payments for Crops Act the Government of Canada will stand behind the producer organizations for 90 per cent of the losses.
Government Orders
The reason we had introduced amendments to make it 2 per cent was that we read Section 9 of the existing act, which now seems to limit that loss to 2 per cent due to an amendment in 1985. Because we had no way as an opposition, or as it turns out did the government, of opening up Section 9 of the existing act because it was not in these particular amendments proposed in Bill C-36, our only option was to propose a limit down to 2 per cent, a liability of 2 per cent, because that is what is now in existence in Section 9, and we thought we would make it at least consistent throughout the piece.
What we would have preferred would have been the same treatment in the Advance Payments for Crops Act as exists in the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act; that is, government being responsible for 100 per cent of the liabilities on those advances not paid back. Because of the legislative constrictions in being unable to open up Section 9 which would have still been there if we had been able to get the number down to zero, we proposed this. The government apparently copied our amendment, hoping for unanimous consent, and I presume it will probably get it. But that explains to all those organizations that wrote in to point out the discrepancy between the treatment of their groups, made up of producers of commodities other than wheat and barley in the western Wheat Board region as opposed to those producers who are getting loans in the Wheat Board district under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act.
There will still be some discrimination, it will be reduced to the 2 per cent, only because of Section 9 in the existing legislation which does not permit that to go any lower.
We have had discussions across the floor. Because of the absence of the minister which was alluded to by the Parliamentary Secretary and because there had been agreement by all parties to discuss this bill today on the understanding that the minister would be in attendance, our understanding now is that the minister can be back from his meetings at three o'clock. is necessary because of the importance of this bill that we do have the minister here to speak on it. So I think that we would agree to this proposal that we call it two o'clock and continue with the report stage of Bill C-36 at 3 p.m. after Question Period.

Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, November 24, I had the honour to
attend the opening of the Bayview Memorial Hospital in Advocate, Nova Scotia, a village far removed from the mainstream of Nova Scotian activity.
This beautiful new hospital is the result of a massive fund raising effort which saw $350,000 raised by this tiny community of 800 people. Most people predicted that it just could not be done, but they did not realize the determination and perseverance of the residents, especially that of Mr. Victor Corbin, the fund raising chairman.
Despite economic disappointments the community of Advocate and in fact the entire Parrsboro Shore have fought for their hospitals, fought for their schools, fought for their wharfs, and fought for their communities in a way which reflects their rich heritage of overcoming hardships related to the forests and the sea.
I take my hat off to these special people, and I pledge to support them in any way I can to protect and expand their wonderful communities.

1989 GREY CUP

Mr. Speaker, the long drought is over. After 23 dry years the Grey Cup has returned to Saskatchewan.
It is with pride, Rider pride, that I join my colleagues from Saskatchewan in exercising the bragging rights that go with the last second victory over Hamilton.
The Roughriders last night were infused with that indomitable prairie spirit. They displayed the determination, dedication, tenacity, and hard work that are characteristic of Saskatchewan people.
Congratulations go to the players, especially Roger Aldag, the veteran from Gull Lake, the coaches, management, and, most important of all, the fans from all over Saskatchewan and Canada who supported the Riders through thick and thin and who now have a much deserved source of Rider pride for years to come-a win in the 1989 Grey Cup, the most exciting Grey Cup game ever played.
November 27, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the feature centrefold of the 1989 annual report of the Canadian Dairy Commission shows a pastoral scene of dairy cows grazing beneath a majestic mountainous backdrop.
The caption reads: "The Rockies provide a dramatic setting for this dairy farm in Agassiz, British Columbia". It is indeed a dramatic setting, one I think the residents of Agassiz would find truly astounding.
The government has made many incredible claims, but I did not know that moving mountains was one of of them. Effortlessly, the government has relocated the Rocky Mountains by moving them some 950 kilometres from the B.C.-Alberta border to the Fraser Valley in southwestern B.C.
How can you blame British Columbians for believing that this government does not understand western Canada when it cannot even get its geography straight?
Most governments are content with simply rewriting history, but this government has truly outdone itself by redrawing our geographical as well as our political landscape.

Capital Commission. While the decision to charge the fees was made secretly in September, unfortunately groups only recently learned of the new fees when they inquired about using the parks and parkways.

The NCC's motto appears to be: "When the going gets tough, do it secretly and behind closed doors and try to implement the decision as quietly as possible".

millions of Canadian homes, will be as great an error as the one just made, if not greater.

The pharmacy changed ownership November 1 and Canada Post offered the new owner, Mr. Eugene Bara-bash, a post office franchise for the price of $40,000.
As you can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Barabash has taken on considerable debt and cannot afford to take on more right now. He will be in a position to buy a franchise two years from now.
Canada Post is bullying him by threatening to sell the franchise to another business although there are no takers. Some 1,000 residents have signed letters and petitions protesting this malicious action by Canada Post.
I call upon Canada Post to renew the existing contract for a period of two years and not to improve service by shutting down a post office one month before Christmas, affecting thousands of residents of Edmonton Strathcona.

1989 GREY CUP

Mr. Speaker, as the member for Hamilton Mountain I rise today in the House to congratulate the Saskatchewan Roughriders on their 43-40 victory of the Hamilton Tiger Cats.
The 1989 Grey Cup left Canadians on the edge of their seats until the last seconds of the game when the foot of Saskatchewan field goal kicker, Dave Ridgeway, secured the win for Saskatchewan with seven seconds on the clock.
It was football at its finest, and it was played in the true spirit of Canadian sportsmanship. Being from Hamilton my loyalty and support naturally lie with the Tiger Cats, yet the Saskatchewan Roughriders have not won a Grey Cut since 1966.
