speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
With Eastern Europe at a crossroads today in history Canadians must do everything we can to assist the reform movement, to assist the tens of millions of people pushing for freedom in a number of countries. In order to make that urge for freedom realistic we have to ensure that there is some opportunity for economic success.
Our government has promised only $42 million to Poland and Hungary, which pales by comparison with commitments made by other western nations to these countries.
Why has Canada so far failed to provide our proportionate share of aid to Poland and Hungary? Where are the serious offers of economic help and a commitment to serious investment in Poland, the Soviet Union, Hungary, East Germany, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia?
When, incidentally, will Canada have a diplomatic presence in East Germany and in Bulgaria?


Oral Questions

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend, the Leader of the Opposition, referred this morning to our contribution to Poland, and he referred to an earlier comment by Mr. Walesa.
He forgot the comment that Mr. Walesa made at his press conference as he left Ottawa, saying that he was deeply impressed by the commitment of this government to the well-being of the people of Poland and that he was very, very grateful for the leadership and the strong support that the government and the people of Canada provided the people of Poland.
He said that but of course the facts just provided to the House by the Leader of the Opposition are, to understate the case, very incomplete.
In point of fact the $42 million is a one-year commitment which compares very favourably on a per capita basis with amounts now being considered by the Senate and the Congress of the United States.
Moreover, it does not take into consideration the fact that Canada is the fourth largest creditor of Poland, the debt being $2.6 billion, and in the process of rescheduling Canada will probably save over the next 18 months the people of Poland some hundreds of millions of dollars in hard currency. That is very appreciated by the Prime Minister of Poland and by Mr. Walesa and all others who believe that we have an obligation to provide this kind of assistance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians will remember what Lech Walesa said, that our efforts so far to Poland are like placing a beautiful tie on a corpse.
The government's White Paper on defence, still defended by the minister of defence, was misguided when it was introduced and is now completely out of date.
Will the Prime Minister acknowledge that the political declaration he signed in Moscow with President Gorbachev now represents a complete contradiction of the whole message behind the government's White Paper on defence?
When will he give a more up to date view of his government's policy both by way of a policy paper on defence and a policy paper on whatever is his current foreign policy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition would come back and refer to the statement of Mr. Walesa about the Canadian contributions "placing a tie on a corpse" which he made in the morning to a parliamentary committee and which in the afternoon at a press conference across the street he very substantially modified and corrected. He paid a great compliment to the government of the people of Canada for its generosity and he expressed profound gratitude. I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition continues to denigrate the efforts of the people of Canada to help the people of Poland.
With regard to the political declaration that was signed, I refer to a statement by Minister Shevardnadze in an interview that he granted Isvestia last Friday where he said and I quote:
The political declaration signed by the leaders of our states is an intellectual and political breakthrough into the new, interdependent world which has left the obstructions of the "cold war" behind and is confidently looking into the future. A document of this calibre and significance could emerge only in conditions of perestroika in the Soviet Union and in fundamental changes in the surrounding world.
That is exactly the position of the Government of Canada. That is why we were able to conclude this historic document and that is why I count on my right hon. friend for further support as we try to proceed with confidence-building initiatives such as the open-skies conference that will be held in Canada on February 12 next, due to the insistence and the hard work of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think what Canadians recognize is that in appreciating what is happening in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, they are miles ahead of their government and they want their government to get up to date.
Perhaps the Prime Minister might be good enough to forward a copy of the declaration which he has recited to the Minister of National Defence so that he can have his colleague up to date on the current posture of his government.

Mr. Speaker, in the political statement the Prime Minister signed with the Soviet Union, and earlier in his speech this morning, the Prime Minister did not say a word about security in the Arctic. He made no definite proposal about demilitarizing this region. In this morning's speech, the Prime Minister failed to make a serious proposal on behalf of this country, in response to a

Oral Questions
proposal for creating a peace zone made two years ago by President Gorbachev. After talking about co-operation in the Arctic with the Soviet Union, why was the Prime Minister unable to advance any new ideas for disarmament in the Arctic?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:

Yesterday afternoon, however, after lunching with Prime Minister

courage" and substantial assistance Canada had offered. "The Prime

When the Leader of the Opposition quotes, he should quote completely and not selectively.

His allegations were inaccurate. And it was just this morning, when I said that in Moscow, I also discussed with Mr. Gorbachev the proposals he had made in his speech in Murmansk several years ago, about arms control in the Arctic. I pointed out that Mr. Clark had responded to his proposals on several occasions, but that we were entirely prepared to discuss with the Soviets a number of refinements they might wish to add to their original proposals. I also told Mr. Gorbachev that I continued to think that the present permanent talks on arms control between the two superpowers and the two alliances had been productive and would remain the best way to make any progress in this area. This completely rebutes the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition. speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance must have some idea today what Canadians felt like when they were hit with his goods and services tax proposal. He has been blindsided today by Blenkam. I would like to ask him a question.
The House committee on finance has now brought in its recommendations.the Conservative majority is recommending that we reduce the tax on $1 million homes and increase the tax on $100,000 homes. Will the Minister of Finance tell us today whether he can support a 5 per cent tax on subsidized housing, low income housing and senior citizen housing, or is he prepared to clear up the chaos and confusion that has been created in this country as a result of this report and tell us that he is going to reject this proposal to impose a 5 per cent tax on every roof on every house and on every other residence in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to comment on any specific element of the finance committee majority proposals. They are, I think, a very useful piece of work in terms of looking at the broad range of things which can or cannot be done as far as the GST proposal is concerned. I am grateful to them for the range of recommendations that they have made and I think it is a productive part of the whole tax reform proposal.
What did disappoint me, quite frankly, was the total cop-out on the part of the Liberal minority report which was full of criticisms but had no alternatives, no productive suggestions as to how to move forward with the GST proposal.
What puzzles me is that in the last Parliament when they had finance critics that spoke out in a responsible way, they stated: "The Liberal Party acknowledges that the existing sales tax must be reformed. A broader based sales tax would stimulate economic growth. The Liberal Party is not opposed to the introduction of a new sales tax". Raymond Gameau said: "Proceeding immediately with the sales tax reform is important. We would manage to make our tax system more progressive and still maintain lower tax rates".
November 27, 1989

The current Whip of the House, I hasten to remind him, said: "A multi-stage type of sales tax sounds to me like an idea which the government should have proposed when it brought in fiscal reform. In addition to proposing it, it should have implemented it".
We are going to implement this tax. We are appreciative of those who are giving us positive proposals for reform, not the reactionary work that is being done by the Liberal party in its response to the sales tax system.

Mr. Speaker, I think the minority report reflects the views of Canadians and sooner or later the Minister of Finance will recognize that or he will go the way of his predecessor in New Zealand and become the minister of police.

Mr. Speaker, Conservative Members sitting on the Finance Committee have recommended that the government impose a reduced goods and services tax on homes worth 1 million dollars and at the same time increase the tax on homes worth $100,000.
My question to the Minister of Finance is this: Will the Minister of Finance today advise Canadians that at least as far as proposing a tax on all homes, all residences in Canada is concerned, he is going to reject that? Or does he intend to support the Tory Members on the Finance Committee who want this tax to apply to all residences across the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe there are some 86 separate recommendations by the Conservative majority on the finance committee. The hon. member is asking me to identify and comment specifically on one. I think that he understands the fact that the GST proposal is a proposal for a sales tax system. It is not just one tax or one rebate. It is a broad proposal to make the sales tax system fair, more effective and more productive in terms of creating new jobs.
I am not going to respond to a question on one specific proposal. I will review the whole of the finance committee report. Once that is done, I will make a specific response on the whole report.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister can at least respond to some
Oral Questions
basic mathematics. Will the minister confirm that the chairman of the finance committee is really starting a full-scale war on the first-time home buyer in this country by suggesting that there be an increase in taxes in comparison to the technical paper by $5,000 on a $100,000 home, by $8,000 on a $160,000 home, but a cut of $40,000 on a $1 million mansion. Will the Minister of Finance confirm that, and will he agree that the chairman of the finance committee is even more regressive, more conservative and more repugnant than the minister himself.

Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to my hon. friend that he should not tempt me in that way.
I have listened to the critics of both opposition parties.
I appreciate the support that they are giving to the government's proposal on sales tax reform. I hope that support will continue as we move into the legislative process.

I have another question for the minister of evasion, Mr. Speaker. I will give him one more chance.
The chairman of the finance committee and the Conservative majority are saying that the number of dollars for the tax credit for low-income people in this country should be cut by one half, from $2.4 billion a year to $1.2 billion. Like the minister, the chairman does not want the index to be a credit for the poor.
Will the minister agree that in terms of treating the poor in this country, the chairman of the finance committee is even more mean-spirited, even more greedy than the minister himself by cutting back or suggesting we cut back on the tax credit for the poor by some 50 per cent, making the poor in this country even poorer and will he reject that recommendation as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member should be reviewing the arithmetic on this. I have not gone through this carefully, but my understanding is that the logic behind this is as the rate has dropped from 9 per cent to 7 per cent so has the need to offset the impacts of sales tax reform in the hands of low-income Canadians so that there is a balance here. I believe that that is the rationale for what the Conservative majority in the finance committee proposed.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the chairman of the finance committee has also copped out in guaranteeing that the existing manufacturers' sales tax be passed on to the consumer.
I know the minister was not able to guarantee us that the existing MST would be passed on to the consumer. I want to know whether the minister will stand in his place and assure us that there will be some guarantee, some mechanism, that if he proceeds with this bill that the existing manufacturers' sales tax will indeed be passed on to the consumer. If he cannot do that, will he do the sensible thing and listen to 87 per cent of the people out there who say "no tax, no GST" and withdraw the proposition.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened carefully to what the polls have said. The polls are really reflecting a simple question: "Do you support a 9 per cent GST?" Obviously, if it is not put in any context, the answer to that question is as you would expect.
What if I put the question to Canadians: "Would you support a tax that is currently a hidden tax on exports? Would you support a tax which penalizes Canadian production, one that imposes one-third less tax on imports? Would you support a hidden tax that is deeply hidden in the manufacturing process? Would you support a tax that is complex, that requires 22,000 separate deals for the 75,000 taxpayers to make it work? Would you support a tax that is subject to a large amount of tax avoidance which is what the existing federal sales tax is?" I think we would get a very different response because the goods and services tax is designed to address each of those five separate problems with the existing system. That is why the majority members on the finance committee have supported a change to the goods and services tax. That is why this government is committed to proceeding with that proposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister going back to his statement this morning on his visit to the Soviet Union.
I think the Prime Minister will agree that one of the most important ways in which this country and others can
support the liberalization taking place in the Soviet Union is to have it become a member of a world trading community, particularly the General Agreement on Thriffs and Trade.
Can the Prime Minister tell us if during his discussions with Mr. Gorbachev he offered that Canada would support the involvement of the Soviet Union in the GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, either as an observer or as a full participant? Perhaps more important, when he visits the United States this week, will he press the United States administration to drop its present opposition to Soviet Union involvement in the GATT as a way of welcoming the Soviet Union as part of the world trading community?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes, indeed, we put forward the view that the Soviet Union might be interested in observer status at the GATT as a step toward a greater degree of participation in the international economy.
We put forward the view that the outgoing chairman of the industrialized summit should meet every year with President Gorbachev to exchange views and policy prescriptions as to how this integration might best come about.
I am not aware of any hostility by the United States whatsoever to this suggestion. The general view, I believe, is quite supportive. It is certainly a matter that I will raise with President Bush as we explore all possible avenues that would liberalize and improve the relationships between the east and west, but in the process to provide some real tangible assistance from the west to the east as the Soviet Union proceeds with its program of historic reform.

Mr. Speaker, there may not be hostility, but there is opposition. The stated position of the United States has been to oppose the membership or involvement of the Soviet Union in the GATT. I simply ask the Prime Minister if he intends to press his colleague, the United States President to drop that opposition, as he said, as a gesture of the new kind of economic regime we are in.
The question I would like to pose to him is more directly related to the interests of Canada. As you know, the agricultural trade between our two countries is perhaps the most essential link between the two.
November 27, 1989

This year there has not been any indication of major Soviet grain purchases from this country, causing widespread speculation or inquietude among the grain farmers and the shipping industry. Did the Prime Minister discuss the ongoing relationship of Canada and the Soviet Union on the grain trade? Can he tell us whether the Soviet Union will be making an announcement of a major grain purchase from Canada this year? Did the Prime Minister discuss the necessity of having another long-term grain agreement signed and ratified with the Soviet Union after the present one expires in a year's time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had extensive discussions with President Gorbachev and Prime Minister Ryzhkov with respect to the agricultural situation generally and the desirability of maintaining the grain sales from Canada to the Soviet Union. We have agreed to work very closely on a process that, hopefully, will ensure that that continues.
They were very grateful for the visit of the Deputy Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture. They asked us to consider some innovative thoughts as to how the Government of Canada and the Canadian agricultural producers could participate more actively in the process of expanding economic opportunities for us in the Soviet Union while at the same time bringing about beneficial results for Soviet Union consumers.
I suppose the best answer to my hon. friend is to tell him that the priority outside of East-West relations that was given by the Soviet Union and responded to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself was the field of agriculture and how this could be developed and expanded. I responded on behalf of the Government of Canada and on behalf of the agricultural producers of Canada with great enthusiasm. I gave them the assurance that we are going to work with them very closely to improve our market share.
Oral Questions ARCTIC POLICY

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister announced with great fanfare a new series of Arctic-related initiatives during his visit to the U.S.S.R. We all remember the last time a similar attempt was made by the Secretary of State back in 1985. Many of the initiatives announced then by the Secretary of State have either been stalled indefinitely or have never been implemented.
Will the Prime Minister assure this House that these latest initiatives will be fully implemented, and to that end will he accept the recommendation that my leader made this morning to appoint an ambassador of circumpolar affairs to co-ordinate Canada's arctic policy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take it that the references by the hon. member to undertakings that were given in 1985 have to do with actions that this government would take to establish Canada's sovereignty in the north, actions that we have taken, actions that had not been taken by previous Liberal governments United States that would guarantee our sovereignty with respect to the transit through northern waters of U.S. vessels. That also has been done. We have signed a number of agreements with the Soviet Union on which we look forward to acting.
In addition to that, the House may be interested in what I think is one of the significant developments of the discussions in Moscow. When the Prime Minister asked Mr. Gorbachev to be more forthcoming, to be more detailed in his suggestions in the Murmansk speech, which was a fairly general speech at the time, Mr. Gorbachev replied by indicating that he would want the matter to be under more regular review between myself as Canadian foreign minister and Mr. Shevardnadze.
We agreed to that immediately because we think that will provide us with the opportunity to make proposals and provide the Soviets with the opportunity to make proposals, and as well provide an occasion for them to be looked at on a very high level.
I have one last comment quickly in response to the question. To give credit where it is due with respect to the proposal for an ambassador I think that came from a

November 27, 1989
Oral Questions
the proposal for an ambassador I think that came from a recent conference sponsored by the Centre for Arms Control here in Ottawa. I have arranged for a meeting sometime in the next few weeks with the chairman of that centre, and I look forward to discussing the proposals of that conference, including the question of an ambassador who might be involved particularly in circumpolar affairs.

Canada has never recognized the annexation of the Baltic States by the Soviet Union. Prior to his visit with President Gorbachev, the Prime Minister indicated that the matter would be brought up in the normal course of his visit.
Did the Prime Minister raise the future of the Baltic States with the President of the Soviet Union, and did he receive any assurance that the Soviet Union will allow Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia to hold free elections without any outside interference from Moscow?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

I also made it clear that we were watching very closely, both governments were, Parliament was and Canadians of origin in the Baltic States, the attitude of the Soviet government toward developments in those regions, and that we would be particularly concerned if there were to be anything resembling a "crackdown" was the word I used. Mr. Shevardnadze replied categorically saying there would be no crackdown. I found it interesting that not only did he say that the foreign ministry was intending none but he was specific to say that the police were intending none, the army was intending none. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Right Hon. Prime Minister. The Prime Minister will know that one of the things all of us share about events happening in eastern Europe is that the Soviet Union has decided to allow people who live in its geographical backyard to determine their own futures, politically and economically.
The Prime Minister will be soon visiting President Bush of the United States. I wonder whether the Prime Minister would be prepared to say today to the House that he intends to suggest to Mr. Bush that it is about time the Americans took the same view toward their backyard in central America and stopped the military aid to El Salvador, to the people who are actually running that country, the military, so that peace could finally be negotiated and the violence come to an end in El Salvador.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it goes without saying that there is great concern in this House and across the country about the situation in El Salvador which is now, in effect, a civil war. It also goes without saying that Canada has to explore every avenue open to us, and there are better things that we can do than simply give advice to other countries as to what their policy would be doing.
I had the opportunity since coming back on the weekend to consult with my colleague, the Minister for External Relations, and senior officials of the department. We have begun close consultations with the OAS.
November 27, 1989

I will be in touch with the foreign ministers of both Venezuela and Costa Rica later today because they are involved in an effort right now to try to bring some resolution to the situation.
I intend to call in for a meeting, I hope this week, some of the Canadians who have been on the ground in El Salvador in recent days, some of whom the Government of Canada has helped to secure freedom so they could come back. We think that their advice will be valuable to us.
We intend also to make representations to a number of governments and organizations in the region, including obviously the Government of El Salvador, the Government of Cuba, and we intend to be speaking to representatives of the FMLN on a senior public servant level.
When the Prime Minister meets President Bush later this week, he is naturally going to draw attention to three elements that are of particular concern to Canada. One, the lives that are being lost. Second, the very grave threat to human rights in the region. Third, the grave threat that has now been created to the possibility of success of the peace plan, including the United Nations ONUCA activities. The Prime Minister will be raising that with President Bush, and we will be working with Americans and other members of the Organization of American States to try to bring peace to El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government gives advice to all kinds of countries. The Canadian government has given advice for 40 years to the Soviet Union with respect to eastern Europe. Fortunately, it has now heeded that advice.
Why is there this exemption for the United States? Why is it that we cannot entertain the notion of giving advice to the United States of America, of stating the Canadian position on American aid to the military in El Salvador?
I ask this question of the Prime Minister, with all due respect to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who will not be meeting with Mr. Bush, what does he, the Prime Minister, intend to say about continuing military aid to El Salvador and the destruction that it involves?

Mr. Speaker, I plan to tell the President of the United States

what the Secretary of State for External Affairs very eloquently stated, which is exactly the position of the Government of Canada.
I will also draw to his attention a story in The Toronto Star for November 24, where it states "The Nicaraguan Envoy lauds Canadian Peace Efforts". The quote from the ambassador-

November 27, 1989
Oral Questions
The Soviet Union has already provided a positive response to three recommendations of the panel on Arctic arms control made before a public forum, the Canada-USSR conference on Arctic co-operation four weeks ago regarding security and sovereignty in the Arctic.
Will the Prime Minister make a commitment to this House that Canada too will give a similar response and that in the spirit of building, as he calls it, a new and durable peace Canada will push for the adoption of other panel recommendations that include the establishment of a central Arctic demilitarized zone and promotion of verification procedures to ensure superpower compliance in the area?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated a few moments ago that I have asked my office to arrange a meeting between myself and the chairman of the agency which organized that panel. We intend to take a very careful look at all of its recommendations.
But let me make a point very clear. We believe that the world has found in the INF negotiations the great advantage, if we are serious about getting levels of arms down, of respecting and working within an alliance to alliance framework. That is also a view that has now been recognized by the Soviet Union, by Mr. Shevardnadze in our discussions, a view indeed reinforced by Mr. Gorbachev's observations to the Prime Minister that this would not be the time, this would be precisely the wrong time to undermine alliances.
Having those questions negotiated on an alliance to alliance basis obviously does not preclude them being discussed between countries that have a particular interest, as Canada and the Soviet Union do. That is why Canada responded quickly to the suggestion by Mr. Gorbachev that it would be useful to have very high level continuing meetings between Mr. Shevardnadze and myself to look at any proposals respecting the Arctic that might come from the Soviet side or that might come from the Canadian side, always on the understanding that any negotiations would occur on an alliance basis because that is the way that negotiations lead to real reduction in weapons.

Mr. Speaker, I realize it is better late than never, but Canada has already demonstrated its ability to act without being prompted by its allies when it rejected the nuclear submarine option, as a number of experts have observed. Furthermore, the Prime Minister acknowledged that his government's policy on national defence and external affairs is no longer up to date and that a thorough reassessment is necessary. Will the Prime Minister give the House the assurance that in the course of this process, he will consult the committees of the House, the various groups concerned and the experts in the field, and could he indicate the timeframe within which this reassessment will take place?

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-36, an act to amend the Advanced Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advanced Payments Act, as reported (with an amendment) from a legislative committee; and Motion No. 5.

Mr. Speaker, I had the floor when the House suspended and I do not wish to hold it unduly. I understand that we have a tacit agreement in the House, since the minister is now here, to move very quickly to a minister for the short period that he will be available to the House. I do not want to take away time from other members.
Perhaps we could get right to it, if that is the understanding, and begin by asking the minister to briefly justify the move to take away the interest free cash advances which have been part of the scene in western Canada since John Diefenbaker was Prime Minister. The rest of the country received them some time later but they have been a part of the agricultural scene for a very long time. They are also a fact of life in our competing countries, particularly in the United States, and we have great difficulty understanding the rationale for cancelling them.
A couple of years ago there was a move by the government, by regulation, to deem the loans received through the Cash Advance Act as a loan for tax purposes, rather than as income. That opened the ground work for a possible charge that people were taking advances, turning them into investments and using interest free money to gain income. That was not possible when the advance was considered to be income on the year it was taken. As long as advances were considered income as well, there was no abuse of the
November 27, 1989

program because people only borrowed enough money to pay their bills and to keep current, because to do otherwise would have changed their tax position for that year.
I wonder if the minister would explain why they have made this change, in light of his own government causing the problem that his parliamentary secretary described as being one of the reasons for the change. We heard from witnesses that the amount saved, some $27 million, would very likely be offset by increased payments to the Agricultural Stabilization Act and other programs. In fact, the very day that the bill was reported back from committee, the government brought in the Supplementary Estimates, asking for another $25 million to augment the Agricultural Stabilization Act. This gives more credence to the argument that was made by producers of fruits and vegetables from across the country, but most particularly from groups in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia.
I will stop with those two basic questions. Why is the government doing this? If it was having a problem, why did it not simply go back to deeming the advances to be income, as had been the case through the long period of practical use of the program?
Second, since the program does not seem to be really saving the government any money anyway, why did it bring it in? There seems to be an offsetting amount of agricultural stabilization money required because of the depressing effect that removal of this program will have on the markets.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And now he believes it. Well, okay. Now we know where he stands.
What we have here is a budgetary item. It was included in the budget on April 27 which was approved by this House. As a result of that, the legislation that flows from the approval of the budget has to be implemented.
At that time the Minister of Finance outlined the very serious financial situation that Canadians face, the large and growing public debt for which all of us has to bear some responsibility. I know that the members opposite would like to shift the burden and blame on to this particular government which inherited a $200 billion national debt, $200 billion in fiscal year 1984-1985. It has been growing ever since because of the tremendous cost in servicing the debt.
Lest there be any doubt as to how this debt was accumulated let me point out that I came to this House 21 years ago. The last time we had a balanced budget was, I believe, in 1969. There were successive Liberal governments in office at that particular time. We got into office in 1979 and tried to reverse that trend. The NDP and the Liberals kicked us out and since that time, from 1980 to 1984, the debt rose by about $100 billion. That is the legacy we have had to deal with, that is what we are trying to deal with.
We have been more than balancing the budget on government programs. That is for sure. We have a surplus. The hon. member would not understand that. After listening to his rationale for opposing this, I am not sure he would understand it.

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
As the Minister of Finance pointed out, the debt is accumulating at the rate of $80 million a day or half a billion dollars a week. All Canadians, including agricultural producers, who are taxpayers as well, view this with grave concern. We as members of a government and members of Parliament have to deal with this issue. Everyone is being asked to share in that particular burden.
The other reason that this proposal is being advanced at this time is the fact that the interest-free advances as they are presently in place have had the effect of distorting markets and subsequently have had the effect of lost sales. The impact of that has had the effect of scaling down or even closing oilseed processing facilities and it is to some extent having an impact upon our ability to be a reliable supplier of grains and oilseeds.
You know what happens when Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier of grain and oilseeds becomes tarnished. It takes many years to build up that image of reliability and anything that is done that tampers with that has a tremendous cost not only on markets today but markets in the future.
The result of this had the effect of holding back product for an unreasonable period of time and thereby the loss of sales and markets. As a matter of fact, the 1988-89 crop year was an example where farmers literally held canola off the market for the entire year. The result was lost sales, the closing down of canola processing plants and the scaling back of canola processing plants.
I have a letter-
Put it under the Wheat Board.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know what that has to do with the Wheat Board. Just because there are some organizations and producers that want the freedom to market their product in the way they desire, certainly the NDP should not take offence at that. In eastern Europe they are making great progress in developing their own freedoms and liberties. These guys would like to go back to the dark ages. That should be a lesson to them. The United Oil Seeds Products, for example, said in a letter to me on October 30, and I quote:
It is our view that the interest-free advances have distorted markets
by allowing farmers the financial strength to hold product off the
market for unreasonable periods of time. The 1988-89 crop year was a good example where fanners held canola off the market for the entire year.
This particular canola processing plant has been closed down for eight months. Jobs have been lost, delivery opportunities have been lost for those farmers who want to deliver. These people across the way have the luxury of criticizing everything that we try to do that is constructive. They would rather play politics with this issue. By their stalling and filibustering on this particular bill, they have denied farmers the opportunity to take advantage of the facility of advance payments.
Why didn't you answer the question?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member asked me why we are doing this and I am in the process of answering. I know that it disturbs him very much.
The Manitoba Wheat Pool wrote a similar letter to me in February, 1989. They said:
The Advance Payments for Crops Act has been a major benefit to the producers in the past when the delivery system was taxed to the limit to allow marketable grains into commercial positions.
The delivery opportunities have changed during the past few years and there are generally fairly high opening quotas on oilseeds and within a reasonably short time there has been space to accept deliveries into the system. The crushing industry in western Canada is in a position now to accommodate a sizeable delivery shortly following harvest. The original reasons to have advance payments for the oilseeds has, to some extent, disappeared.
The ability of the producer to get some financing without delivering the product (even though there is space and opportunity to do so) is creating some difficulties for the crushing industry and for the export marketers. Producers, with an advance payment, are holding stocks at the farm hoping to achieve a higher price later in the year. As you may well appreciate, this is shorting both the crushing industry and the export market. In many cases, markets are being missed or lost, never to be recovered.
Those are the reasons. Quite clearly, only 2 per cent of all canola produced in western Canada was covered by an advance. This is too small an amount to substantiate the point. The producer organization is considering changing the marketing system to rectify this problem. The pools have since backed off. That is what I hear.
So, here we are again. The situation, since it has become an issue, is one of to and fro, but the fact of the matter still remains that there has been distortion and dislocation in the market-place. That, together with the fact that this was a budgetary item, is clearly a reason for
November 27, 1989

this particular initiative to be advanced at this particular time.
I should say as well that the issue of safety nets, stabilization programs and the kinds of support systems we need to support agriculture is something that is going to be considered in a very comprehensive way during the course of the policy review. I would hope that things such as this could be considered at that particular time.
In the final analysis, the idea is to improve the mechanisms in our programs to ensure that producers have the opportunity to rely upon support systems and safety nets while at the same time reading the market signals and making their decisions on that basis; and making their decisions based upon the knowledge that they will have some shield of protection which is really the bottom line in advancing the policy review, particularly in the field of safety nets.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

My understanding was that we would handle this section like we do committee of the whole House, since the minister was unable to attend the committee stage, and that a series of questions would, therefore, be permitted.

A point of order, Mr. Speaker. I assume that we are on Motion No. 5.1 would like to comment on it in light of the minister's remarks.
I was very interested in the Minister of Agriculture's comments in regard to Bill C-36. He talked about agriculture producers being very concerned about debt because the provisions of this bill provide very little financial support, especially at cropping time, and this is being taken away.
My concern is that support is not only being taken away, but the government is taking it away unilaterally. There was an understanding with our trading partners in the United States, with whom the government signed an agreement a year ago, that the support programs and subsidies outlined in that free trade agreement would be reduced and there would be a negotiated reduction.
Government Orders
Clearly, there has been no negotiating in that regard. This is just a straight removal of a major program which is of major benefit to Canadian producers. It provided some $27 million a year, which provided $300 million or $400 million in cash flow for those producers. They are very concerned about their own debt and how they will be able to cope with it with this program removed.
The minister quoted a couple of groups which he thought were supporting his position. If we look at the letter sent to the Prime Minister on October 2, we see that some 20 farm groups across the country are opposing the government's position. The government majority in the legislative committee on Bill C-36 refused to allow them all to make their presentations. Keystone Agricultural Producers, the United Grain Growers, the Flax Council of Canada, the Ontario Corn Producers, the Ontario Soybean Producers, the Manitoba Pulse Producers, oppose this proposed legislation by the government.
When the minister is quoting who supports it, he selectively forgets who is opposing it. He mentioned the canola producers in the prairies. I would just like, for his information, to quote a letter from Max Pond, President of the Manitoba Canola Producers, dated October 20, when this bill was being debated, in which he says: "We would like to encourage your continued support for the reinstatement of interest-free provisions on the cash advance program. Without reinstatement of the said provision, the program holds little benefit for Canadian farmers. With respect to oilseeds, the interest-free cash advance has contributed to orderly marketing".
This directly opposes what the minister said just a few minutes ago.
The letter goes on; "It contributes to orderly delivery by moving the pressure on producers to sell at harvest at a time when prices tend to turn downwards.
Further, one of our board members happens to be the person responsible for administering the Canola Cash Advance Program offered under the Prairie Canola Growers' Council. His calculations show that with the fee which must be charged to cover the cost of administering the program, the true cost of the advance would be prime plus at least 1 per cent to 2 per cent because the administration fee is a fixed amount no matter the size of the loan".

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
The shorter the period for which the loan is held and the smaller the amount borrowed, the higher the actual interest rate becomes, making it more economical for farmers under those circumstances to borrow directly from a lending institution. As a result, the cash advance will lose all usefulness.
Clearly, the Canola Producers from Manitoba and other areas are opposed to this, as are practically every other group.
One area that the minister has not dealt with, and I do not know whether he has really focused on it, is the importance of improving the value of the crop harvested. The Ontario Corn Producers have calculated that the cost-benefit ratio is 15 to one. For instance, in 1987-88 they estimate that for the cost of the program, a little over $1 million, the benefit to producers was some $16 million.
Obviously, this is a good program that the government should not be cutting out at this time and I would hope that the minister will still change his mind. It is a program that has great advantage to it. Our American friends have not indicated that they are going to do away with their similar program. Surely, if this is going to be negotiated away, it should not be at a time when net farm incomes are dropping anywhere from 20 to 38 per cent as they are in various parts of the country this year.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while it was not a House order, I understand that there was an understanding among House leaders that hon. members would be allowed to put questions similar to a committee of the whole process and that I would respond to them. speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member, I would submit that these amendments will improve the orderly marketing of agriculture commodities in Canada. Farmers will still have the ability to have advance payments.
As a matter of fact, the amounts will be increased. They will be able to make those arrangements to carry crops from harvest time to delivery. In fact, the improvements with regard to this flexibility and the security would provide greater opportunity to merchandise their product in such a way that they could use this facility in a proper fashion.
I think it is important that the decisions are made on market signals and sound business principles rather than simply on the basis of managing a financial portfolio. They will still be able to use the provision to help smooth out the seasonal price fluctuations. They will still be able to use this facility for those farmers who want to prepay their fertilizer bills before the end of the year. They will still have the guarantee. The guarantee level is being increased to 98 per cent from 90 per cent, including the interest.
My sense is, quite frankly, that the system will be improved and there will be a built in discipline. Interest rates will be negotiated at anywhere from one to three percentage points below prime. Producers now want this facility to be used so that they can get on with the business of running their farms.
Let us talk about support for the agriculture industry. In 1984-85 this federal government committed $2.8 billion to Canadian agriculture. In 1985-86 it was $3 billion. In 1986-87 it was $4.4 billion. In 1987-88 it was $6 billion and in 1988-89 it was $4.5 billion, for a total of roughly $20.8 billion provided by the federal government to support agriculture; for drought, crop insurance, dairy subsidy, Canadian Wheat Board losses, advance payments and the agricultural stabilization program.
When we look at what has been done to the grain and oilseeds sector for that same period of time, 1984-85 to
November 27, 1989

1988-89, a total of $11,777 billion, almost $12 billion, was provided to the grain and oilseeds sector.
With regard to supporting agriculture, I just looked at the editorial page of the Ontario Farm Women's Network News Letter of June, 1989, where it was pointed out that it was rather unbelievable that the money spent by the provincial government of Ontario on agriculture was no more than 1.25 per cent of the total budget. Of the total budget, Mr. Speaker, 1.25 per cent. The hon. member will agree that agriculture is pretty important to the province of Ontario. It is, but it certainly is not a priority with that provincial government.
In the last year, 1987-88, the federal government poured $2.1 billion into the province of Saskatchewan. The Saskatchewan government put in $166 million. Federal government support was 93 per cent while Saskatchewan's was 7 per cent.
In 1987-88 the Manitoba government put in $72 million while the federal government put in almost $800 million. The ratio was 92 per cent federal, 8 per cent provincial.
Alberta put in $445 million while the federal government put in $1.3 billion for a ratio of 25 per cent versus 75 per cent in favour of the federal government.
Those are not small picayune figures. Here we are talking about a measure that is less than $20 million compared to billions and billions of dollars that we have poured into agriculture to support the family farm, the rural communities and everything associated with agriculture. It showed up in the 1988 realized net income which reached an all-time high in spite of all the difficulties.
Alberta, for example, exceeded $1 billion for the first time in history. Saskatchewan was the highest at over $1 billion since 1981. Quebec averaged over $900 million in realized net income between the period 1985 to 1988. Ontario achieved a realized net income in agriculture of $1.4 billion, the highest record ever achieved by the agricultural industry of Ontario.
To suggest that this government is drawing back and withholding support for agriculture is absolute nonsense because the facts and figures belie that. I will challenge anyone to argue with these figures because the facts are clearly there. We have supported agriculture in an unprecedented fashion and the farmers of Canada know it. But there comes a time when there has to be a little bit of pulling back, a little bit of belt-tightening and, like all other good citizens, we are asking the farmers to
Government Orders
share in that process. Now what could be more fair than that?
What the farmers are asking today is for us to get on with the business of governing and get this piece of legislation passed so that they can get on and make the cash advances, hopefully before Christmas. The opposition have seized upon this opportunity to try to make political hay. They have not hurt us, they are only hurting themselves and the farmers of Canada. I would ask that they cease and desist and get on with the business of passing this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to be very explicit in my question to the minister. Hopefully it can be answered with a simple yes or no. I have before me a letter from the B.C. Vegetable Marketing Commission. In that letter the commission says that the APFC program is very useful. However, the elimination of interest-free advance payments will more than likely render the entire program inadequate to meet the producers' requirements.
Can the minister advise the B.C. Vegetable Marketing Commission, which has expressed this grave concern, if he is planning to eliminate the interest-free advance payment plan which would be devastating to that industry?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member can answer that question herself. It would be provided for in this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the farmers will be glad to know they are doing so well. I found it very difficult to believe that the Minister of Agriculture is suggesting that this advance payments program, if there is interest charged on it, can take the place of an interest-free program.
I am going to use canola as an example because it is something I know is a major crop in the minister's home area. In the canola industry right now there is enough canola in place, backed up, unpriced, to last well into January or February.
The farmers in my area and in the minister's area are delivering canola at the present price of $5. There is no guarantee that within the next three months there is going to be any increase in canola. Even if the advance had been in place, those farmers could not afford to pay the interest, prime plus one or two or whatever the government decides to put on that, over a period of time on the hope that maybe the price will go up enough in the next couple of months. Only if canola was under the Wheat Board, where the price would level off for the

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
year, would it be possible to do that at that particular time. It cannot be done under this present system.
While we are talking about money, two years ago the government backed off of the two-price wheat system at the rate of $270 million a year, about one-tenth of what it costs to keep the advance payments interest free. Why is some of that money not being used? Why is a portion of that money not used to allow this, at least for this year?
We have legislation that is in place that could be used. The government is withholding that money now under legislation that is in place and could be used. I know the minister tries to blame the opposition for this not being through, but he does have the instrument by which the money could be sent out. Why not use some of this money and let it go?
If the minister wants to talk about changing the legislation, next year is a good enough time to do it. Pass it now but let them have their money when they need it under the circumstances which they have planned for.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member, I think that one of the reasons that the back-up in canola deliveries is as he described is the fact that this legislation has not been available and has not been able to be utilized by the producers.
