Interest free right now.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know they do not support the bill, but that is no reason to hold the farmers to ransom and to hijack the farmers. The fact of the matter is that this provision was passed when the budget was passed and it has to be implemented. The back-up is caused-and I know my hon. friend will take issue with this-I am sure, in large part by virtue of the fact that they saw fit, and it is their right to do so, to withhold passage of this legislation, to delay it. I think that is regrettable, particularly because after the budget had
been passed, it became a fait accompli and it was going to become a fact of life.
They should not have misled farmers into believing that there would have been some deviation from that. Notice was served in April that this provision was going to be withdrawn. We had hoped that through the co-operation of members opposite we would be able to get this bill through, hopefully before the end of June, and if not the end of June at least by the end of September. They chose not to and so we have this kind of chaotic condition.
The hon. member never listens. He talked about the fact that farmers could not afford prime plus 1, 2 or 3 per cent. I said just the opposite. I said it would be prime less 1 to 3 per cent. That is what we are really talking about.
He wants to talk about canola being under the Canadian Wheat Board. That is another issue. It is an issue for another day. I know what the hon. member's position on that would be. I am not sure what the position of the producers is. It varies from area to area and from year to year.
I know that hon. members opposite are opposed to this legislation and they certainly have every right to oppose it, but I would plead with them to allow us to get on with the job so that the facility that is enshrined in here can be used and the farmers will be able to take advantage of it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the minister a question. In view of the fact that he has said that the opposition parties have held up this bill, I think we should follow this through in sequence. The original bill was tabled, I believe, on June 26 or 27. The budget was brought in in late April. The bill had to be withdrawn, as he is well aware. This particular bill, Bill C-36, was re-introduced in the House on October 3 and that is when the debate commenced.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: So it couldn't be passed in September, could it?

There is no way it could have been passed in September. As a matter of fact, five months after the budget he saw fit to introduce the bill in a form that they felt could be accepted by the House. Consequently, the delay was not caused by the opposition
November 27, 1989

parties. We are within a period of less than two months and we are going to vote on final reading this afternoon. He certainly cannot suggest to us that it was held up in committee either because it went through committee very expeditiously in view of the content of the bill.
The soybean harvest in Ontario was well under way before the bill was even introduced on October 3. The com harvest was well under way and the prices dropped because the bill was not there to even out the flow of grain to market. Soybean producers had to sell their crop in order to get cash in hand. Will the minister consider compensating those farmers for the loss they took when they had to harvest the beans at that low price? I think the price has recovered by about 40 cents a bushel since October 3.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy the hon. member because he has had a lot of experience in this House. I would not want him to leave the impression that there has not been a willingness to negotiate and facilitate the passage of this bill. He will know and his Whip will know that we have made several attempts.
The reason there were delays is because there were some improvements made to the bill. There were several attempts made, all of which were aborted because the members opposite wanted to have a little fun with this thing. This bill could have been passed a month ago. It is not a complex bill, it is fairly straightforward. It was introduced on September 27,1 am told. Had there been a willingness and a desire to assist the producers about whom he is now so concerned, I am sure his generosity would have prevailed and we would have been able to do something.
Unfortunately, we are at the stage now where it is too late to consider that. I hope that we can get this bill passed as quickly as possible. I hope that he will have some influence on his friends in the other place and that they will not foot drag so we can get this legislation in place. It is my sense that while a lot of producers would rather have interest free cash advances, they are now interested in getting this legislation in place so that they can use it to full advantage and it will be used to fuller advantage because of the flexibility and improvements that we have put in it.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, during his earlier comments the Minister of Agriculture made an excellent case for his use of this particular legislation as a means to keep farm prices down so that processing plants could remain open. He quoted a couple of processing operators who he indicated were in favour of the removal of the interest-free cash advances prior to it being done, which was proposed in the budget of last April.
Could he tell us, in the spirit of consultation which is supposed to be the spirit in which this government entered office, whether in fact he had any meetings in this regard with the farm organizations? Could he report what they told him? In the letters that we have received during the course of this legislation being before committee, we have not found any farm organization that has approved of doing away with the interest-free cash advance. We were only able to call three before us because of the time constraints imposed on us by the Conservative majority in the committee, but we did not hear from any groups that were in favour of the proposal.
Who did he consult with prior to the budget proposition and what farm groups, if any, were behind it? We know that the processors appear to like it because they are hoping it will keep farm prices down to the point where they can have a margin to stay in business and show a good profit processing. What farmers liked it?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member attempts to mislead again. He said that the only people whom I quoted or referred to were a couple of processors. I referred to one processor; it was United Oilseeds in Lloydminster, and that happens to be owned by the United Grain Growers which is a co-operative, I think. The other one was from the Manitoba Pool. That is a co-operative too, is it not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: As far as I know.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Where does he get off with this nonsense of me listening only to the processors. I thought that the Manitoba Wheat Pool was a co-operative organization composed of farmers and I thought the United Grain Growers was a farmer co-operative organization. I am not sure how the hon. member gets off trying to suggest that all I am listening to are processors.

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
You're making processor arguments, not farmer arguments.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, now, Mr. Speaker, they are making processor arguments, not farmer arguments.
The processing arm was the people you were listening to, right?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, I see.
Well, read the letter again.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I guess he is now suggesting that farmers, because they do not haul to canola crushers, are not interested in processors. Is that right? Is that what the hon. member is saying? Is that the new NDP farm policy?
The question was: "What farmers?" It's lowering farm prices. You have admitted it's lowering farm prices.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Okay, now we are getting into the second part of the question. I will respond to that.
The hon. member asked what farmers we consulted with before we brought this budgetary proposal down. When you bring down a budgetary proposal, you do not consult. I think that has been a tradition and part and parcel of our parliamentary democracy.
That was not what you said when you came into power.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The budget was presented; the budget has been ratified. This is legislation that is flowing from the budget.
The hon. member said there are no farmers who want to pay interest. I agree, that is probably correct. But I will tell you what farmers want. They want to see interest rates come down, they want to see the deficit come down and they want to see us tackle the national debt.
The hon. member opposite has been around here a long time but, boy, when it comes to exercising responsibility, they are here hollering in the House every day: "spend, spend, spend". Today we are at the stage where we cannot spend, spend, spend any more and even farmers are now being asked to bear a portion of the burden. That is what we are doing in a very modest way here. In addition, we hope that through this we may remove some of the distortions and dislocations that take place in the market-place.
What farmers are wanting and expecting of a government is sound and proper fiscal management to get the Canadian books of account into shape. That is what we are trying to do and we are asking everyone to co-operate and to assist in this process by sharing that burden. I am sure the hon. member would agree with that.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the comments of the Minister of Agriculture. There is one concern which he can perhaps clear up just by being Deputy Prime Minister.
A lot of farm groups suggest, as did the letter I read this afternoon from the Manitoba Canola Producers and the letter which we received from the Ontario Com Producers, that the interest rates well may be 2 per cent above prime. The minister has talked about them being 1 or 2 per cent below prime. I wonder if he could give the House a guarantee that the Department of Finance and the Department of Agriculture will ensure that the resulting loan guarantee will result in rates below prime by 1 or 2 per cent.
That clearly would be a significant step because it would provide to farmers using the program some significant advantage, using the power and the financial resources of the Government of Canada, whereas if it is 2 per cent above prime, if the person is in a reasonably good financial position he can probably borrow at the bank at that rate. He is certainly not going to have to put up $2 in security by way of crop in the bin in order to get $1 loan through a producer organization. If the minister could clarify that it would be very helpful.
He talked about the canola plant, I believe it was owned by the United Grain Growers in Saskatchewan, that was supporting the bill. In fact, the United Grain Growers were one of the organizations which wrote the Prime Minister an urgent letter in early October demanding that the government abandon the bill and let the funds which had already been approved by Parliament go forward. I would be very surprised if that canola plant was really that concerned.
I note as well that the minister's colleague and counterpart in the province of Manitoba, Mr. Findlay, wrote the minister a letter dated September 19 urging that the advance payment be provided to farmers, and
November 27, 1989

stating that the cash flow problems currently felt by Manitoba producers could be alleviated by this bill.
The last point I want to put to the minister is the one made by Cliff Leach, the president of the Ontario Com Producers, in a letter to the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds just after he spoke in the House on October 4 in which, besides refuting most of the points that the minister had made in the House when he intervened in the debate, he puts the question about which I think all members are concerned.
He said:
Finally we must repeat our underlying criticism that Bill C-36 represents a reduction in federal support for Canadian farmers when no commitment has been made to reduce comparable assistance elsewhere-and specifically in U.S. Farm Bill loan provisions available to American farmers.
I think that is the concern of a lot of producers, not just the advance payments bill, Bill C-36, but the whole list of items-I believe there were six-that were in the budget on which action has been taken by the government that were listed as subsidies in the FTA.
The Americans have not made any reduction in their agricultural support programs whereas on the Canadian side we have about six, everything from reduction in crop insurance to doing away with the two-price wheat system, a significant number of which we have moved on. This one is quite important because the Americans have a loan program whereby they provide interest for farm stored wheat and major crops. We seem to be doing away with these unilaterally rather than negotiating them bilaterally under the subsidy code provisions of the FTA. Since this question was put by the president of the Ontario Com Producers, I wonder if the Minister might respond to that question put in the letter to the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to respond to the hon. member because it does provide me with an opportunity to correct an impression that I left with my friend in the NDP when I may have said 1 to 3 per cent below prime. That is not correct. It is probably 3 per cent below the current going rates.
For example, the Canadian Wheat Board does borrow at a rate below prime. We think that we will be able to get an almost similar rate although there may be some small charge for administration handling. I apologize and
Government Orders
regret that very much. We are basically looking at 2 to 3 percentage points below the going rate of interest which would be roughly in the area of prime or slightly above.
The hon. member raises a point about what support programs from the agriculture industry are the best. It is obvious that our grain stabilization program and our crop insurance program and some of our agricultural stabilization programs have been insufficient to meet the tumultuous period of time we have just gone through. That is precisely why we are looking at a new crop insurance program. That is why we are looking at the issue of safety nets to see whether we can design safety nets that will be more permanent, more reliable and more predictable and that will be in place on a permanent basis rather than on the basis of having to design them on an ad hoc basis.
I think the fanners want to make their plans with some degree of confidence. They want to plant their crops knowing that they can make the decisions reading market signals, weather patterns and trends. At the same time they want to make sure there is some kind of safety net, some kind of shield that will be there so that they can make those kinds of decisions.
That is our ultimate goal and objective. That work is proceeding and we hope very much that during the course of the comprehensive agriculture review that we are currently undertaking we will be able to come up with some programs that will be more appropriately and more fittingly designed to meet the 1990s and the 21st century based upon some of the experiences that we have encountered over the last four or five years.
I do not think there is any secret in the fact that the last four or five years, in terms of drought conditions for example, were probably equal to or worse than the 1930s. I think it really speaks very well of the producers of this country who have been able to survive. I think it demonstrates a tremendous degree of resilience that they have been able to survive this very difficult period with, of course, the aid of governments.
Ad hoc programs are very difficult to design and very difficult to administer. Usually you end up not pleasing everybody. You end up with inequities from one region to the other, from one township to the other, from one county to the other. We are trying to overcome that if we possibly can. .

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
We hope that in the course of the review we will be able to deal with this issue with everybody around the table trying to sort this out in order that we can come up with programs that will be properly cost-shared and will be fiscally sound but permanent, reliable and effective.
The hon. member says that this is part of the free trade agreement. I am not sure how long we are going to have to be around here to get off that kick. There is nothing in this that is being directed by the free trade agreement whatsoever. We are our own sovereign country. We do what we have to do to meet the challenges and the conditions of the agricultural community.
One would ask whether the $20.7 billion or $20.8 billion that we have poured into agriculture as a federal government over the last four or five years was dictated to by the free trade agreement or not.
I suppose the hon. member is now trying to say that if we reduce that by $100 he is going to blame it on the free trade agreement. We did it because we had to respond to a need. Fanners know that we have responded to the need. Farmers also know, if you really sit down and talk about it, that this government has been pretty generous to them.
The hon. member reads figures just as well as I do, so he will know that in 1988, in terms of realized net income, it was the best year that farmers ever had. I know that there are difficulties and there are areas that are hurting. I know that.
I serve a rural constituency just like the hon. members opposite, but figures do not lie. The fact of the matter is that there are pockets where the hurt is substantive, while there are other areas in which things are going a little better. That is not to say that everything is well.
I am not trying to paint a rosy picture for agriculture. What I am saying is that we are trying to deal with this with the limited resources we have available. We are trying to respond effectively and we are trying to respond with some degree of sincerity. The last thing that farmers want is a return to the 22 per cent, 23 per cent and 24 per cent interest rates that were the hallmark of the party and the government that member was a part of.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: You are not serious.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am serious. I will tell you-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: And they are serious.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that when it comes to difficulties on the farm 97 per cent of all the farmers who are in difficulty today are in difficulty because of the 23 per cent and 24 per cent interest rates which that government brought about and inflation that heads up to 15 per cent. The inflationary psychology was on a treadmill.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Absolute nonsense.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These guys say it is absolute nonsense. That goes to show you how much they know about farming. We are trying to avoid a repetition of the disasters inflicted upon the farm community by the Liberal government.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear that the Minister of Agriculture and the Deputy Prime Minister are attempting to head off a disaster with high interest rates as we saw in the early 1980s. I note that we are now a full four percentage points above United States interest rates, something that even in those terrible days we did not achieve for very long.
Consistent with his arguments about attempting to keep down inflation, would he advise the House what his government's intention is with regard to the amendment for each of the two acts that are being dealt with and put forward by myself to limit the amount of loans to just $50,000 from the current $30,000?
That way they would go up from $30,000 to $50,000, as a means of combating this inflationary psychology. It would also be a means of limiting the amount of liability the Government of Canada will have basically to the banks in this country. Given the opportunity of turning a quarter of a million dollars of their own liability on to the Government of Canada, lending institutions will encourage some of their customers whose accounts are getting a bit shaky to go and take out the maximum cash advance for grain. That way, if they should happen to fall into bankruptcy or receivership, the government will be held responsible and not the bank.
Can the minister tell us whether members on the government side will be supporting a more modest kind
November 27, 1989

of approach to move from maximum loans of $30,000 up to only $50,000 instead of the $250,000 million that was originally in the bill?
In keeping with his espoused attempts at abating the inflation psychology, certainly it seems to me that one of the more inflationary things a government could do would be to move this ceiling on loans from $30,000 up to $250,000 all in one step.
We do not know from the witnesses we were able to call just how many loans hit the ceiling, but from the witnesses that we were able to hear it appeared that very few people actually applied for the maximum loan.
We were unable to get the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee to come because government members refused to allow us to hear from those witnesses. Therefore we do not know what proportion of the population using cash advances went to the maximum. We were told by the witnesses we heard that a very small percentage indeed took the maximum of $30,000.
I repeat my question to the minister: If he is so interested in abating the inflationary psychology, why is the government proposing to move from a maximum of $30,000 to a maximum of $250,000 for these loans?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member's whole purpose of engaging in this debate was to point out the fact that farmers needed money to pay off their bills and to smooth out the markets of their commodities when prices were low. In that way they could take an advance based upon the market signals and on basic sound business principles.
Now I hear him saying that they do not need too much money; they just need about as much as he would prescribe. I do not share that same philosophical view.
I do not believe that farmers are irresponsible. I believe that farmers are good business managers. I think that they can best make the decision whether they should borrow $30,000, $60,000 or $100,000. I would leave it in the hands of the producer.
I have watched in my lifetime a dramatic change occur in the agricultural industry. As one bom and raised on a farm, I have witnessed the transition from horsepower to mechanical power. If there is one thing that stands out in
Government Orders
my mind about the agricultural industry in Canada it is its ability to adapt to change.
The reason we are successful in agriculture today and have been able to survive as one of the leading agricultural countries in the world is that our farmers have been able to adapt to change. When farmers adapt to change it means, at least to me, that they are sound business managers.
They are good business managers and they can make the best decisions. I would rather leave it in their hands so that they can diversify and use this for a multiple series of crops. They will make the decisions. We will provide the tools with which they can make those decisions, and I will rely upon their good sense and sound judgment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to get back to the need for money by farmers right now.
The minister makes the point that the decision was passed in the budget, but that does not etch it in stone. It is not necessary for the government to take that position, continue with it, and run with it.
The government has changed its mind before on issues that have been in the budget and passed in the budget. I point to one particular example, that is, the deindexing of the seniors' pensions which was brought forward in The Budget Papers and was changed when the government shifted its position. This was not too long ago.
Why not pass this bill on to the Senate but use the old bill to get the money out to farmers now? Let it go to the Senate, and you will have your bill for next year which is a logical time to get it. I ask the minister: Why not use this approach, get the money out to farmers now on the old bill, and use the new bill next year?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been through that argument before. I have tried to lay out the reasons for the need to pass this bill at this particular time. It is a budgetary provision.
The member says that governments have changed their minds before. I am sure that opposition parties would have wished they had changed their minds.
I remember in the budget of 1979 when we were in government that we proposed a modest 18-cent a gallon increase in the price of gasoline. The NDP and the

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
Liberals voted together to defeat that particular measure and the price of gasoline went up.
You raised it $1.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Gasoline went up over $1 a gallon and we accumulated an additional burden of debt to the tune of about $100 billion plus during that period of time. The only reason we are accumulating it now is that we are paying the interest on your debt, which we cannot afford. That is what is wrong. We are still paying for the litany of mismanagement caused by that government and supported by that gang over there.
From $68 million to $200 billion.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know the hon. member for Prince Albert is genuine and sincere when he makes his plea. I am sorry to disappoint him. We have to move with this legislation at this particular time. I will go to the extent of telling his constituency that he fought a good and lofty fight in the process.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great care to the genial Minister of Agriculture. It occurred to me that he is having great pressure from groups in Saskatchewan and across the prairies. Groups like the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee have been pointing out that a lot of crop this year is of low quality due to wet periods during harvesting. A lot of it cannot be delivered because of the demand for the lower quality wheats, barley and so on. That is a very important argument.
The other group in Saskatchewan is the Saskatchewan Municipal Association that has been doing studies which show a very deteriorating situation with regard to loss of farms, farm foreclosures, and debts that cannot be serviced. This was pointed out dramatically in the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan Pool in which it said that at least $500 million will be required before spring planting next year. That has been reinforced by a letter from the premier of the province saying that additional funds would be required.
It seems to me the advance payment money would be one way to put funds into the hands of producers on an interim basis. I do understand that there has be some kind of emergency funding arrangement for this purpose.
Assuming that no permanent arrangement with regard to additional funding is made, I am wondering if the minister has considered responding to those requests from Garf Stevenson, President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool or Premier Grant Devine as these advance payments would provide several hundred millions of dollars of cash flow at harvest time.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I hope I understand the purport of the hon. member's question correctly. Is he saying that if we were to bring forth interest-free farm cash advances that that would satisfy the premier of the province of Saskatchewan and Mr. Stevenson, the president of the Wheat Pool? I sort of gathered that that is what he was trying to say. He may want to clarify that a little later.
He also said that farmers have grain of poor quality, and there is not much market demand for it at this particular time. That is all the more reason why this legislation should be moved forward quickly, because they will have the opportunity to take advantage of this instrument to take out advances and in the process improve their cash flow.
He also left the impression that this instrument was a tool to finance long-term debt. It was never intended to be that. It is intended to be a marketing tool, to use the facility of a cash advance, to improve your cash flow, and to arrange your marketing so that you can maximize your returns. That is what this issue is for.
It is not to finance long-term debt or intermediate term debt. It is a marketing tool. It is there to facilitate orderly marketing and to ensure that the producer gets the best market return possible. I regret the hon. member is leaving the impression that if this particular piece of legislation were to be withdrawn all would be well.
We know that there are still problems in western Canada and in other parts of Canada in the agricultural community. The premier of the province of Saskatchewan represents his farmers very well and makes representations to us on a regular basis when he considers there is a need. Of course, we will be responding to his request. We will be analysing and assessing the magnitude of the difficulties, whether they be drought or other conditions, as we have in the past.
November 27, 1989

I want to assure my hon. friend that our record speaks louder than words. In the process we will examine the extent. I know that last year about this time everyone was screaming and hollering about the need for drought payments.
We will not get statistics in from the crop insurance people until the end of January, February or March. It is very difficult to try to make guestimates of the extent of any losses because when you do you sometimes miss the mark.
Obviously, we will be monitoring the situation very closely and responding to the premier in some detail indicating how we intend to monitor the situation. We will seek his co-operation as he will ours. Once again, no one in the province of Saskatchewan speaks louder and clearer and with a more articulate voice than the premier of the province of Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, I think everyone in the House is aware that this is not long-term financing of farm debt. It only exacerbates the situation if the government responds in a positive way to the Sask Pool and to the premier in providing assistance later this winter or early next spring.
This $400 million or $500 million worth of interest-free loans is not available, and that is why the whole situation is being exacerbated this fall. Clearly, we have heard the cries from the Canadian Wheat Board, from the municipal leaders, and from the pools. I suppose that if the minister continues to press this legislation through it only puts that much more pressure on him from the premier of Saskatchewan. He has already outlined that and of course we are very familiar with it from the 1986 provincial election when the demand came in at 6 a.m.
I just think that it does worsen the situation for these producers, especially at harvest time when we have not, apparently from what the Prime Minister said today, been able to conclude new shipments and agreements for the sale of wheat to Russia. The situation is aggravated by the loss of this provision.
The minister would agree that in the negotiations over the subsidy code there was a list of subsidies which was not subject to the countervail. Most producers, including farm producers, soybean producers and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, only three groups allowed to
Government Orders
speak before the committee, could not understand why we were destroying this unilaterally when it would lend itself in the negotiation of a subsidy code with the United States to giving away certain support programs through agriculture well before negotiations had started to take place.
It is my understanding that they are not going to take place until 1991. I would say to the minister that removing this is a very unfortunate thing at this time. It is his decision and his difficulty, perhaps with his good friend the premier of Saskatchewan, because it will only exacerbate pressure for special interim payments at a much earlier time than might have been necessary because of the level and quality of crops in the prairies this summer.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. Minister of Agriculture have a reply?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will reply because the hon. member made reference to the first special Canadian Grains Program and to a telephone call that occurred in the middle of the night. I want to say this to you and to other members of the House who may not have been here at that time: there was no one who was more disappointed about the federal government coming up with a special Canadian Grains Program than members of the Liberal party. It pulled the rug right from under them. They tried to distort the program by suggesting it was a loan. They wanted to know whether it was new money or old money or whether it was phoney money. It was hilarious to watch them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Their old leader told them to sell their own grain. They were used to that.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That's right. They were used to that because they did have a leader who told farmers what to do with their wheat.
This has nothing to do with the subsidy code. The hon. member keeps insisting that he has to drag the trade agreement into this issue. He has absolutely no basis upon which to make that statement at all. This has absolutely nothing to do with it whatsoever.
We have a gentleman across here who purports to speak for agriculture. He fails to realize that the agricultural community is very heavily reliant upon the export industry. Some 50 per cent of our agricultural market receipts are achieved through the export market. We are a world player in the export market. We have been

Government Orders
caught in the crossfire of a price war between the European Community and the United States.
It was the Prime Minister of this country who brought the issue of agriculture to the top of the agenda in the GATT proceedings to deal with this debilitating situation that was destroying the export oriented industry of agriculture in Canada. What we see now is the attention of all agriculture producing nations directed toward dealing with the gradual reduction of trade distorting subsidies, which incidentally in world terms total somewhere between $250 billion and $275 billion.
Quite frankly, if we are going to be asked as a trading nation to pay our share of those dues, we cannot stay in that business. It is incumbent upon us to work together with other agriculture producing nations to bring about a gradual reduction of the trade distorting subsidies that have played havoc on a very important segment of the Canadian agricultural industry.
The hon. member speaks out of both sides of his mouth. The fact of the matter is we have to ensure that our export oriented industry and our domestic oriented industry are fairly treated. That is the kind of balance we are trying to achieve.
It is worthy to discuss this issue on an intellectually honest basis, but when he keeps throwing red herrings are being thrust across the floor, bringing the subsidy code into this particular issue, it does not speak well of the hon. member. He and I came to this House at the same time. We have enjoyed each other's company, but there are times when he lectures me and I have to lecture him. Today it is my turn to lecture him.

We have also said, and this is well known at GATT, that Article 11 of GATT has to be clarified and strengthened. That should be sending a strong signal. I believe we have the support of the Canadian Dairy Commission and the dairy fanners of Canada in the strengthening and clarifying of Article 11 of GATT. They know that that has to happen. But we are working together with the producers to do these things. That is where the success is going to come from, by working with the producers of these various crops.
The hon. member talked about oats being removed from the Canadian Wheat Board. It is my understanding that the Canadian Wheat Board did not market an awful lot of those oats.
He talked about the two-price wheat. Many of us in this country have forgotten why the two-price wheat system was brought in in the first place. It is my understanding that it was brought in for the protection of Canadian consumers because the price of wheat was much higher on the domestic market.
The hon. member mentioned St. Lawrence Starch. From newspaper articles, the company claims that the com countervail was the reason that they were taking a look at their operation and the decisions they had made. None of us probably know the real reasons why St. Lawrence Starch is moving, but we could all speculate and this is not the place to speculate. We would certainly not want to do that.

We are not going to stand back idly and see our producers hindered or tramped on by actions taken by the U.S.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider developing special initiatives, in consultation with Aboriginal peoples, to response to the serious employment, education and health needs of aboriginal youth.
He said: I think there is an interpreter when I start speaking Inuktitut, Mr. Speaker.
[Translation from Inuktitut]
I am pleased to have this opportunity today to speak to the concerns of aboriginal youth. I submitted this motion as a subject for debate out of a deep concern for both the present circumstances and future prospects of the young Inuit, Indian and Metis men and women in this country. I hope my remarks today will do justice to their concerns, their hopes and their dreams.
To the members of the Private Members' Business committee I would like to express my appreciation for having designated this motion a votable one. I am pleased that they view this issue as seriously as I do.
What does it mean to be young and aboriginal and living in Canada today? Last year, the annual report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission made newspaper headlines with this grim statement: "An Indian youngster in Canada has a better chance of being sent to prison than of completing university."
Many parliamentarians and Canadians were shocked at the time, and rightly so. But the alarming headlines disappeared after a day or so. How many of us bothered
to wonder why the situation exists, or asked what could be done to help change the situation? Headlines come and go, but the problems faced by aboriginal youths remain.
[Translation from Inuktitut\
I would like to quote from a letter I received from Mikkel Panaktalok, the secretaiy of the Tuktoyaktuk Youth Committee on the issue of law and prison.
If we knew what the law meant, we would not break it because our community and families are much too important to us, to hurt them in any way. We also don't want to go to jail because we don't want to get sent away from our parents. Sometimes though we feel that the only way we can get help and counselling is to be sent away, because we don't know how to get this help in our community, because of the lack of education programs. We cannot make choices unless we have the information we need.
In order to bring out a problem to get help, we get into trouble. Youth do not want to do this anymore. We never did want to do it intentionally.
We think that the RCMP, health services and social services are only there only when you are in trouble. No one tells us about prevention programs. We need help in using these agencies. We want to work together, but these agencies isolate us. All they do is react instead of prevent.

What are some of the stark realities of being young, aboriginal and living in Canada today? Statistics tell us that a young aboriginal person has fewer economic and employment prospects than a non-aboriginal person. They tell us that the young aboriginal person will not achieve as high an education and will earn less income than a non-aboriginal youth.
The health of the young aboriginal person is poorer than the non-aboriginal youth. The aboriginal youth will live about 10 years less than his or her non-aboriginal counterpart and is more likely to die a violent death.
Study after study has documented the continuing social and economic discrepancies between aboriginal and non-aboriginal peoples in this country. Although there have been improvements over the past few years in life expectancy, housing, sanitation and post-secondary education the disparities remain unacceptable.
An article which appeared in the The Canadian Family Physician in July of 1988 assessed the health of the Indian and Inuit in Canada in the 1980s and the 1990s. It revealed that Indian infant morality rates are more than
November 27, 1989

twice the Canadian rate. Inuit infant mortality rates are more than three times the Canadian rate.
There remains a 10-year discrepancy in the life expectancy between aboriginal people and non-aboriginal people in Canada.
[ Translation from Inuktitut]
The rate of tuberculosis among aboriginal people is still 7 to 10 times higher than the national average. In some communities in the Northwest Territories, where epidemics have broken out in the past couple of years, the rates are over 100 per cent higher than the national rate.
Violent deaths are still a significant cause of mortality among aboriginal people. In 1933, 31 per cent of all Indian deaths and 34 per cent of all Inuit deaths were violent deaths. Of these violent deaths, suicide is the most important cause of death in young adults.
The aboriginal youth of Canada are killing themselves at a shocking rate. The statistics are horrifying and demand the attention of all of us.
The Inuit of the Northwest Territories are committing suicide at a rate four times the national average. More than half of the 172 suicide victims in the Northwest Territories since 1978 have been in the 15 to 24 age group, and the vast majority are males.

Between 1978 and 1988 the rate of suicide amongst Inuit in the Northwest Territories averaged 53.4 per 100,000. The suicide rate was 22.3 per 100,000 for Indians, and 20 per 100,000 for others.
The average Canadian suicide rate over the decade was about 14 per 100,000.
Factors contributing to the high rate of suicide among aboriginal youth include poverty, alcohol and drug abuse, erosion of traditional values and stress associated with cultural transition. The cultural turmoil in many aboriginal communities especially affects the young people and many feel they have no hope for the future.
Aboriginal youth must be able to see for themselves a positive future within their communities. They must be part of the decision-making in the development of solutions.
Private Members' Business
I would like to return again to the letter I received from the Tbktoyaktuk Youth Committee and what they would like to see happen in their community:
We want to get something done for the youth in the community of lUktoyaktuk. We need national, regional, and local youth programs. We need funding- If we had other communities to work with, we could see what they are doing, and have different exchange programs with other communities. We could break down trouble between different places and get new ideas. Sometimes other youth might be doing things that we would like to do.
There is no place for the youth to go to. No drop-in centre, no place to hang out, nothing happening in the evenings for the youth in our community. There isn't enough recreational programs. Right now, the youth are getting into trouble because of not enough things to do. A drop-in centre would really benefit our community.
We need to be given responsibility and be taught how to use this responsibility, and given the power to make decisions.
There is not enough, if any, substance abuse or alcohol programs that are for youth in the community. We do not have anyone our age who is trained in this area. Unless we do, the message does not get through. We need our peers to teach us what happens. We need someone our own age that we can look up to. They are trying to use programs for adults, and these programs do not work for the youth.
Improving educational attainment levels is essential. Educational attainment levels among aboriginal people are still significantly lower than among non-aboriginal people. Grade 9 attainment for the general population is 80 per cent. For Indians living on urban reserves it is 66 per cent. For Indians living on rural reserves it is 51 per cent.
[Translation from Inuktitut]
In the Northwest Territories, 63 per cent of aboriginal people have less than a grade 9 education. Only 2 per cent of aboriginal people in the Northwest Territories have attended university. School dropout and failure rates are still high. Less than half of the students enrolled in grate 10 in the Northwest Territories graduate. It is at this stage that most young people quit school because most of them are reluctant to leave their home communities to attend high school in one of the major centres.
While it is true that attainment levels have been increasing over recent years, there is still much more to be done. And what are the employment prospects of these young aboriginal students once they graduate? Not good.

November 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
I am concerned we may have an aboriginal youth employment crisis of major proportions very soon unless some priority attention is given to this issue.

The aboriginal population of the country is growing at a much faster rate than the non-aboriginal population. The 1989-1990 estimates of the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs indicate that the Indian population has been growing at a rate three times as fast as the Canadian population as a whole. This rate does not even include the increase in the Indian population due to Bill C-31, passed a few years ago by Parliament, which has restored Indian status to thousands of Indian people who had lost this status under various discriminatory provisions of the Indian Act.
This growth rate has resulted in a population which is very young. Almost two thirds of the Indian population is under the age of 25, compared to less than one quarter of the Canadian population as a whole.
Internal documents of the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs point out the serious employment consequences of this young and growing population. Between 1987 and 1997, 140,000 young aboriginal people will become eligible to join the labour force. According to the department, the problems this will create cannot be understated. Just to maintain employment rates at present low levels will require 8,000 plus new jobs annually. Most of the new jobs will be required in rural areas where opportunities to date have been very limited.
In the Northwest Territories, where I am from, the picture is similar. The population growth rate of the Territories aboriginal people is 3 per cent annually. Over half of the total population of the Northwest Territories, about 53 per cent, is under the age of 25. About 43 per cent of the NWT population is under the age of 20. In the Northwest Territories, there will be 600 potential entrants to the labour force every year for the next decade.
Current unemployment rates among aboriginal people range from 35 to 50 per cent. In remote communities, the rates are higher. In the Northwest Territories, most of the almost 30,000 Inuit, Dene and Metis live in small, widely scattered villages where the prospects for growth
are limited. Unemployment rates in some of the communities reach 50 per cent and higher.
In the NWT, in the winter of 1989, the aboriginal unemployment rate was six times higher than the nonaboriginal rate. Unemployment was highest for young people aged 15 to 24.
Regionally, youth unemployment was 49 per cent in the Kitikmeot region, 34 per cent in the Baffin region, 31 per cent in the Keewatin, 28 per cent in the Inuvik region, and 20 per cent in the Fort Smith region.
The population boom in the aboriginal communities has outstripped the number of jobs being created. For example, in the Northwest Territories aboriginal communities, the working age population increased by 2,600 people between 1981 and 1986. Over the same period, employment in those communities grew by only 1,185.
The challenge of establishing conditions which will enable young people of these communities to have an economic future and lead productive lives is an enormous one.
I am encouraged, however, by the many signs that aboriginal youth are increasingly taking matters into their own hands. Last February the Aboriginal Youth of Canada held a conference here in Ottawa. The purpose of the conference was to bring together aboriginal youths from throughout Canada to provide a forum for discussions and opportunities for consensus on the course of action. The theme chosen for the conference was: "From the past, in the present, and for the future". The theme was chosen to reflect the reality that in order for aboriginal peoples to attain their goal of self-determination in the present, it is necessary to respect the traditional ways and have a clear vision of what people want to be in the future. The Aboriginal Youth Council of Canada would like to have another such conference in the new year, and I would encourage the government to support this request for funding.
In closing, I would like to express my wish that as many Members of Parliament as possible from all three parties speak to this motion. I have corresponded with many members already, inviting them to participate in this debate. The more these issues are discussed and the more people become aware of their importance, the better will be our understanding.
November 27, 1989

In conclusion, I will return to the comments of the Tuktoyaktuk youth committee which stated: "It is the hope of the youth of Tuktoyaktuk, that the concerns we have put down on paper, will be taken to heart by the politicians in Ottawa. We want to work together, to help the aboriginal youth of the north and south. The government in Ottawa has the final say that is very powerful-we hope the government in Ottawa will help us with our concerns, issues and problems." Imaginative efforts are needed to address the concerns of the aboriginal youth of Canada. I am sure that everyone will agree that it is in the national interest to ensure that the productive and creative potential of these young people is harnessed and not wasted.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Nunatsiaq. I cannot help but commend him for his concern and his care about the well-being of aboriginal peoples in Canada. His is a concern that is shared by this government and by me personally, and it is shared by a government which is striving to accomplish real progress and bringing new hope and dignity to native Canadians.
However, I must say that while the member himself is unquestionably sincere and a man of honourable motivation, it is unfortunate that the political party he represents is astonishingly hypocritical in its dealings with this matter over the past century.
Throughout most of the past century, successive Liberal governments have demonstrated a tremendous insensitivity to the needs of the aboriginal peoples, and I bring this up because it is relevant to the policies that we have to deal with today. Liberal policies have slammed the doors on the aspirations of natives. Liberal thinking relegated the first Canadians to an existence that was separate and apart from the mainstream of modem life.
Instead of educating the young and employing the vibrant, vital, adult population of the day, these policies created what was a destructive and soul-destroying system of welfare and hopelessness where identity and self-respect were stripped away, leaving behind a very sad and weakened shadow of the proud people who once held dominion over this land.
Private Members' Business
Since 1984, this government has been working to bring some order out of this chaos. We have had to return to the very fundamentals of the relationship between Canada and its aboriginal people, and we have done so in our continuing search for answers to address these wrongs.
First, there is the issue of land claims, many of them outstanding for over a century. Since taking office five years ago, this government has settled 40 specific claims and is working on 140 more. We have also achieved agreements in principle on two comprehensive claims, and are on the brink of signing a third. As well, we are negotiating six others and the groundwork has been laid for negotiations to get under way on several more. This issue is critical to the self-esteem of the native people, who gave way to the European invasion believing, because governments told them that this was so, that there would be a place for them that they could call home. Therefore, as quickly as we can, we are working to settle these claims and deliver on that promise.
Second, there is the issue of self-determination, what some call self-government. Quite simply, our effort toward self-government means that we are returning to the people their birthright, the birthright that is expected by all human beings, to make their own decisions over their own everyday lives, and this is necessary because the paternalistic attitudes of past governments gave Indian Affairs officials a most extraordinary and almost Orwellian control over the lives of Indian and Inuit people.
This big brotherism must now be reversed so that Indian and Inuit people are enabled to take their rightful place as equal participants in the affairs of this country, and that they do so having honed their skills through the experience that they have gained in running their own lives.
In the past, bands have been restricted as to what they may or may not decide without reference to the federal government through the Department of Indian Affairs. They have been unable to deal with such simple things as local problems like control of the dog population. They have had virtually no control over administration of funds used to provide basic services to a reserve. Direction over the welfare of their children was wrenched

November 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
away from them, frequently as were the children themselves.
Certainly, the questions of schooling and access to health care were totally under the direction of government bureaucrats who often made decisions according to their own perceptions rather than in response to the actual needs of the people.
All these things are being reversed under the progressive policies of this government and the leadership of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. We are sensitive to the need to introduce these changes with great flexibility and with concern for the specific needs of each band, group or community. We know that what works for communities in the south in the highly populated areas will not always be appropriate and will not always apply to people in the more remote areas. Nevertheless, we also recognize that we must proceed at all levels without delay so that the degradation of the first citizens of this land is halted at once.
Our objectives are clear. We are fully committed to a full return of local decision making and power over local self direction to Indian and Inuit communities within the framework of the Constitution. This includes control over programs delivered by the federal government, and we have made great progress in these areas. For example, administrative control over funds provided for postsecondary education has been turned over to the Indian communities in Manitoba and in many other jurisdictions.
Many bands disperse social assistance on their own and run local municipal type services such as water, sewage and firefighting programs. More and more bands are running their own schools, employing educators and setting the curriculum according to community objectives and values. Bands are running housing projects, administering mortgage funding and planning community development programs. Bands own and manage construction companies, building schools, roads and other community facilities.
Out of these initiatives is growing a self confidence that will allow these native people to take full advantage of the new Canadian Economic Aboriginal Development Program introduced by this government in June. This is a program that over the next five years will see the injection of $874 million into the aboriginal community.
This will help to establish a renewal of the entrepreneurial spirit that is so natural to a self motivated people.
This is a program that is designed to help develop an economic base that will allow aboriginal people to grow and to thrive in financial independence. I am proud to say that there are hundreds of successful, incipiently successful, and looking forward to being successful Indian entrepreneurs out there, proving once again that the initiative is available when the opportunity is offered.
This is good news for many, many reasons, but most important because it puts the lie to the stereotypes of the aboriginal people that so many people have. These stereotypes are being put to bed in 100 different ways right across this land. They are evident to me as I travel from place to place visiting aboriginal communities throughout Canada. What I see is a people who are struggling to take hold, to gain control, to provide then-children with a new sense of tomorrow. I see successes everywhere I go because now people have what they lacked in the past. They finally have some hope.
Without doubt, there is much to be done and there are many new challenges before us as more and more young people drift into the cities looking for additional opportunities. This government will continue to respond flexibly and appropriately as the need arises.
Canadians at large and as individuals must also assume their own share of responsibility for easing aboriginal peoples over the adjustment period. I would suggest that we begin by learning about what the successes are of our native people and through that gain a new perspective and reflect a new respect for their ability to survive against tremendous odds. I can tell you that the more you know about the successes, the sooner that respect becomes admiration for those who have succeeded against those odds.
It is heartening also to see volunteer organizations such as the Canadian Council for Native Business springing up. It is a private sector organization led by key business leaders across Canada that encourages young native business entrepreneurs through a mentoring system to develop their business skills. In the final resolution, we will need many more such as these in order to complete the process of repairing the damage that past attitudes and policies have created.
November 27, 1989

I said already that much remains to be done. Daily we are learning new approaches through the collaborate process we have established with native leaders. In our five years of experience with the native question, we have not discovered a single magic solution, but we have developed a very strong sense that we are working toward the right goals, and we have many successes to bear that out.
Before European settlement of this land, the aboriginal people were self-reliant, self-governing, and they were totally self-resourceful. We have made some progress in restoring some of that responsibility. The task before us is to complete that process and that we complete it to the benefit of all Canadians.
