subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today in support of this motion put forward by the member for Nunatsiaq which states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should
consider developing special initiatives, in consultation with
Aboriginal peoples, to respond to the serious employment,
education and health needs of Aboriginal youth.
The member has properly identified a key area of concern that requires immediate attention and a greater degree of priority in the government's planning activities. Young people of aboriginal origin face a tremendous challenge as they tiy to find their identity and their place in this large world of ours. Despite natural hurdles, as well as social and economic barriers, these young people must overcome obstacles put in their path by this federal government.
Private Members' Business
We must remember that Indian youth are growing up in a world much different than that which bred their elders. Indian youth are confused and frightened and unsure of their future. They live in a world ravaged by the frustrations of the generations that preceded them, and as they try to respond they receive conflicting messages about how to cope with those frustrations.
Like their elders, every time they witness progress being made on one front, they see a government betrayal on another. These are people who see their elders struggling to survive in a world that seems so much different from the world they see before them on the television signals coming into their homes. The messages they receive from the non-Indian world help to reinforce their feelings of mistrust and lack of confidence in their own ability to initiate change. Into this world of mistrust creeps abuse and victimization and sometimes violence. It is not a pleasant world, and it serves only to perpetuate poverty and despair.
Indian leaders across the country are addressing the problems facing Indian youth as best they can. As they look to the future, these leaders know their children must be armed with the knowledge of their history, their culture and their way of life, as well as the understanding that is necessary for achieving the social and economic goals they set for themselves. Indian leaders have identified, like the member from Nunatsiaq who has brought forward this motion today, that employment, education and health care for young people are the pillars on which their future will be built. Without opportunity, skills, patience, and a strong body, as well as mind, young Indian people will not have much of a future.
One thing I want to make clear in the developing of this motion before us today is the simple definition and interpretation of the word "aboriginal". I want to stress that, as the member who presents this motion represents in the strictest sense aboriginal people in Canada, and I support his motion in that regard. I also support the motion in the context that it applies to treaty people, those people who are the descendants of those who signed treaties with the Crown so that they could retain their inherent sovereignty and live as Indian people on their land forever. Treaty people include many of those who reside in my constituency and are equally concerned with the future of their children, and as such are working

November 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
to improve and develop employment, education, and health care opportunities.
When we as parliamentarians are addressing this government with plans for programs or policies, and we are addressing the needs of aboriginal people, the government must understand that our plans are not meant to distract from the plans or programs of all the people who may be aboriginal in origin, but who may be addressing their own special needs differently. I say this for a couple of reasons, not the least of which is that the government tends in its public relations to regard all aboriginal people as the same, and as such reacts inappropriately with inappropriate legislation.
Chief Rolland Crowe of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations stated: "The actions and words of the present government are totally contradictory. On the one hand it says that Indians must retain and develop their cultural heritage and the political or social institutions; on the other hand the government has repackaged the termination policy as a devolution policy and thereby continues the Crown's apparent deliberate efforts to dilute and eventually eliminate the special status and rights of treaty Indian people!" This government obviously needs constant reminders that its responsibilities are to all aboriginal people, just as they are to all Canadians.
In that context, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw your attention to the position on education that was developed by one of the bands in the riding that I represent, The Battlefords-Meadow Lake. The Little Pine Band believes that education holds the key to the future for their children and for their band which they regard as a nation distinct in its own right. As such, the band is working to an education for their young people that is holistic in nature and encompasses the total and complete preparation of the young for active participation as responsible and competent individuals in society as a whole. The education received must provide not only for mental and academic development but also for moral, spiritual and physical development as well.
Let me quote from one of Little Pine Band's education planning documents: "Education must recognize the distinctive attributes and values of the traditional Indian culture and must seek to develop in young people a knowledge of their cultural background and heritage as well as a pride in being recognized as an Indian in society, both now and in the future. It is important that
young people be taught their special rights as guaranteed through the treaties. They must be helped to understand the spirit and intent of those treaties and to respect and honour their forefathers for their wisdom and foresight in negotiating the treaties which have granted the Indian bands status as distinct nations. People must not abuse their rights by expecting preferential treatment where it is not warranted and in such a way that their own sense of independence and responsibility is eroded. They must understand that these rights were intended to offer them opportunities to become functional, responsible and contributing citizens of their band and of Canadian society."
The Little Pine Band made these comments in a proposal to the Department of Indian Affairs last June. I supported those comments then and I continue to support them now. The department must be reminded of its responsibilities. I say that again, because often it reacts without thinking of those.
You will remember not too long ago when the department was doing what it should have done at the time, Mr. Speaker. A proposal was accepted that would see the construction of a school on Indian land that would prepare Indian youth for specific employment opportunities. That school, the All Nations Institute of Technology, was built on the Thunderchild Reserve, also an area within the boundaries of the Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency.
That school now sits empty and idle because the department forgot about its plan. Money for capital was easily found, but funds for operations disappeared. Money for the building alone will not educate or employ Indian people. The government must remember that Indian youth, to achieve the success they want to achieve, must be provided with the tools that are needed to build the bridges to that success. Those tools include, as the member pointed out, education, employment and health care.
Indian populations are growing and because a significant portion of that population is under the age of 20, it is imperative that further support systems be established to assist students to complete their studies. It is readily apparent by the high drop-out rates, particularly among Indian students in urban schools, that the system is not meeting their needs. A special effort must be made to get an Indian curriculum, Indian teachers, and Indian elders into the schools in the territories, on the reserves,
November 27, 1989

and in the urban centres where Indian populations warrant.
Keeping Indian and aboriginal youth interested in their education is not only an important part of the school system, it is an important part of the development of our society. What use will a good education be to an Indian youth if there are no jobs that will utilize the acquired skills and knowledge? As long as attitudes against the creation of Indian job development programs and economic opportunities persist, there will be little commitment or motivation from Indian youth to follow through and achieve that which is so much desired.
I take this opportunity in concluding my remarks to ask the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs to immediately call together a meeting of Indian leaders, with the simple purpose of creating a special task force, a task force to be made up of Indian people who would have the duty to recommend initiatives that the federal government could take to respond to these serious employment, education, and health needs of Indian youth. If the minister would do this, it would address the concerns put forward by the motion today and, more important, provide us with specific direction and focus on one of this nation's most pressing social and human problems.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to talk about a topic of great concern, not only to the government, but to the people of Canada. While acknowledging the special needs of aboriginal youth, I would first like to applaud the many accomplishments of these young people in many fields.
Aboriginal youth have excelled in the arts, education and are increasingly making inroads in the private sector ventures. These achievements are particularly outstanding, considering the difficulties they often face in health, employment and education.
Given the importance of the aboriginal culture, both to the aboriginal people and the richness of the fabric of Canada, it is important that aboriginal youth are afforded every opportunity to support and to further their unique cultural heritage.
Private Members' Business
Each of us understands that the problems experienced by aboriginal youth are many. Every one of us appreciates that significant measures must be undertaken if we are to break the cycle of poverty in which too many of these young people find themselves trapped.
The future of any society rests with its young people. It is especially true for status Indians. Approximately 54 per cent of their population is under the age of 24, compared with 38 per cent of non-aboriginal Canadians.
The first nations of Canada are rightly anxious that these young people realize their full potential. Mr. Speaker, you will hear many members from this side of the House agree with that sentiment. You will hear us state that we are not at all satisfied with the state of affairs our aboriginal youth find themselves in. You will hear that while there have been improvements in many areas, this government remains deeply concerned about the conditions of aboriginal youth.
More specifically, we readily acknowledge that Canada has a long way to go before aboriginal people achieve the same standards of health, employment and education as other members of our society. But at the same time we are beginning to see positive developments and new opportunities that will significantly benefit aboriginal youth.
I would like to assure this House that the Minister of State for Youth and the Minister of Employment and Immigration remain dedicated to changing the conditions that have prevented aboriginal people from securing their rightful place in Canadian society. But we also acknowledge that a major reason behind the failure of past government efforts to improve the conditions of aboriginal people lies in the basic approach taken. Too often the programs were initiated by social planners who thought they knew all the answers and they were wrong.
It is now evident that the aboriginal people of Canada should assume control of the matters that directly affect their lives. That is why the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs has worked as closely as possible with the diverse groups that make up the First Nations of Canada to promote aboriginal self-government. He is

November 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
committed to a dramatic increase in local decision-making. He is determined to equip aboriginal governments with the increased powers within the framework of the Canadian constitution and he is ready to provide the aboriginal people with increased resources to achieve their objectives.
A key feature of self-determination lies in increasing employment opportunities for aboriginal people. There can be no doubt that we must work to improve the unemployment rate among aboriginal youth which is at 31.6 per cent, much higher than the national average of 11 per cent. We want aboriginal youth to take advantage of our shift in emphasis in employment and immigration, away from the passive income support programs and toward programs and services that will help people secure a stable niche in the labour market.
We want them in these programs because it is clear from all the statistics that aboriginal youth desperately need to be better equipped for the demanding requirements of a modern global economy.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, many training and employment initiatives undertaken by Employment and Immigration Canada have targeted aboriginal people as a top priority. Employment and Immigration Canada is committed to helping those who have difficulty entering or remaining in the work force. That is why the aboriginal peoples are one of the designated groups that receive special consideration in the programs we offer.
Projects have been launched under the Canadian Jobs Strategy all across the country to address the very real training concerns of our aboriginal peoples. For example, a life and work skills training project was recently launched in Vancouver, directed at unemployed native youth who have come into conflict with the law. This project, worth $331,538, was sponsored under our job entry program of the Canadian Jobs Strategy in co-operation with the Indian and Metis Society. It now employs 48 native people and is providing them with supervised work experience. The project provides alcohol and drug counselling and offers social orientation and anger control techniques for those who need it. This is the type of practical opportunity we are providing aboriginal peoples. By participating in these projects they receive important training that will allow them to enter the job market.
The life skills training they obtain in these programs is culturally based. Job placement assistance is provided and those needing further employment related training are directed to appropriate programs.
This is all part of our concentrated efforts under the Canadian Jobs Strategy to begin addressing the many inequities in the education and training that aboriginal peoples experience in Canada. In our concern, we have supported innovative efforts to meet the unique needs of aboriginal youth. In Regina and Winnipeg we have attempted to upgrade literacy among unemployed aboriginal street youth with our "Beat the Street" program. This is a unique undertaking that uses peer tutoring to reach street kids. Unemployed youth are often more receptive to the training offered by people who understand their situation, as the success of"Beat the Street" indicates. Participants in the program who have failed elsewhere have acquired the reading, the writing and the life and job skills they need to successfully enter the world of work.
Other examples of government efforts include the native internship program that has been successfully operated by the federal government since 1976. It is now being significantly expanded and operates under the Summer Challenge program offered by Employment and Immigration Canada. The native internship program creates summer employment and opportunities for aboriginal youth in the Employment and Immigration Canada offices throughout the country. It provides them not only with an income but training and work experience. This gives them the marketable skills that helps them successfully enter the job market. Since 1976 participation has increased from 65 to 586. Every effort is made in this program to provide employment in the federal service that supports the career and vocational aspirations of the aboriginal young people.
I know there is a lot of concern about the deplorable educational record of the aboriginal people in Canada. It is a problem that has bedevilled our government and many previous governments before us. All of our studies show that anyone, aboriginal or not, who drops out of high school severely restricts their economic and work prospects. Education clearly remains as the best way of avoiding unemployment. Yet we readily understand that the aboriginal youth drop-out rate is much, much higher
November 27, 1989

than any comparable group. We are determined to help them develop to their full potential.
One of the ways we do this is through our work orientation workshops, or WOW. These provide early school leavers with guidance on their future participation in the labour market. The WOW program provides a combination of workshops and on-the-job training to both orient young students to the world of work and encourage them to continue their education. It helps them to appreciate the importance of seeking specific skills training based on their future employment ambitions.
These are all part of our over-all approach of assisting youth. The development of comprehensive pilot projects such as the Canada-New Brunswick Youth Strategy and the Canada-Newfoundland Youth Strategy addresses the unemployment problems of youth in these provinces, with aboriginal youth being one of the groups being targeted for assistance.
These strategies address the very real difficulties young people face as they attempt to enter the labour force. For example, a key feature of these strategies is that preventive stay-in-school emphasis. This includes counselling, co-operative education programs and employment projects that will give students a realistic understanding of the workplace and the long-term benefits education provides.
In New Brunswick special attention is placed on high risk students from aboriginal backgrounds who are potential drop-outs. The Youth Strategies co-ordinate the current federal and provincial programs and services for youth; strengthen existing federal programs and services-

Yes, Mr. Speaker.
As I have already mentioned, aboriginal youth receive a very high priority. Recently, for example, we provided $140,000 to the Union of New Brunswick Indians to accept the Maleseet and Micmac youth in taking advantage of the full range of assistance under the Canada-New Brunswick Youth Strategy.
We have also provided almost $100,000 to the New Brunswick Aboriginal Peoples Council to ensure that the off-reserve aboriginal youth can better participate in the
Private Members' Business

I would like to ensure the hon. member who put forward this resolution that we are firm in our commitment to provide aboriginal youth with job skills that will allow them to fully participate in the 21st century. Canada's ability to compete in the global markets of the future depends on the preparations we provide to today's young people. Our young people are our future.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for Nunat-siaq for putting forward this private member's motion on aboriginal youth and for allowing me the opportunity to speak to this very important matter.
Initially, I was going to focus my remarks on education and economic development. However, I must address one other issue before addressing these topics. There have been some extremely disturbing stories recently involving teen suicides in the aboriginal communities in my riding.
We have often heard that the incidence of suicide in the native communities is higher than the national average. There is no question that this statement is an accurate one. But what is being done to lower the rate of teen suicide in the aboriginal communities is another situation. From what I have been told by the native leaders in my riding, there is not much being done. The Shibogama Tribal Council represents six native communities, located in an isolated area of northwestern Ontario. The six communities can only be reached by air. In the past two and a half years there have been 40 suicides in these communities which have a total population of less than 1,800.
The suicide rate in these communities is seven times higher than the national average. Native leaders in this Shibogama Tribal Council area are discouraged by the increase in suicides among their young people. They are most concerned with the increasing number of aboriginal youth who turn to suicide as a way of solving their problems.
The latest suicide occurred last week at Kingfisher Lake. A 16 year old boy ended his life. His death has left a void in the hearts of many residents of that community

November 27, 1989
Private Members' Business
of 300. The parents of this young man are devastated. Losing one's child to suicide is a most difficult experience for parents. Many questions are left unanswered, which makes the acceptance of death all the more painful. The community of Kingfisher Lake has experienced four such suicides in the past two years. While its native leaders continue to work hard at building their community for future generations, they are seeing their young people tom apart by violence, poverty, drug and alcohol abuse.
Earlier this summer I travelled to many of the native communities in my riding. Upon arrival at Wapekeka Indian reserve, the chief and council greeted me at the dock with the news that a 17 year old boy had taken his life the night before. He had been receiving treatment in Kenora at a drug and alcohol abuse treatment centre. I was taken to visit the boy's mother and other members of his family. What I saw has left a profound mark on me. The mother, the grandmother, the brother and sister of this young man were completely shattered by the news of their loved one's suicide. The whole community was grieving with the family. When one member of the community loses his or her life in such a violent and unnecessary fashion, the spark goes out of the eyes of the other members of the community and only pain, sorrow and helplessness are left.
At a native mental health seminar in Thunder Bay last month, Dr. Harvey Armstrong, head of the Canadian Psychiatric Association's native mental health section, said native parents are developing feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy because many of the children are damaging their minds with alcohol and chemicals. At the Association of Iroquois and Allied Indians annual health conference in London, Ontario, earlier this month, native author and clergyman, Arthur Holmes, also related some disturbing statistics. He said 80 per cent of Indians die in either unexpected or violent ways.
Canadians would never accept these kinds of statistics in non-native communities. Cries for help would be listened to and acted upon. So, why do we have a different set of standards for the aboriginal communities? As legislators we must find solutions to the many problems and issues before us.
The 1986 report of the special Senate committee on youth dedicated a complete chapter to native youth and the problems they face. In a section on suicide, and drug and alcohol abuse, the committee said:
We believe that drug and alcohol counselling and suicide prevention programs need to be designed and carried out by native people themselves.
The report goes on to say:
The most successful programs seem to involve young people helping other young people and providing healthy alternatives for solving their problems.
I have been a witness to the success of crisis intervention programs in three of the native communities in my riding.
In 1980 the communities of Grassy Narrows, Whitedog and Whitefish Bay, faced with high unemployment and welfare, were confronted with a major crisis. The young native people were either in the care of the Children's Aid Society, under the supervision of the probation and after-care service or involved in substance abuse. The native leaders recognized the need for crisis intervention programs and they designed programs in their communities which are run by them and for them. With financial assistance from Health and Welfare's National Native Alcohol and Drug and Abuse Program, the the crisis intervention programs in these three communities have been a tremendous success.
Recent statistics from the Grassy Narrows, Whitedog and Whitefish Bay communities show an 80 per cent decrease in the rate of violent deaths, an 80 per cent decrease in the suicide rate, a 90 per cent decrease in young offenders and an 80 per cent decrease in solvent abuse. All of this, over a seven-year period. These are very encouraging statistics and testimony to the statement of the special Senate committee on youth which stated that prevention programs designed and carried out by native people are the most successful.
The communities of Grassy Narrows, Whitedog and Whitefish Bay have proven beyond a shadow of a doubt that they can turn things around in their respective communities with adequate financial and moral support.
While funding for the crisis intervention program in these three communities in my riding has continued to decrease substantially, the programs continue, but with great difficulty. Earlier this year, the crisis intervention
November 27, 1989

programs almost became a target in the federal budget cuts.
The native leaders travelled to Ottawa with me and met with Health and Welfare officials and managed to salvage some of the funding. You see, Mr. Speaker, the crisis intervention programs at Grassy Narrows, White-fish Bay and Whitedog, are not an actual program of the department. This program was designed by the native leaders for their people. Any other native community attempting to obtain funding for similar programs have been turned down. The department has not recognized this program as an "official program".
I honestly believe that funds should be immediately set aside which would allow every native community in this country to design and administer a crisis intervention program which best addresses the individual needs of each community. We would see declines in the rate of violent death, suicide and substance abuse in very short time. We have an opportunity to invest in the future of aboriginal youth in this country. It is recognized worldwide that our youth are the future. We can give aboriginal youth a future filled with hope and future built on hope.
Now is the time for the government to act. Now is the time for us to put our money where our mouth is. We must do so in order to prevent the suicide rate from climbing any further. The cultural and economic survival of the aboriginal people depend on it.
I realize I have very little time left, Mr. Speaker, so I will use it to touch briefly on the education of aboriginal youth. It is no secret that education programs in native communities fall below the provincial standards. For years, native leaders have attempted to design curriculum which is tailor-made to the needs of the respective communities.
As the Department of Indian Affairs prepares for the transfer of education programs to Indian control, it is essential that such a transfer take place with the full consultation of the aboriginal people. There is a great fear among the native leaders that once this transfer takes place the financial resources will not be there for curriculum development. This is why a full consultative process must be established. Curriculum development in
Private Members' Business
native communities is tantamount to the future of these communities.
If the aboriginal youth receive a sound education with curriculum designed by their leaders for them, I believe we will see an increase in enrolment in the post-secondary institutions in this country. The difficulties many of the post-secondary native students have in completing their studies stems from an inadequate curriculum at the elementary and secondary levels. They are literally thrown into a system which is virtually foreign to them and they are not adequately prepared for it.
I would like to see the department provide the necessary resources to allow the native educators the opportunity to begin designing curriculum now, before the transfer of education programs take place. This way, once the transfer takes place, the communities would be ready to proceed with curriculum suited to their needs.
There are so many more issues concerning aboriginal youth which I could speak on. While I have yet to address the issue of economic development, let me say this much. There is no doubt in my mind that tf the government were to provide the financial resources needed which would allow native leaders to design crisis intervention programs for the communities and curriculum for the schools based on their needs and cultural beliefs, we would see a dramatic increase in post-secondary and native graduates who would return to the communities and work for the betterment of their people.
I have seen what economic development can do for a community. People have jobs. They are happy and living life to the fullest. Economic development works in the single industry towns and it works in aboriginal communities.
In closing, I would again like to thank my hon. colleague for Nunatsiaq for putting forward this motion and I call on all members to support it in the interest of aboriginal youth.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in this debate because this country has, at this time, no abortion legislation. It has not had any since January 28, 1988 when the Supreme Court of Canada struck down the existing legislation adopted by this House in 1969.

Mr. Speaker, it took two years and meanwhile, as a result of this government's failure to act, the private lives of Canadian men and women were paraded through the media. We had some flagrant examples of this last summer. We have had two years of stormy, divisive and sometimes even troubling debate. The 1988 election campaign was a time when the abortion issue created some very difficult situations.
For many years I have had a chance to read and listen to the comments of my constituents in Ottawa-Vanier,
and many of them support my position, which is that of a moderate. I have noticed that pro-choice people are not as extreme as people think. They do not necessarily favour abortion on demand. Nor do they consider abortion as an alternative to contraception. The less extreme proponents of pro-life accept or at least say they can accept abortion as a last resort in cases of incest, rape or when the mother's life is at risk.
If I had to indicate where I stand between the two, I think I would qualify as moderate pro-life. I am against abortion on demand, but I realize that in some situations, abortion may be necessary. Of course I would prefer to live in a society where the issue did not arise. However, reality is different, and as a legislator and a Member of this Parliament, I cannot look the other way and ignore the problem.
Bill C-43, the bill before the House today is, in my view, too permissive and unfair in its present form. The bill is ambiguous, to say the least. For instance, some people read the bill and say that in its present form it supports pro-life. Others read the same bill and say that, substantially, it is pro-choice. One doctor, on the basis of his personal values and religious beliefs, might be able to justify and promote abortion on demand. Another doctor, however, either from a different part of the country or even from the same town, might reject abortion on any grounds. In remote areas, where health services are limited, this could become a real nightmare.
In any case, Bill C-43 shifts the whole burden of responsibility to the doctor. The government and this Parliament are asking him to be clairvoyant and to predict the mother's moral, psychological, physical and mental health after the abortion.
Of 65,000 abortions done annually in Canada, nearly 50 per cent were sought by young women under 25. These statistics show that something is very wrong and that something must be done as soon as possible. The legislation before the House today does nothing to eliminate the reasons why women resort to abortion.
To be acceptable, a national policy should urge and enable the parties concerned to make a rational decision. To do so, we must create a secure environment. A good start would be counselling. Although this is certainly not the only answer, it could promote a dialogue and generate a positive attitude to pregnancy. A well structured family policy could also help secure the well being of the child to be bom. What about the daycare we have
November 27, 1989

been promised for two years and which has yet to materialize?
With Bill C-43, the government has, as I see it, tried to please everyone. It has shrugged off its responsibilities by shifting the burden of responsibility to the doctor. Mr. Speaker, is the doctor responsible for making a distinction between legal responsibility and moral values? I don't think so.
I think the potential interpretations of Bill C-43 are as numerous as our medical practitioners.

In a perfect world we would not need to have abortions. In this imperfect world, we have to address this issue. I believe, for one, that legislation controlling abortions is needed.
It took two years for this government to bring forward legislation to fill the legal vacuum created when the Supreme Court of Canada struck down the existing 1969 legislation because it breached the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. After two years of this Conservative Government, Bill C-43 is their best effort. It is far from perfect and it falls short of my personal position on the issue. It needs to be amended in committee.
Some members have told us that they reject this legislation in principle, and will vote in the negative at second reading. I can understand that position. But if the majority believes this bill is wrong in principle and should be defeated tomorrow, then we are faced with the status quo. That is, no abortion legislation. We all know that only the government can bring in enabling legislation and order its consideration by Parliament. Bill C-43, I repeat, is this government's best effort. If defeated, we are not likely to have another bill in this Parliament, thereby confirming the status quo, and that is abortion on demand.
On the other hand, if the majority accepts the principle of Bill C-43, then in my view it should go to committee for study of its clauses. Amendments will be possible to deal with the substance of the bill and redress, I would hope, its imperfections.
I dare say that those who vote against the bill at second reading, being the principle of the bill, will have some convincing to do in committee to substantively amend something to which they object in principle.
Government Orders
Once this bill is in committee it acquires a special status by virtue of it being the object of a free vote for most of us in this House. In committee it will be subjected to scrutiny by backbenchers-no members of the Cabinet will be present-freed from party lines and the discipline of the Whips. Whatever happens to the bill in committee will be the result of our own best efforts, not the government anymore.
As a legislator, I know the great difficulties members will face in coming up with a more acceptable bill. I hope we can meet this very difficult double challenge of respecting, on the one hand, the constitutional requirements as set out in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms with regard to the rights of the women, and also address the legislative demands, in my view, in matters of abortion.
I shall vote for this legislation at second reading and I pray the committee will succeed in amending it.

Mr. Speaker, during my ten years as the Member of Parliament for Peterborough very few issues have been as emotional and morally frustrating or as unnerving as the issue of abortion. With regard to abortion we have been living in a permissive society since the Liberal government passed the abortion law in 1969.
The Conservative government, 20 years later, is now introducing Bill C-43 which will not offer one speck of hope to the more than 65,000 foetuses that are aborted annually. This might explain in part why the present Liberal leader is considering, according to the press, supporting Bill C-43.
Citing Section 251 of the Criminal Code as unconstitutional, the Supreme Court, in 1988, sent a clear message to Parliament to draft new legislation that would balance with the woman's constitutional rights the interest that society has shown in the foetus. Might I point out, Mr. Speaker, that Supreme Court Justice Wilson, in her comments following the Supreme Court hearings, said:
The primary objective of the impugned legislation -
-speaking of the current legislation-

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
- is the protection of the foetus. This is perfectly valid legislation as an objective. It has other ancillary objectives, such as the protection of the life and health of the pregnant woman and the maintenance of proper medical standards.
The value to be placed on the foetus as potential life is directly related to the stage of its development during gestation.
Finally, from Supreme Court Justices McIntyre and Laforest:
Historically, there has always been a clear recognition of a public interest in the protection of the unborn and there is no evidence or indication of general acceptance of the concept of abortion at will in our society.
It is my contention that Bill C-43, which is packaged in pro-life terminology, is legislation which calls for nothing less than abortion on demand as a legal right. Bill C-43, I regret to say, puts society's permissive call for personal comfort and gain ahead of society's call for respect of human life at every stage of its development. I consider Bill C-43 to be morally repugnant. It mirrors a time in history when blacks were slaves and society held a higher regard for their own personal comfort and gain than they did for the rights of slaves held in bondage and not considered to have any rights whatever.
Today's legislation needs to reflect a society that supports life at all stages of development and which will enable children to be raised with dignity. In the drafting of the bill I had hoped for a closer adherence to the direction of the Supreme Court in the Morgentaler decision, that the interests of both the woman and the foetus could be considered. The legislation before us manages to dance around this requirement and does absolutely nothing in reality to protect the foetus.
The bill states that abortion is illegal at all stages of pregnancy and then it goes on to say, except for all circumstances of health. By allowing a woman to have an abortion on mental, physical and psychological health grounds the government is giving women carte blanche rights to have an abortion for any reason they so wish by simply convincing a medical practitioner that the reason warrants such action.
Very few people in my riding support abortion for socio-economic reasons. Under Bill C-43, or under the former bill by the Liberals in 1969, it can be easily shown that strain on the mother results in serious psychological
impact on her health and consequently she can be granted an abortion for psychological reasons.
With Bill C-43 in place all that is needed to have an abortion is a pregnant mother, Dr. Morgentaler and a free-standing abortion clinic. These three ingredients are now available in Ontario and Quebec and will continue as they are with the blessing of this Parliament and the provincial governments of both Ontario and Quebec. Nowhere in Bill C-43 do we offer any protection whatever for the rights of the foetus, only for the mother's rights to have an abortion.
Only two short weeks ago, on November 16, the Supreme Court justices, in presenting their reasons for overturning the injunction against Chantal Daigle in August, refused to comment on foetal rights outside of the province of Quebec. The same court, however, in the Morgentaler decision gave the government an indication that foetal rights could be provided under new legislation. The government, in my view, has failed to take up this challenge with Bill C-43.
I must now indicate my unwillingness to support or to endorse Bill C-43. The only possible legislation that I could support would be that which makes abortion illegal at all stages of pregnancy except in the case where the life of the mother is seriously threatened.
Here is the reason why I do not feel we can move along by approving second reading and expect major substantial changes either in committee, in the House as a whole or at third reading. As it is mandatory for cabinet to vote for this bill with no options, it is obvious to me that any substantive changes such as I would require as a pro-life supporter will never come to pass. Therefore, I cannot and will not support this legislation at second reading, report stage or third reading. I feel that although it would be possible to enact a law which would protect all human life from the moment of conception to death, to attempt to do this within the realm of the legislation before us would require such a deviant move from the underlying principles of the bill that it would be virtually impossible.
The Minister of Justice is on record as saying that the government will not accept any amendments that further restrict a woman's access to abortion, according to The Toronto Star of November 25.
November 27, 1989

I spoke earlier about our permissive society that puts people's personal comfort and gain ahead of people's rights and needs. I would like to close with a short quote from the former president of the Catholic Conference of Catholic Bishops, Archbishop Hayes. He said:
Abortion is the destruction of human life. The challenge is to change our society's attitudes toward life and to channel the energies and strong emotions involved in this debate toward correcting mentalities and situations that lead to abortion. We need to create a society that supports life and enables children to be raised with dignity; a society that puts other people's rights and needs ahead of personal comfort and gain; a society that respects human life at every stage of its development.
As a Member of Parliament, and as a man who just two weeks ago became a grandfather for the fourth time, I could not agree more. We must, therefore, defeat this bill, defeat it at second reading, and concentrate our efforts on a piece of legislation that will provide the unborn with significant rights as a human being. I remind this House of elected representatives that when last given an opportunity to vote on this issue more Members of Parliament from all sides of this House supported a pro-life position than any of the other options that were available to us at that time.
So it is important that we defeat the bill. With our free vote I would like to show the Canadian people that Parliament wants to offer more protection to the foetus and reduce abortions in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great sadness, and indeed considerable anger, that I rise to address this House on the subject before us, namely, the recriminalization of abortion in Canada.
I have given a great deal of thought to what I would say on this sad day, both in response to Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, and in response to speeches made by some of the spokespersons supporting this criminalization legislation.
Most have spoken with great sincerity. Some have spoken to rationalize their compromise of basic beliefs. Some have done so to retain positions of power, and the saddest part is that they should even have to make that choice.
Equally sad is that many women must often face bearing a child not of their choosing, but what is tragic is that they must, if this bill passes, make decisions with the threat of criminal sanction.
Government Orders
In addition, a woman must approach her doctor who also has the weight of criminal sanction to contend with, and the doctor must decide whether an abortion for her is legal. I contend that the choice is no longer one of whether or not abortion is the appropriate course of action for the woman, but whether or not, if an abortion is sought, it will be legal in her circumstance.
I have spent most of my working life advocating, in one way or another, for women; most often low income women. I have seen the great distress women have faced with unplanned and unexpected pregnancy. I have seen the results of incredibly difficult decisions. I have known women who died because abortion was not legally available and, in desperation, they had put themselves in the hands of back room butchers.
I have seen women who carried to term and delivered children that they allowed to be placed for adoption, in the hope that the child would have a better life, and then spent a lifetime of torment longing for that child. I have seen women who faced pregnancy from failed birth control, or the inability to afford birth control, left alone with the consequences.
I have seen women who have made a difficult choice, harassed and harangued by people who claim to care about them, not just outside clinics, but daily in the media. And along with all Canadians, I watched the tragedy this past summer of young women dragged through the courts, having every intimate detail of their lives dissected on the evening news.

To my sisters from Quebec, I would like to say that I am glad the Supreme Court has guaranteed our right to choose under the Quebec Charter. And it is a right we hope to preserve for all women in Canada.

I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the whole question of abortion has been elevated to the level of emotionalism that we have seen in the past few years by a concerted and a sustained effort, but the true underlying question before us is the question of power.
Throughout history women have been the subject of control by men. The dictionary definition of power is "a position of ascendancy over others". Throughout the history of religion and civilization women's place has

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
been assigned by men based on their reproductive capacity.
Often women's position has been elevated. Women have been put on a pedestal, so to speak, to control their actions and participation in society. For example, women did not work outside the home because it was not their place. The fact that this only applied to women who came from well-to-do circumstances had nothing to do with society's attitude. Poor women, who have always worked, were not in the equation. Women, until 60 years ago, were not considered persons. Society has finally recognized how absurd this attitude was and few today would dare advocate turning back the clock. Twenty-five years ago women could not have access to birth control unless they were married. Men had access but not the societal responsibility for the outcome.
Today, in some jurisdictions, a woman still must have signed permission from her husband for a tubal ligation, but her husband is not required to seek her consent for a vasectomy.
Some of these practices have been codified in the past. Some are merely practices. But in either case, they are norms established by men for women. They are norms established by those who have always participated as partners in the process that leads to pregnancy but have never, to this very day, been required to participate in the consequences of pregnancy, much less be required to take responsibility for these consequences. Indeed, men are physiologically unable to face the same consequences as women.
Elere we are today faced with yet another law, another criminal sanction, drafted, debated and passed, mostly by men who will never bear the consequences of their decision.
Throughout the discussion in this House, men have stood and passed judgment on women and their ability to make thoughtful, responsible choices regarding reproductive rights. They have demeaned women. They have cast them again on a false pedestal saying: "We know what is best for you and we will decide what is good for you". In other words, they are saying: "We will continue to exercise power over you".
One of my colleagues, earlier in the debate, said: "One would wonder if this type of bill, based on this concept of women, would be before this House if this
House were made up of 255 women and 40 men instead of its present make-up of 255 men and 40 women".
The Minister responsible for the Status of Women stated in this House:
The last time I spoke in this place on the issue before us, I began by saying that I speak on behalf of those women who have been faced with bearing a child not of their choosing. Once again, I rise on behalf of those women.
She went on to say:
Since I first uttered those words we have no law in this country regarding abortion. In the view of many women including myself the absence of legislation appeared to respect what I believe, that the judgment of women faced with a difficult decision and their capacity to make a better decision than anyone in this chamber on their behalf was respected in that environment.
I concur with the minister's statements. I find it impossible, however, to believe her later remarks that to provide a framework for women in the world as it is, and not as we would like it to be, the solution is to support this motion to re-criminalize abortion.
If women in the past had been prepared to live the world as it was and failed to struggle for the world as we would like it to be, we would still not be persons, we would not have the vote and some of us would not be Cabinet ministers.
The criminal sanction is dressed up differently than past laws. Its greatest distinction is that it is purported to please no one. I suspect that it will possibly secretly please those who would maintain power over women.
This criminal sanction says to women: You are not capable of making your own moral decision. You must attend your doctor on the basis of a medical decision. Your doctor will make the final choice. If that choice is deemed wrong, your doctor will have to prove to the satisfaction of the courts that the procedure was legal. In so proving the legality of his or her decision it is you and every detail of your personal life that will be examined.
The Minister of Justice and Attorney General, when he introduced the bill, said:
The proposed new abortion law is understandable, it is workable and it is fair.
I suggest it is not understandable. It is not understandable to me why this government feels compelled to re-criminalize abortion. I suggest it is not workable. It is not workable because it is vague and creates the requirement to establish a whole new set of jurisprudence and risks withdrawal of doctors from performing abortions, especially if some are charged under this law. It is not fair. It is not fair to present a law that completely takes the final choice out of the hands of the woman and places it in the hands of her doctor while the threat of
November 27, 1989

criminal law looms overhead. As well, this legislation to re-criminalize abortion is unacceptable for Canadian women.
One of the special things about this House is the respect members accord each other. We address each other as honourable, knowing that we try to acquit ourselves with dignity, honour and integrity. I plead with the hon. members in this House to accord the women of Canada the same respect, knowing that they will acquit themselves with dignity, honour and integrity.
In this world, as women struggle to establish their rights and freedoms, I submit to all hon. members the words of J.S. Woodsworth: "What we desire for ourselves, we wish for all".

Mr. Speaker, after listening very carefully to Hon. Members whose speeches reflected widely divergent opinions; after reading Bill C-43, an Act respecting abortion, a subject that has been extremely controversial for many years; after long discussions with many of my constituents in Ahuntsic, people whose opinions are varied and diverse; after a thorough study of the impact on abortion of our society and the moral, ethical, social, economic and demographic aspects of this issue, one which compels Canadians to examine their democratic conscience as well as their moral values; and after consulting experts on the subject such as physicians, legislators, lawyers, priests and ministers, Catholics, those of the Orthodox faith, Protestants and atheists, today, Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to give my opinion of this bill, and be as objective as I can.
First of all, I would like to say that as a Member of Parliament, a woman and former nurse, in other words, someone with a respect for life, I will vote in favour of this bill which provides a judicious and clear response to all the concerns and questions I may have had since the debate started in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, my support for Bill C-43 is not just a matter of subjective
Government Orders
emotion and deep-seated feeling, it is a reasoned and rational decision.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, coming as it does after the Supreme Court's judgment in the Morgentaler case in January 1988, is intended to fill a legal vacuum, in response to demands by Canada's modem, pluralistic society. Since our society is not monolithic, its members holding various beliefs and views, it was imperative that this legislation should strike a balance between women's constitutional rights and society's interest in protecting the foetus. This means, Mr. Speaker, that these two fundamental rights are entirely compatible: the right of the woman to control her own body and her own destiny, and that of the foetus which, although unfortunately, it has yet to be recognized by the Supreme Court, is nevertheless a moral value that no normal society would be able to reject indefinitely.
Mr. Speaker, at a time when legislators, human rights activists and even the United Nations are talking about children's rights, minority rights and women is rights, a perverse selfishness that stifles all feelings of compassion and generosity leads us to ignore the rights of the foetus which is, at whatever stage of its development- embryology and the latest scientific techniques such as ultrasound prove it-a being in essence, in other words, a human being that is genetically alive. To talk about the rights of this fragile and voiceless being is, according to some people, tantamount to preaching in the wilderness and having opinions that are reactionary and outdated.
If, as these modernists claim, morality changes as new scientific discoveries are made, then I say those who speak for the unborn are pioneers, working towards a future where the rights of all will be respected, including the rights of the foetus. What future is there for a society that is unmoved by its own voluntary extinction and does not fight for its survival? What future is there for a country that, if it does not pass laws on such an essential issue, is doomed to a geometrical decline in its birth rate? The primary objective of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to reconcile two fundamental rights that are complementary and equal.
The second objective of this legislation is to provide fair and reasonable access to abortion, while preventing abuse and charlatanism. We know that many women, especially young women, left to themselves, accept willingly or are forced into some abortion practices that endanger their own physical and psychological health. For all the reasons that have already been given, abor-

Government Orders
tion must not be a form of birth control. It is therefore our duty as a responsible government to protect the life and health of the women in our country. This bill does so by removing several administrative obstacles, such as therapeutic abortion committees. These took a long time to make a final decision and thus prevented women from fully exercising their right to a legal abortion, thereby infringing on their physical and psychological health.
But, as I see it, Mr. Speaker, what is most important and what convinced me that this bill is positive and fair is the doctor's involvement in this big decision. For me, this is not paternalistic; the doctor will not tell the woman in an authoritarian way what choice or decision to make. Whatever decision she makes, she will always need to call on a doctor to perform an abortion and thus abortion is first and foremost a medical procedure. Who, Mr. Speaker, is in a better position than the doctor, with his scientific knowledge, professional ethics and practice, to make a definite decision that will take into account the woman's health, the foetus' rights and society's responsibilities?
Furthermore, the doctor who performs an abortion as prescribed by law for medical reasons related to physical, mental and psychological health is, according to the generally recognized standards of his profession, responsible for monitoring the woman after her abortion. He is inevitably involved and takes part in this process, like it or not. The bill simply confirms his deep involvement in providing an abortion. He is not acting as a moral adviser but as a qualified professional trained to make such a dicision. This decision is not unilateral but is made together with the women, for health reasons and with full respect for her freedom.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, some groups stubbornly criticize the criminalization of abortion. The Government has no alternative, since placing abortion in the Criminal Code was the only way for Parliament to regulate abortion nationally.
If abortion is performed in the legal framework, in accordance with legislation that is in the interest of our civilized society and defends the rithts of both the foetus and the women, I do not see how one could deliberately go against such a piece of legislation, because it is a reasonable compromise among all the opposition tendencies in our society. Bill C-43 is based on consensus, unity, not division, reconciling basic differences and
eliminating unyielding opposition. It is a bill which, like our country, is built on compromise and dialogue. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I support it with all my heart and all my mind.

Mr. Speaker, life is precious. Some five days ago I found I had reason to believe this more and more as just three hours ago I left the hospital with a health problem.
I wanted to take part in this debate because during the 15 years since I was first elected to Parliament in 1974 there have been only a handful of issues which have touched the very soul of this nation, issues which have required that we look inside ourselves and make decisions which affect not only us but which will affect all of our fellow citizens for generations to come. I would list in this category capital punishment, the Constitution, the free trade bill, and now abortion.
Abortion has been discussed for many years not only in this nation but around the world. There are a few things I would like to make clear at the outset. I speak today not only as the representative of the people of the Welland-St. Catharines-Thorold riding; I also speak as a grandfather, a father, a son and a brother. I speak as a friend to all those people who have entrusted to me the duty to speak on their behalf. Like other members in this House I too have searched very deeply into my own soul.
I have sought advice from friends and scholars, from people whom I respect a great deal, from people who are in favour of abortion and from people who are opposed. After having digested all of this information I have decided the course of action which I will follow.
Abortion is no more and no less than the taking of human life. This bill fortifies the idea that there can be in this country abortion on demand. I base my thoughts on logic. You see, life must begin sometime. There are those who argue that life begins at the moment of conception. Some will say after 12 weeks and others will say after 20 weeks. The legal definition is that life begins at the moment that you come out of the womb and from that moment on you have the protection of the law. As for me, I believe that life begins at the moment of conception for if I do not believe that, then life must begin at some arbitrary point. I say "arbitrary" because you can take any time, from one week of gestation to 12
||

November 27, 1989

weeks to 30 weeks, but you must always go back and say that life begins sometime.
If life does not begin at conception, then why can we not legislate that life begins one hour after you come out of the womb? In that way if someone were to be bom with a deformity or illness then we could destroy this non-human and our consciences would be clear. Why do we not say that you are not legally a person until you are one-year old for greater certainty that there would not be any problems with the child? To me, Mr. Speaker, life begins at conception. To take any step back from that is not logical.

If life begins at conception, as I believe, it follows that this person, or entity that is becoming a person, must enjoy the same rights as I, who have been bom. I believe that the foetus has inalienable rights, in particular the right to be born we all have and the right to security of the person.

To say that the foetus is not a human until a certain time is to condemn ourselves and future generations to arbitrary decisions as to when we are or are not human. Let me explain.
It was not so very long ago, approximately half a century ago, that one madman declared that there were certain races which were superior to others. Then so decreeing he sought to have a final solution for a whole race of people: the Jews.
But he did not stop with the Jews. He went on from there to clean the streets of what he called cripples, homosexuals and the mentally handicapped, people that he and his henchmen determined undesirable. Their solution was simple. It was to kill these people. To hide their heinous crimes they burnt them in the hopes that the bones and ashes would never be found. As I contemplate these clinics and hospitals in which we abort our young, whether it be at four or thirty weeks, I see the remains thrown out like so much garbage. I am moved to
Government Orders
wonder: could not one of these or some of these have helped our society to become a better place?
They say we should abort because a child would be bom into circumstances where they would not be wanted, where they would be subject to physical punishment, where indeed they would be emotionally scarred. I am not unaware of this. I know that children who are not wanted are bom into this world, that they are not cared for, and that they are abused. Even with this in mind I know full well that there are people who have survived these circumstances and risen above them. Should they not have a chance, just as you and I have?
Is there anyone here who had a perfect childhood? Is there anyone who did not have his cuts and bruises and emotional scars and yet we go on as best we can? Abortion is wrong. Abortion is morally wrong. I believe that we were put on this earth because we have a destiny to fulfil. Our destiny, I believe, is to live good lives as best we can and try to help our fellow man, not destroy him.
Women often resort to abortion because they cannot see any other way. There are other ways. We should help them during pregnancy. We should give them the choice to keep or to give their child to couples who want to adopt. We the government should be helping them, not hindering them.
If you asked me where there are any circumstances under which an abortion could be performed, I would say to you yes. I believe that an abortion can be performed when the physical life of the mother is in danger. That means that you will or you want to save the life of the mother. You do not will or want the death of a child. The child's death is incidental to the good that you want to accomplish.
There are those who say: "Well, can't the mother make a choice on her own"? Once again, I am hard pressed to answer. But would you grant the mother the right to kill a child if she no longer wanted the child and the child was three, four, or five years old? The child belongs to her and although the child is outside her, does she not still care for it? Is the child still not her responsibility?
In this debate, Mr. Speaker, you will hear many voices raised in the defence of the rights of women. What we

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
have here are really two conflicting rights: the rights of women and the rights of the unborn. I have tried to straddle the fence. I have tried to find a compromise, but there are some things in life, my colleagues, for which there is no compromise. An abortion is one of them.
I respect those who in this debate will speak about the rights of women. I surely have no quarrel with them, but I have chosen to speak for the unborn because to my way of thinking you cannot satisfy both. I know full well in taking this decision that it will not be politically popular. It is a sans dire that it is women who vote. There are no votes among the unborn.
But this decision is not a political one, nor do I say it is a political one for you, my colleagues. It is not made to garner votes or to try to appease one side or the other. This decision is made because I believe it is the right decision.
In the final analysis whichever way we decide collectively, the fact is I must still live with myself. I would ask you, my colleagues, before you cast your votes to reflect on another issue which is at the other end of the life spectrum. It is a nice sounding name. It is called euthanasia.
If we decide today to kill at the beginning of the life spectrum, I wonder how far we are away from deciding to kill at the other end. In Norway they used to have what they called passive euthanasia, passive mercy killing. Now they have, shall I use the word progressed or regressed to the point where they are using active euthanasia.
Will the day come when we will decide that someone who reaches 100 years should be killed even though he or she is healthy? How long will it be before we lower that age until it is 80 or 70 or 60, all under the guise that this planet cannot support so many people? And, how long will it be before we look at our mentally, emotionally and physically handicapped and say, no, only the strong will survive in our society, you must be sacrificed? I suggest to you that these things will occur in the lifetime of rtiany of the members who are in this House now.
There are those who shy away from the word "murder", but I do not. The word "murder" is defined as an action causing the destruction of human life which is regarded as morally wicked, whether legal or not. Further down it says, it is a terrible slaughter and a destruction of life.
Is there anyone in this House, is there anyone in Canada who will deny that abortion is the destruction of life? Is there anyone in Canada who will deny that the taking of an innocent life is wrong? I base my stand on the fact that life does begin at the moment of conception and life is so precious that it must be defended all the way through the life process.
If we deny the rights of the unborn today we will be denying the rights of all Canadian citizens in one way or another tomorrow. I will have no part of this action. I will vote against Bill C-43 and everything that is in it.
To those of you in this House who say that history will be your judge, I leave you to history. My judge has been around a little bit longer.

Mr. Speaker, it is with heartfelt concern that I rise today to join in the debate on abortion.
At this point in the debate it might seem that every point of view has been covered and that we need not hear more, but I believe it is important for each member to be heard on this issue so that our constituents might know that whatever decision we have come to we have not come to it lightly and that we have taken into consideration all the various points of view presented to us in the last few months.
I believe that life begins at conception. This is one of the biggest problems that I have with Bill C-43. Certainly it implies that life begins at conception since it purports to provide some protection to the foetus from the moment of conception until birth. However, there is precious little protection there, and there is no explicit statement that the life in the foetus is a life like any other life including that of its mother.
This means that the fundamental test, the health of the mother, is not balanced by the other fundamental test, the health of the foetus, when the doctor and mother are making their decisions. This is the core of the abortion debate. It is a debate about rights, the rights of mothers, fathers and unborn children. On the one hand, there are those who believe that the mother has the right to self-determination, to make choices that concern her own body and her future. On the other hand, there are those who believe that the unborn child has a right to life and that this right must be protected.
November 27, 1989

Any bill that would receive my support must recognize explicitly this right of the unborn child. I believe the rights of women and all Canadians to control their own bodies and to shape their own future must be secured. However, just as my rights are limited by the fundamental rights of others, I also believe that a woman's rights over her own body are limited by her unborn child's fundamental right to life. This balancing of rights takes place every day in our society to prevent chaos, to protect life, and to defend the democratic nature of this nation. I believe it must also take place in the case of abortion.
As far as choice is concerned, I believe that choices must be made before conception, not after. For this reason, despite grave misgivings, I am willing to consider abortion in cases of rape or incest as I do not believe that a woman should be forced to carry a child that she has been forced to conceive.
I also believe that abortion can be considered where a mother's life is in real danger. These are examples of the difficult decisions that must be made when rights are balanced for I fully concede that the foetus is never a guilty party.
There are many things about this bill that bother me, not the least of these is the fact that we appear to be approaching the problem from the wrong direction. One of the most serious factors contributing to abortion is what might be called the crisis pregnancy. It can happen at any socio-economic level in society, as we are all well aware. The crisis is defined by each individual woman's own situation.
This bill treats abortion solely in criminal terms, but what we need is much broader access to programs which focus care on people in need and which make raising and having children a primary aim of our society.
There are many programs which could reduce the apparent demand for abortions. I am thinking of some simple things such as better access to psychological counselling and birth control education, of tax laws that do not discriminate against parents who wish to stay home and raise their children, of laws which do not make it difficult for single mothers to get an education and child support; simple things like the need to reverse the trend which discourages adoption by mature couples in
Government Orders
favour of encouraging young women to keep children that they are not ready to cope with.
One of my main reasons for getting into politics was a desire to make things simpler. I am well aware that this bill, Bill C-43, appears to be simple and straightforward. I am very concerned that it is just a simple band-aid on a very complicated social illness and that we are doing almost nothing to solve the basic problem which to my view is that society has begun to accept abortion as a quick fix, not recognizing that the very decision to have an abortion is a fundamental symptom of many problems.
I do not delight in the polarization of this debate. I am well aware that those on both ends of the spectrum present their views in terms of love, care and compassion. I understand fully that no right thinking person takes a decision in favour of abortion lightly.
I will not be one of those to condemn those who have made or who may make decisions with which I disagree. Whether this battle is won or lost, I believe we must continue to speak for and promote the development of resources which can help people grow toward healthy, life giving relationships wherein responsibility for birth control and parenting is shared by both parents. We must encourage schools and employers to support women who are pregnant, not to expel or discriminate against them. We must continue to speak out against and deal with family violence so that children may be raised in safety. We must develop more efficient and fairer means of distributing support for child care. We must continue to support the development of preventive or crisis counselling in the areas of sexuality, pregnancy and family planning. Finally, governments including this government must encourage adoption as an alternative to abortion.
One of my hon. colleagues from the other side indicated a few minutes ago that 60 years ago women were not persons, and today they are. I am very distressed that many of those same persons who received their rights 60 years ago are now denying the rights of the foetus.
This debate is about abortion and how to deal with it in a pluralistic society. In the last few days we have heard many well-intentioned arguments on both sides of the question. I return to my first point: we cannot discuss abortion unless we first acknowledge clearly that life begins at conception and then develop a clear, rational approach to the balancing of rights, an approach which

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
recognizes the foetus as a fully human entity, doing so with compassion and a full understanding of the difficulties that each person faces. I do not support this bill. I cannot imagine supporting it, even in an amended form.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start by saying that this last year of my life has probably been one of the most exciting. I cannot believe, quite frankly, that I am here tonight in the Parliament of Canada. I feel it is the greatest honour of all to serve for your country. At the same time I want to say that the last 24 hours has been very tough for me. I am not a doctor. I am not a lawyer and I feel humbled in addressing this issue.
I have listened for the last year and a half to people on all sides of this issue. I have met them in my constituency office. I have met people in my office on the Hill. I noticed one thing that all parties have in common. All the people I met with were approachable and caring; they had integrity and they were passionate about their views.
That makes the dilemma even more difficult. I realize it is a dilemma that most politicians from all parties are facing, because many of us are finding that our personal beliefs are in conflict with the majority of our constituents, at least as many of our constituents perceive our responsibility to be.
I personally refer to this issue as the Thomas More dilemma. Few of us, and certainly not I, would pretend to have the learning or courage of Thomas More, but I believe after listening and watching people in this Chamber for the last year that they also have and stress the value of morality, honour and integrity.
Today, when we are struggling with an issue like this, that kind of integrity, that kind of trust, is so important. In fact, I think that trust is the central issue in this debate. It is the trust that our constituents have with each one of us. I take that thought with me as I approach this issue of abortion because we have a choice between acting as a representative of our constituents and voting as we perceive the majority would wish us to vote. In my constituency a majority would wish me to vote in favour of this bill or abortion in whatever limited form it would be allowed.
The other option is that we can act as a delegate of the voters and vote for what we consider to be right. If I were to take the first course, then I would apparently gain the trust of the majority and certainly lose the trust of a significant minority who are against abortion, and I use the word apparently advisedly because I do not think anyone would ever trust me if I really gave in and gave up on deeply held convictions, especially one like this.
I want to speak personally for a moment about my convictions because I believe that human life begins at the moment of conception. This is not a religious conviction; all the medical evidence supports this belief. However I am not a member of the pro-life movement. I question their emotive use of the term.
Who, after all, is in favour of death? My belief is a quiet personal belief. It is important that we have strongly worded legislation to protect the unborn. At the same time we must have the political will to put in infrastructure to support women facing the prospect of an unwanted pregnancy. We must discuss this issue with genuine empathy for the plight of pregnant women. They are often lonely, afraid, deserted, poor and particularly stigmatized, so we must be innovative in our solutions to make it easier for women to continue with their pregnancies.
In listening to this debate for the last few days, I do acknowledge the hon. member from British Columbia when she said it was mostly men who were speaking on this issue. I have to refer to two of my colleagues who are women who spoke on this issue last Thursday, my colleague from Western Arctic made the following statement:
My position is one for life. I choose life. I do not belong to the pro-life movement, but I belong to a people who believe that life is sacred and always have under the harshest of circumstances.
I also believe in people who are willing to take the unwanted; I believe in the people who adopt. I am an adopted child. I celebrate my mother and I am the oldest of 15 children. I celebrate my mother because she brought 15 of us into this world, under the harshest of circumstances, with great poverty and difficulty.
She went on to say:
I cannot take the chance of having this legislation pass. I will vote against it. But I can tell you once more, that for my people, children are important, people are important, and life is the most valuable gift you are given.
November 27, 1989

My colleague, the member from Northumberland made a similar statement. She said:
