Because I believe in and try to live in the spiritual, sacred, mystery side of my, in my intellectual weakness I submit to the view that it is probable that the sacredness of life begins at conception. Therefore, I cannot accept abortion at any stage of life from conception onward.
She went on to talk about companion legislation.
What am I going to do? For me the choice is clear. I shall vote against this bill. I may have to answer to the voters as long as I am in politics, but I have to answer to my own conscience for the rest of my life. I let my belief in this issue be known through the last year and a half. For me, governance is to look after the disadvantaged and for me there is nothing more disadvantaged than an unborn child and, in my opinion, this bill does not pass the test.

Mr. Speaker, no subject is more troubling for any reflective person than abortion. No other issue since I arrived here in 1979 has evoked more letters, phone calls and personal visits from concerned constituents and non-constituents on both sides of the issue. It cuts right to the heart of what human beings, religions of all kinds, pluralism, the proper scope of our criminal law and representative democracy are all about.
In the case of members of the present governing party and the Official Opposition, at least our whips will not tell us how our respective party hierarchies want us to vote. If it is true, as indicated, that the Prime Minister intends to force his cabinet colleagues to vote en bloc for Bill C-43,1 trust that the right hon. gentleman will allow them to vote their consciences on various amendments which will be proposed both in committee and at the report and third reading stages of the bill.
Let me say now what I find to be positive and what I find to be unacceptable about Bill C-43. First, the more positive. The bill says that Parliament has sufficient respect for unborn children from conception in that it orders that no such child can be aborted unless a medical doctor "is of the opinion that the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened".
Second, the bill requires that henceforth for legal abortions in Canada only medical doctors can perform
Government Orders
them. One of the consequences of the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Morgentaler is that in terms of federal legislative sanctions, at least, a person performing an abortion need not currently even be a trained medical doctor.
Third, I personally share the presumed view of the drafters of this bill, that the person charged with inducing an illegal abortion should be a doctor, not the woman. I wonder, though, how doctors across Canada can reconcile performing abortions because, a husband or a boyfriend demands that one be performed, with the Hippocratic Oath taken I gather, by every practising physician across Canada. One part of that oath says, and I quote: "I will not give to a woman an instrument to produce abortion".
Fourth, the doctor's opinion that a continuation of the pregnancy would threaten the health of the pregnant person must accord to "generally accepted standards of the medical profession", not his or her own notions about the matter.
Fifth, I believe as a lawyer that this bill is constitutionally unassailable under the Charter of Rights.
What is illegitimate about the bill? First, it can be said to be pro-life in form; it is clearly strongly pro-choice in substance. Second, and closely related, in terms of the world's realities, it appears to me to pay only lip service to the all important issue of balancing the interests, assuming that they can conflict, of perspective mothers and this Parliament's interest in protecting unborn children. I say this as someone who has worked professionally with the provisions of the Criminal Code for many years both as Crown counsel and defence counsel, and who worries that the member for York Centre has probably characterized very well what will result, in practice, across Canada. The member reportedly said at a press conference, after the bill was introduced, and I quote:
-what has been attempted here is really nothing more than to provide a fraudulent cover for abortion. What is being said is, "Ladies play our game, go to the right doctors, give the doctors the right story, and you'll have nothing to worry about".
Mr. Kaplan went on:
That, to my mind, is not the honourable kind of solution that
should be brought forward considering all the various interests and
all the various rights that are at stake here.

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
In other words, there are, unfortunately, probably enough medical doctors practising across Canada today who take a less than literal interpretation of their Hippocratic Oath and who favour abortion on demand, that abortions on demand, legalized by the Morgentaler case, will in most communities continue unabated.
Will a single one of the 60,000 unborn girls or boys who now perish each year in the present legal vacuum, survive if this bill becomes law in its present form? Canadians generally, and my constituents in particular, as I understand their views, want a major reduction in the number of abortions being performed across Canada. That at least was the major conclusion I drew from approximately 5,000 questionnaires received from constituents in the spring of 1988. Fully 2,865 or 60 per cent of my constituents, indicated that they wanted "drastically reduced" the number of abortions. Approximately 2,000 or 40 per cent, indicated in effect that they wanted abortion "made more fully accessible".
May I pay particular tribute to the speech made in this House by the member for Ottawa South which voiced many of my own concerns and views. For example, his quote from Mario Cuomo about the need for society to assume that the right to life does not end at the moment of birth. Proper housing, education and nutrition for all children must be the priority of all of us who profess to be pro-life. Also, that of the member for Welland who spoke earlier tonight.
My 10 minutes is going fast. Let me urge all members of this House who are on the pro-life side of the spectrum not to vote against this bill on second reading. If enough of us private MPs do so in this Chamber, the government's bill, flawed as it is from a pro-life point of view, will die and the status quo, that is, abortion on demand will continue across Canada in all likelihood until the next election and possibly beyond.
The only Canadians who will benefit from that possibility would be the 25 per cent to 35 per cent in all 10 provinces who, opinion polls suggest, favour abortion on demand at all stages of all pregnancies.
In closing, I would urge all colleagues to consider carefully and to vote to send C-43 into a legislative committee where, hopefully, the government majority there will recognize the bill, as is, is more pro-choice than a substantive majority of both Canadians and MP's favour. If enough carefully drawn amendments are
accepted, C-43 could be moved significantly closer to the government stated objective of balance in the interests of society, the protection of unborn children and the interests of some mothers in not continuing a pregnancy in defined situations.
Finally, if such amendments are not accepted, and I put this to my friends on all sides of the House who are pro-life, the majority of us in this House who believe that human life is sacred could then vote against the bill on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak strongly against Bill C-43, an act to recriminalize abortion. I was reluctant to even participate in this debate because I am so angry that it is occurring at all. I, along with my New Democrat colleagues, opposed this bill on its introduction because abortion is a private matter, not for doctors or judges to decide, but for the woman who must live with the outcome of the decision for the rest of her life.
This is not a matter for criminal law. This is not a matter for the 255 male members or 40 female members of this House to decide. It is a matter for the woman involved.
This whole debate and the bill which is at the centre of it is based on a false assumption. That assumption is that controls are necessary, that women are unable or incapable of making this painful decision without some sort of state control. I utterly reject this assumption. Women have always, through time, and in different cultures, made these painful life and death decisions.
There is another assumption implicit in this debate and it is that this debate will somehow bring some resolution to this dilemma which confronts us. This, too, is a false assumption. I doubt that there is a legislative resolution to this question. In a pluralistic society, how can we legislate the solution to abortion?
The question of abortion is a moral question. We all bring our own life's experience, differing religious beliefs and philosophies when considering such a question. We as legislators, acting in a pluralistic society, know there is no legislative resolution to this issue. No law will end abortion. In this instance, I mean political in the crassest sense. It is, as my colleague for Victoria pointed out in last week's debate, a bill designed not to respect women or their decisions, nor in that false polarity, fuelled by
November 27, 1989

this debate, is it a bill to protect life. It is, to be blunt, a bill to protect politicians.
Some speakers in this debate have characterized this bill as a compromise. At the beginning of this debate I rejected that idea. But now I have come to agree. It is a compromise. But once again I mean that in the crassest sense. It is meant for many in this House to compromise their principles. So in this bill we do have a political compromise flowing from political expediency.
For the record I should state that that last sentence was spoken with contempt. I will now turn from speaking about the debate to the broader discussion of the issue.
The issue of abortion challenges us at the very core of our being. Abortion is a statement of failure. At the individual level, this could mean failure of partners accepting responsibility in expressing their sexuality, or failure in contraception, or failure in a relationship.
At the societal level, abortion is also a statement of failure. It is our society, despite rivers of rhetoric, saying that we do not welcome children, we do not treasure children. In the society we live in today, that message is loud and clear. It is stated in child poverty, which our leader so eloquently addressed in his last statement before this House. It is stated in the lack of resources given to child care. It is stated in overcrowded classrooms and the lack of housing where children are welcomed. There are few enough housing units where children are accepted, even fewer where space for children and those who care for them are included in the planning. These are the reasons I say abortion is a statement of failure. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, women have always recognized this.
For women, this issue is not abstract-it is very real. It is a women's issue. It is women's bodies and women's lives being controlled by this legislation, not men's. Women are the ones who ultimately decide this life and death issue. They have done so since time began and in all cultures. They have done so alone, in fear and secretly, often protecting the men in their lives from the enormity of their decision because they were aware that men have little ability to handle life and death decisions unless these decisions are depersonalized such as during war. They will do so no matter what this House does. I suspect that much of the anger surrounding this issue is based in recognition of this fact because ultimately this
Government Orders
issue is about power. Women exercising their power of choice challenges that unstated premise on which our society is based, that men know best, that they are morally superior. If you doubt that assertion, just consider the continuing debate surrounding the ordination of women. I can understand that this challenge is very threatening, especially to those who are reluctant to share power with women. If women cannot be controlled, what will become of us?
Women are not morally deficient. I respect women's rights to choose. As a woman I feel betrayed by this bill. I feel betrayed by some of the formerly pro-choice women of this House. This issue is too important to flip-flop on. I implore all of the formerly pro-choice members of this House to reject political expediency and instead stand in pro-choice solidarity against this bill. Canada has signed the United Nation's Convention on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination Against Women. Paragraph 4 of the Convention calls for signatories such as Canada, to:
Repeal all national penal provisions which constitute
discrimination against women.
This bill before us discriminates against women. It does not control men's sexuality and reproduction; it controls women's sexuality and reproduction. It does not limit men's right to choose whether or not to have children; it limits women's right to choose whether or not to bear a child.
As critic for the New Democratic Party on international development, I am appalled that Canada says one thing abroad and practises another at home. I have become very angiy at the arguments used and abused in this House to justify this bill. Some members whom one once would have called pro-choice are saying now that they will support this bill because it proposes a national standard for abortion, a national standard for access. This is utterly outrageous. This bill does not prevent the harassment of women outside clinics. It does not create community health centres where abortions can be performed. It does not prevent restrictive laws such as the one we are currently seeing in Nova Scotia, nor will it lead to abortion services being made available in Prince Edward Island. The only national standard it sets is one of fear of being charged under the Criminal Code. This bill does not meet international standards and it does not promote a national standard. All it does is hurt women. I would have hoped that some formerly pro-choice cabi-

Government Orders
net ministers would have at least had the integrity to admit that.
In conclusion, I want to say that this is the issue that made me a New Democrat. It is only my party which has had the courage to tackle this issue and determine a party policy. This policy was achieved not without pain. Only the New Democrats gave the issue the priority to work through that pain and come to a position on the issue. Our detractors use this as evidence that we do not individually struggle with this issue, that we blindly and unthinkingly follow party policy. Our party speakers during this debate have made it clear that this is patent nonsense. Each one of us have brought our own life's experience, our religious beliefs and philosophies and come to a common conclusion. We, as New Democrats, respect women. We believe that abortion is a private matter for a woman and her conscience. We are confident that each woman is capable of making the right choice.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to speak on Bill C-43, which deals with a matter that has caused a great deal of controversy and debate from coast to coast in this nation.
When we choose to enter public life, all politicians know that at times they will be faced with tough decisions. The subject of abortion is, without a doubt, one of these occasions. For example, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources even considered quitting politics rather than support a liberal new abortion bill. This vividly illustrates the agonizing nature of reaching a decision on what is very clearly a moral, ethical and personal matter.
I have never been one to shy away from making my views public on difficult policy matters, and the same is true for the abortion issue. I have made my personal position crystal clear ever since I was elected to the House of Commons 17 years ago. I am against abortion on demand. However, I feel the life of the mother is all important and should be given top priority.
I also feel that an abortion should be made available in cases of rape and incest. When I say rape, I mean especially the rape of a minor. Not allowing abortions in these instances is tantamount to condoning these atrocious acts.
At present, we have no abortion legislation in place. This has put the federal government in a no-win situation. An abortion can now be performed at the end of the ninth month, and this is frightening. I believe at least 70 per cent of the people in Canada agree that an abortion should be available under certain circumstances. In all probability, under the circumstances I mentioned earlier.
It is my feeling that the legislation presently before this House presents a reasonable solution to the complex matter of abortion. While I am somewhat concerned that the legislation involves an amendment to the Criminal Code, I realize this is the only way the federal government can ensure a national approach to the issue of access to abortion. Under the proposed legislation, any woman seeking an abortion will have to consult a medical practitioner. If the medical practitioner feels the pregnancy would threaten the life or health of the woman, then an abortion can be performed.
Pro-life supporters have stated that the legislation is not strong enough. However, they should note that with the new legislation, a woman or her doctor can receive a maximum penalty of up to two years in jail if they breach the provisions of the law.
At this point, I would like to stress that the legislation does not provide for abortion on demand. The medical practitioner is required to determine, in accordance with generally accepted standards of the medical profession, whether there are health reasons to justify an abortion. According to these standards, abortions are rarely conducted after the foetus becomes viable, unless there are compelling foetal or maternal complications.
A sad reality is that at present a woman may feel that no alternative to an abortion exists due to her economic or social situation. It is imperative that we do whatever we can to help these individuals avoid the problem in the first place and to provide all the possible alternatives to abortion in cases where unplanned pregnancies have occurred. For this reason, I was heartened by the

November 27, 1989

measures which the Minister of National Health and Welfare has planned to put in place to reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies in this country. These include increased research into family planning, including contraception, continued funding of planned parenthood and measures to encourage more pregnant women to consider adoption in place of abortion.
It is my sincere hope that these measures will enable us to deal with the startling facts of teenage abortion which have recently come to my attention. In a recent issue of one of the Ottawa newspapers, for example, it stated that of the 800 girls aged 15 to 19 who became pregnant in Ottawa-Carleton in 1987, 62 per cent had abortions. Across Ontario, in the same year, 46.9 per cent of the estimated 12,800 pregnant girls in that age group had abortions. Clearly, this is an unacceptable situation.
In preparing the legislation before us, the justice minister had to keep in mind the issue of the Charter of Rights. If the government presented legislation that was too restrictive, then the Supreme Court could strike it down as it did in the Morgentaler decision. In this decision, Chief Justice Dickson wrote:
Forcing a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to
term is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus an
infringement of the security of the person.
I am confident that Bill C-43 has responded to these concerns.
As the justice minister stated in this House, we are not asking the people of Canada to change their opinion on what they think is right. Each and every Canadian is entitled to his or her own value judgment on this very moral issue. We are merely asking Canadians to respect the views of others and to respect this new law.
Canadians will never be unanimous about what abortion laws should be passed, but it is clear that some federal legislation must be passed. If the bill is defeated, we will be right back to square one with abortions available right up to the ninth month. Clearly, this is unacceptable to the majority of Canadians.
This is a tough decision, but governments are elected to make tough decisions. The federal government has never backed away from its responsibilities and has acted to bring in a bill that strikes a moderate and balanced approach to the veiy sensitive abortion issue. For this
Government Orders
reason, Bill C-43 should receive the support of this House.
I am hoping, and I think a great many other members share that hope that certain amendments may be tabled before committee and at report stage. It would then be more acceptable to some of those who have misgivings about it in its present state.
I might point out that down through the years, since I have been a member of Parliament, I have had many delegations coming to my office, primarily in Ottawa but also in my constituency office, and I will concede that the great majority of those were groups of pro-life people who were worried about the previous legislation even before it was struck down.
It is rather unusual that, in the last number of months, I had requests from members of the pro-choice group which is the first time I had ever had that in all my years here. I know we have a very difficult situation before us and I can assure you that a great many of us are worried considerably about it. As I stated, I have made my position clear not just in the last few months but down through the years since I have had the privilege of being a member of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and privilege to contribute to the deliberations of the House of Commons this evening on this very emotional topic. I have listened to many of the speeches during this debate and have read those that I did not hear.
Before I begin my remarks, it is important to remember that we are speaking tonight on second reading debate. If the bill passes second reading, otherwise known as approval in principle, it will go to committee for discussion and attempts at amendment. I cannot support it. I will now explain why.
On November 7 this year, the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby urged us to "speak to our mothers; speak to our sisters; speak to our daughters; speak to our wives". I have done so. I have gone further. I have spoken to my constituents. I have spoken to Canadians all across the country. My mother, my wife, my daughter, the majority of women on my riding executive, the overwhelming majority of people, both female and male with whom I have spoken and the vast majority of those who have written to me, have said no to abortion on demand. The question is not whether we should have

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
restrictions but, rather, the nature of the restrictions that we should have.
Of course, there are some of the opposite view. In today's mail I received a letter from a constituent. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, I quote:
No man has the right to tell me to carry what amounts to little more
than a parasite in my body. A foetus lives off the woman cartying it.
This so-called human life can cause diabetes, high blood pressure, let
alone discomfort, nausea and pain.
I cannot and will not subscribe to this view of the unborn being akin to a tapeworm. If this person's own mother thought as she does, perhaps she would not be alive today to write to me.
I am opposed to this bill. I believe it should be defeated tomorrow on the vote for second reading and the issue sent back for further consideration by this government. Why? This bill is the spawn of the entirely unsavoury union of hypocrisy and cowardice. With origins such as this, it must be condemned to the dustbin. Let us examine the bill.
It says, "Every person who induces an abortion". What does that mean? What is so objectionable? After all, there is no law prohibiting appendectomies or tonsillectomies. Why a law to prevent abortion? Is it not just a medical procedure like any other? Well, logic would suggest that we look to the bill for definition of what we are talking about. There is no definition. This is cowardice, this failure to deal squarely with the fundamental issue of abortion. If there is no definition, how can we possibly know what the bill is pretending to outlaw? In the absence of a definition, look to the dictionary. The shorter Oxford English Dictionary, based on historical principles, third edition, being the abridged version of the massive Oxford English Dictionary, says about abortion that it is "the procuring of premature delivery so as to destroy offspring". Offspring is defined by the dictionary as "a person's child or children". That is what abortion is. The destruction of human life, nothing less.
This bill pretends to ban the procuring of premature delivery for the purpose of destroying one's child. Does it really do so? Here begins the hypocrisy. The destruction of a human being is permitted if the medical practitioner, and that is any medical practitioner, and only one, such
as Dr. Morgentaler, is of the opinion that: "The health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened'*. "Likely to be threatened". Not "will be threatened". Just a mere possibility. It is totally subjective and completely open-ended.
It is interesting to note that notwithstanding the fact that the word "abortion" is not defined in the legislation, the word "health" is defined. Surely, this is further hypocrisy. This wide-open definition with virtually no restrictions is really nothing more than abortion on demand under the guise of what some misguided individuals believe is an implicit recognition of the humanity of the foetus.
The Supreme Court of Canada unanimously in the Daigle case has told us and all Canadians that the foetus has absolutely no rights in Canadian law whatsoever. You only get rights once you are bom alive. But it went further. It said that if Canadians wish the foetus to have rights, then these rights must be explicitly, not implicitly, spelled out in legislation by the House of Commons.
I was speaking of hypocrisy. I will mention two situations only, due to time constraints, and let you be the judge as to whether there is hypocrisy or not.
First, on May 2, 1980, a member of this House of Commons proposed a private member's bill concerning an act to amend the Criminal Code, Bill C-293. It proposed that the procuring of a miscarriage, as abortion was then known, would be permissible only if the continuation of the pregnancy would be likely to actually, physically or mentally, endanger the life of the pregnant woman. This same member now supports Bill C-43, the abortion-on-demand bill. Who is this member? It is the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Simcoe.
Second, the Prime Minister has said he personally opposes abortion, but he will not say why. I know why. It is because he knows that abortion is the destruction of human life. If this is not why, then I challenge him to refute me tomorrow in his speech and tell us all why he personally opposes abortion.
He has said this about life:
November 27, 1989

II is wrong to take life. I can think of no circumstances except selfdefence to justify it-I will resist with all my strength, all of my life, any
action that would diminish that reality and would lessen value.
Those are noble words, applicable in his mind to convicted murderers but apparently not to unborn human beings. This is a man who promised a free vote and yet has forced his ministers to choose between loyalty and conscience only to have them demonstrate apparently that loyalty overrides conscience. This is a man who is so weak of will on this issue, indistinguishable in principle from the issue of life he so vigorously defended in the capital punishment debate, that he follows rather than leads. Not only does he not have the courage of his convictions, but he insists that his ministers abandon theirs.
This bill, being a concoction of one part hypocrisy and one part cowardice, is a drink designed to be distasteful to all. It cannot in my view be amended without direct explicit recognition of the humanity of the unborn child, something which the rules of this House will not in my opinion permit by way of amendment.
It must be rejected with the admonition to the government to return with legislation which does three things: explicitly establishes the humanity of the unborn human being, protects the unborn human being from conception and is coupled with companion legislation which, as my colleague the hon. member for Northumberland has said, supports pregnant women and their children and deals with the underlying causes of abortion in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by saying that it is very difficult to add anything of real substance to this debate on the second reading of Bill C-43 respecting abortion in Canada.
I had the honour to precede you very briefly in the chair, Mr. Speaker, at your request. I was very grateful that I had that opportunity because it enabled me to listen to speeches from members on all sides of the House. In the short span of time that I sat in the chair, I heard a defence of what might be called the pro-life stand and a staunch defence of what might be called the pro-choice stand.
While I have my own views on abortion and the need for a law with respect to abortion, I want to say very clearly and add to the record that I think all of us have to respect those who support either view. There is no right inherent in any of us to condemn those who approach the abortion issue from a pro-life standpoint or from a pro-choice standpoint. It is only with an understanding of all the views that pertain to the issue of abortion in
Government Orders
Canada that we can come to any national reconciliation on the issue.
In that respect, I want to point out that I understand that there is no compromising on the issue of abortion. I understand that many regard it as the killing of an unborn child, while others regard the act of abortion as saving and protecting the woman whose rights must be honoured. It is difficult to compromise on those two positions.
What we have to do is achieve some kind of balance of rights because we are, after all, legislators. We are here to legislate in the interests of all the people of Canada. To the extent that we can effectively legislate and create some reconciliation among all Canadians on the issue, that is our challenge. Our challenge is not, in my opinion, to stand here and provide support for our own particular view, or to represent any particular point of view, but rather to achieve some kind of resolution of this problem.
In that connection, let me say very quickly that I believe there has to be a law on abortion. I think that that is in the interest of all Canadians. I respect the rights of women. I understand the difficulties faced by pregnant women who want their pregnancy terminated. But I think at this point in our history it is in the interest of all Canadians to have a law on abortion.
There may come a time in the future when we will not need a law on abortion, when we have the social instruments that will preclude unwanted pregnancies or take care of unwanted pregnancies when they do occur so that we can avoid this issue of abortion. But in the meantime we have to recognize the void that exists in the law of Canada. If we can possibly remedy and fill that void, then that is or obligation. That is why I want to spend my time reviewing the law.
We had for many years in Canada complete prohibition against abortion. It was contrary to the Criminal Code. Then we allowed, by virtue of Criminal Code provisions, abortions to be performed under certain circumstances.
We cannot neglect and avoid the fact that this House of Commons, this Parliament of Canada, with the consent and concurrence of the provinces, enacted a Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We gave to the courts of Canada and to the Supreme Court of Canada the right to interpret that Charter, and the Supreme Court did so. It exercised the mandate to determine what the rights were under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It said that the existing abortion law, the law restricting abortion, providing for hospital committees to approve abortions, was not valid.

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
We have to recognize that that was the right of the Supreme Court of Canada to make that decision. We have to answer the question, what are we going to do about it to give it the exercise of that right in the Charter.
I have heard members say that we cannot approve the law as enacted by Bill C-43, that it does not go far enough, that it does not protect the foetus, that it does not recognize that life begins at conception, or any of the positions taken by people who espouse a pro-life point of view. But you have to recognize what the Parliament of Canada is permitted to do under the law. Very few of those members who take that position referred to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and recognize that we must amend the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms if we are to provide rights to the unborn. It is a constitutional issue.
The member from Scarborough talked about a law that defined the rights of a foetus. We cannot enact that law in Parliament. It has to be by way of amendment to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We can only do what the law permits the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada to do, that is to enact a law that does not violate the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada. If I had the opportunity to enact a law, I would do so.
I presented Bill C-203 to the House of Commons in the first session of the thirty-fourth Parliament. It indicates, I believe, the strongest law that can be enacted with respect to abortion, but I do not think that the government and many lawyers will accept the fact that that law would pass the test of the Supreme Court of Canada.
My point is simply this. In Bill C-43 now before the House of Commons we have been presented with a law that restricts abortion in Canada. It may not restrict abortion to the extent that many members want, but I cannot accept that as a reason to vote against the bill. I can understand that those who espouse a pro-choice position will vote against that bill. They believe that a woman should have a right to an abortion if that is her decision with respect to a particular pregnancy. I understand that they would vote against the bill, but I do not understand a person who is interested in protecting life voting against Bill C-43 at second reading. I do not understand that position. If this bill is defeated in this House of Commons, there will be in Canada no law on abortion and no real possibility of enacting a law. Is that the position that members want?
Yes!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
I have said very clearly that I believe that Canadians want and require a law on abortion. It is not ah overwhelming majority but it is the consensus of opinion in Canada.
Why do I think that? Because I do not think most Canadians desire and want what is happening in Halifax, Nova Scotia at the Morgentaler clinic. I do not think that Canadians want abortion reduced to the level of walking in off the street and having it over and done with and forget about the consequences.
I believe that Canadians want consideration. They want the sanctity of life protected by a law. Whether or not this should mean that women will be denied abortions in reasonable circumstances is another matter. I believe that at this stage in our history the law while restrictive must conform to the Supreme Court of Canada decision. We really do not have that choice without a constitutional amendment.
My purpose is simply to remind members of the state of the law, to recognize what the House of Commons, the Parliament of Canada, can do and cannot do with respect to abortion.
I believe Bill C-43 represents a measure that the Parliament of Canada can take, not a measure that will satisfy those who believe that life begins at conception and under no or very, very extremely limited circumstances can a pregnancy be terminated. I recognize their position, but it is not one that we can implement in this House of Commons today.
The expression comes to mind like half a loaf is better than none at all. I know it is considered to be unsatisfactory. I think the fact that the bill is opposed by both pro-life advocates and pro-choice advocates indicates that it does effect some kind of balancing of rights. I
November 27, 1989

think all we can do at this stage of our history is balance rights.
We can and we will have the opportunity to add amendments to the bill. I think that abortion should be performed in an accredited hospital. I do not think it should be left to the parties to decide where an abortion can be performed.
As far as the bill having no real effect, that is not true. It would be very unwise for a medical practitioner in Canada if this bill is enacted to perform an abortion without having objective criteria to adjudicate whether or not health was affected. I think a medical practitioner would be very unwise to not have a second opinion on an abortion. I say that to the people who advocate that pro-choice view. That is something that they should consider. It is possible for a woman to be prosecuted under this provision. I do not think that we should hide behind the fact that a woman may not be prosecuted because under the existing law pregnant women were specifically mentioned and they are not under this bill.
I think we should look at this provision realistically. It does restrict abortion. Do not make any mistake about that. There is not a doctor in Canada who will rush in and perform an abortion just on his own say so that the health of the mother is in jeopardy. They will get second opinions. They will go through processes. It is going to take time and effort to get an abortion. Those people who regard the provisions as meaningless are mistaken in my opinion.
I am not supporting in any way, shape or form the pro-choice group. I want to point that out. The bill does restrict abortion. It restricts it in a way that is valid under the Supreme Court of Canada decision. It is all the Parliament of Canada can do at this stage in history. I would urge members to support the bill and propose amendments at the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate this evening on the crucial matter of abortion facing not only this Parliament but, indeed, this country. It is, of course, an extremely delicate and complex subject matter which has aroused and will continue to arouse the passions of Canadians from coast to coast and lead them to explore this most fundamental dilemma.
Government Orders
In any discussion on abortion several parameters need to be drawn. First, most Canadians would acknowledge that this issue is not an easy one, for such fundamental questions of life and death strike at the very foundation of our society.
Second, the issue is a multi-faceted one which involves the social, moral, philosophical and religious forces of the day, as well as pits the rights and the choice of individual women against the collective rights of a society and, indeed, the rights of the unborn.
Thus, because the equation is a multi-dimensional one, the challenge becomes one of distinguishing the order of importance among the competing variables. Which is the most important variable? Which is of paramount priority?
Third, there are few issues like abortion which create the polarized extremes which seem to colour this particular debate. Consequently, the traditional Canadian way of compromise or building bridges between these two polarized shores is made extremely difficult, if not nearly impossible.
Under these three parameters any discussion will prove difficult and challenging to say the least. But, at the same time, it requires an extra investment on our part as a Parliament and as a society to ensure that our response to the issue rises in honesty and in clarity to the occasion.
I had the opportunity during the previous Parliament, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, back in July of 1988 to voice my thoughts on the question of abortion. Therefore, I will try not to repeat the arguments that I made some years ago, but yet, in the 10 minutes allotted to me this evening, I will take the opportunity to specifically focus on the government's proposed abortion legislation and thereby share with my constituents and my colleagues my views and feelings about the quality of the current legislative response to this emotional issue.
In the last Parliament when we were asked to choose among a multitude of motions I supported the one motion which was considered to be the pro-life option. I did so with conviction and deep belief and without any regrets or apologies. I did express, however, my deep reservations with three specific exceptions which I simply was not prepared to overlook, namely, where an abortion was performed in a case where the life of the mother was seriously endangered; where the pregnancy was the

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
result of rape; and where the pregnancy was the result of incest.
I was not able under those three conditions to carry through with simply the one view that the pro-life option was not prepared to take into consideration the sense of compassion and fairness. That was my position then and that remains my position today.
Consequently, I am not pleased with the proposed legislative response by this government today. I believe the bill is a poor, inadequate attempt at addressing and accounting for the many delicate issues that define the abortion discussion and the abortion debate. I, therefore, will not and cannot support this bill at second reading under any circumstances.
Let me illustrate briefly why I will vote against this legislative measure. First, for me, this proposed law as written is paramount to abortion on demand. The proposed law would make it very easy and very open-ended for the vast majority of women in Canada to obtain and secure an abortion. It is open-ended for any health reason which is loosely defined as including physical, mental and/or psychological factors. It is open-ended for any medical practitioner to approve the abortion. It is open-ended for ending a pregnancy at any stage of a woman's pregnancy. Really, is there a major difference between this bad law and no law at all?
Second, there is absolutely no reference, no effort in defining the rights of the foetus, the rights of the unborn. There is no attempt to define at what stage in the pregnancy that right, that life becomes paramount.
What about the past Supreme Court decision which requested and indeed challenged Parliament and parliamentarians to toil with this issue in order to provide guidance and leadership to both the country and our courts? Was this not to be a central premise in this current debate? Do we think that as a Parliament by avoiding the issue it will go away by itself? I do not believe it will. I believe with a deep sense of commitment that the majority of Canadians feel the same way. They would have in fact greater respect for us and this place as an institution if they believed and sensed that we really toiled over this emotional dilemma.
Third, with regard to women who do not wish to continue with their pregnancies, how does this proposed legislative package help to offer an alternative other than abortion? Where is the incentive, the resources and the support to encourage the birth alternative? Does an unwanted, unwarranted pregnancy have to mean an unwanted baby? Clearly, it should not and does not. Therefore if we wish, as a government, as a Parliament, to encourage women that they can and should give life to their unborn without having to jeopardize their own lives, then we must commit to effective counselling, for instance, to rebuild a woman's self-esteem and self confidence. We must provide nurturing and homes for women whose families may not be willing to accept an unwanted pregnancy.
We must provide medical assistance to meet those sudden physical and medical needs that may legitimately arise. We must provide career and educational programs to allow those women to resume their career or academic studies. We must provide necessary financial assistance for the expenses inherent in that pregnancy. This bill, however, does not even begin to discuss any kind or any type of support mechanism whatsoever. It is bankrupt of any commitment or compassion toward those women in severe difficulty.
Fourth, why is there no discussion, no reform of our adoption procedures as a possible answer and option to the unwanted child as an answer and a bridge of understanding to the growing number of childless Canadian couples who would dearly love to experience the special gift of parenthood? Why is the bill silent on these concerns when couples presently cannot find children to adopt in this country? If you are the chosen and fortunate few, then the process takes years, not months and clearly not weeks.
Alternatively, if these couples look for parenthood opportunities abroad, they will not only find a flourishing expensive business, but a very complicated bureaucratic process be it overseas or be it in this country.
Are we to have no answers at all? Unfortunately, Bill C-43 is silent on many issues. Yes, these questions are difficult. Yes, these questions are challenging. But, by the same token, it is far too easy for us as a Parliament and for the government to hide from them. That is precisely what this bill does. It runs away from making the necessary difficult decisions. Instead, it attempts to please superficially the two ends of the current debate.
November 27, 1989

For the pro-life element, this bill in the very first sentence of the very first paragraph makes abortion an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment.
Yet, in the very next breath, at the very end of that first line in the first paragraph for the pro-choice element the bill basically says: "Don't you worry, because if you get approval of any medical practitioner on any health reason, then abortion is legitimate and not an offence." I cannot, and I refuse, to support that type of cheap rationale.
Moreover, I cannot accept the challenge or the arguments of those who say: "Well, I don't like the bill at all, but I will support it at second reading. Let it get into committee and then we have a chance of amending the bill to our liking". That kind of rationale has two faults. First, it fails to recognize that Bill C-43 is bad legislation, that it is a fatally flawed document that does not merit that compromise. It is, for me, far better to make a strong unequivocal statement that Parliament and Canadians deserve better, that the government ought to bring back a proposed piece of legislation that is more worthy, more responsible to the challenges that confront us as a Parliament.
Second, the government has made it abundantly clear that it will not tolerate any loosening of the woman's free choice to choose. When this overriding point of view is complemented with the parliamentary committee process that does not permit amendments outside the purview of the bill, then what is the point of this charade at second reading? Is it to prove to the government that it was able to get the bill to second reading? Is it to delay the ultimate showdown to third reading? If it is, how better off are we going to be as a country if, after a lengthy process at committee stage, the amendments for either the pro-choice or pro-life elements are refused and the resulting shift in votes assures defeat at third reading? How would we have advanced the cause for a mature and rational law which would govern abortion and which would define the rights of the unborn?
In conclusion, both the issue and Canadians deserve better. Let us involve Canadians in a process where, in the end, the process will yield positive results, tangible results, and not a process that risks producing a
Government Orders
stalemate which would only further aggravate and frustrate the respective passions intensively felt on this issue.
I will vote against this bill at second reading. I truly hope a majority of my colleagues will be joining me.

Mr. Speaker, as I stand here I wonder why it is that I am standing here speaking on a bill that concerns women. When I watched in the last Parliament the last debate on the abortion issue, what I saw was a number of middle-aged men once again trying to tell women how they should arrange their lives. At that time, as I sat in my home in the comfort of my living-room watching the television, I wondered why it was that a male-dominated Parliament should be once again trying to control or continue to control a significant part of Canada's population.
When is the male population that I am a part of going to realize that women are capable of managing their own affairs without interference from us, the men of Canada? Life, death and all of the terms and times in between are of concern to me. But when I look at Bill C-43, it does nothing to accomplish what must be accomplished and what already has been accomplished by the Supreme Court of Canada in its recent decisions. It struck down the criminalization of abortion in Canada. In the period of time since then, women have once again proven to all in the world, and particularly all in Canada, that they are very capable of arranging and controlling their lives. There has not been a massive increase in abortions within Canada. There has not been what so many of those against choice for women have said will happen. I repeat that women have proven once again that they are very capable of managing their own lives.
In trying to grapple with the very issue that is before us and has been brought once again before Parliament, even though it was already dealt with through Bill C-43, I had to look for help from those who would be affected by the legislation. One of the people I looked to was one of my constituents who wrote to me. I would like to read to you today what she said to me: "I am one of your pro-choice constituents and I am also definitely one of your pro-life constituents. No dichotomy exists in being pro-life and pro-choice. I have two children and support any woman's right to bear children. However, I also support any woman's right not to bear children. Women will always have the final say on abortion. No legislature or Supreme Court justice can change that, all they can

Government Orders
do is make it illegal or difficult to obtain. All that politicians or members of the judiciary can do is force women, mainly poor women, to suffer the indignities of hurdling barriers designed solely to harass them. Access to reproductive health care for a woman should not depend on geography or a bank account."
If we analyze what this constituent has been telling me and I pass on to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the people of Canada that it appears that what is in fact going to happen through Bill C-43, and through any legislation that criminalizes the termination of an unwanted pregnancy, will force more and more people, more and more women, poor women, into the back streets for their abortions, with the problems that we have seen so often in those areas.
I deeply respect and value all life on our fragile planet, but denying women access to safe therapeutic abortions will not in any way enhance our communities' respect for human life. Desperate women will seek illegal abortions at the hands of back street abortionists, or use methods themselves which endanger their own lives.
Under Italy's harsh anti-abortion laws, repealed in 1978, estimates placed the annual number of illegal abortions as high as 800,000 per year with 2,000 women dying annually of complications.
Limiting access to abortion will not reduce the number of abortions in Canada, but will cause a significant increase in maternal mortality and injury. This surely constitutes disregard and not respect for human life.
I must also point out that we on this side of the House have never advocated abortion as an alternative to contraception. The decision to have an abortion is an agonizing one for any woman, yet it is ultimately her own choice determined by the dictates of her own conscience and in consultation with her physician. It cannot be a choice determined by the legislators.
I certainly acknowledge the complexities and sensitivity of this issue. I also recognize the importance of reducing the number of abortions in Canada. This can be accomplished by improving the availability of contraceptive information and materials, ensuring better sex
education programs, and providing increased funding for birth control research and family planning programs. This position was taken as long ago as 1971 by the Canadian Medical Association and supported by many other well respected organizations and individuals in Canada, including the United Church of Canada.
In supporting childbirth by choice, I am supporting the principle of freedom of choice in planning one's family. This principle was recognized by the International Conference on Population and Development and sponsored by the United Nations Fund for Population Activities. I fully support this principle that they have enunciated, and believe that it is a responsibility of government to provide alternatives to abortion, such as counselling, prenatal care, child care and adoption assistance. Funding these types of services, rather than restricting access to abortion, will do more to help decrease the number of abortions than will a return to criminalization.
I cannot support this bill because of that.

Mr. Speaker, it is both my pleasure and duty to participate in this most important debate on abortion, and I welcome the opportunity to do so tonight. It is a subject which has provoked incredibly intense feelings on both sides, and has tortured the heart and soul of millions of people across this country. The argument has been one in which emotion has often transcended reason.
That having been said, it is incumbent upon us as members of Parliament to deal with this most sensitive of issues. We must fulfill our responsibilities as legislators. We must provide leadership and direction, and we must formulate a law which is moral and just.
During the year which has passed since I was elected to represent the riding of Egmont, I have received hundreds of letters and visits from constituents on this issue of abortion. It has been a great comfort to me that the vast majority of those who took the time and trouble to write and speak to me share my views on this matter.
I consider the question of abortion to be one of public as well as private morality. It is a question which involves the sanctity of human life and the civil rights of all
November 27, 1989

human beings. It is a question the answer to which provides a measure of our country as a civilized country.
In introducing Bill C-43, the government took the simplest course available to it, other than doing nothing. It declared that abortion is a matter between a woman and her doctor, but with penalties for abuses of the law. Symbolically, it makes abortion illegal. Effectively, it provides abortion on demand. There is no protection for the unborn child.
Who is responsible for the protection of life in our society? Upon whom does the onus lie to protect all members of that society? Who, if not the state? I consider this bill an abdication of that responsibility. The youngest, the most innocent, the most defenceless members of our society have been abandoned. Our laws are a reflection of our morality. How sad it is today that we are being asked to support legislation which legitimizes the killing of the unborn. A law which permits the killing of human beings is uncivilized and thus unacceptable.
The Minister of Health and Welfare in his remarks to the House said: "We have been elected by Canadians to choose the course which best balances the rights of everyone concerned."
I contend that every one concerned has not been considered in this bill. One group has been omitted, left unprotected. The unborn have been left to the mercy of their mothers and their doctors. They have been given the authority to pronounce the death sentence on unborn children. It is an appalling situation.
My colleague from Leeds-Grenville, in one of the coherent and reasoned speeches of this debate, referred to that kind of situation as an extension of our throwaway society. When something is inconvenient, get rid of it. He asked, is it moral for the strong to destroy the weak? Remember that two people go into a Morgentaler clinic but only one comes out.
Our society generally embraces and upholds the sacredness of life. We resist the threat to life posed by the world's nuclear capabilities. We resist the threat to life generated by racial strife and by poverty. We in this country have resisted capital punishment. I believe that we have developed a consistent life ethic in our nation.
Government Orders
We pride ourselves in that. We consider ourselves the most civilized of societies.
Any society that calls itself civilized will have as its highest value the preservation of human life. It logically follows that legislators in such a society will have as then-highest priority laws which serve to protect that human life from its beginning to its end.
Medical technology has proven beyond any doubt that life begins at conception. Where else could it begin? Given this fact, I cannot accept that from the moment of conception until some optional time during the pregnancy, we are prepared to give a woman and her doctor the legal right to arbitrarily terminate that life. We cannot say that terminating a life is okay up to a point, but from that point onward it is a criminal offence. I contend that there is a serious flaw in the logic of this process, a flaw which is embedded in Bill C-43. It also makes one wonder what the future holds for the aged, and for the physically and mentally handicapped.
An American writer, Shelley Douglas, raised an interesting point. She states: "We have been so busy arguing over the right to choose that we have lost sight of whether the choice itself is a good choice for people to have to make". Much of the discussion now is not on whether abortion is right or wrong, but rather on the woman's right to choose. Abortion is now cast as a struggle of power, domination and control. Mercy and compassion are disappearing. The idea of abortion as a moral failure is lost on many people. For some, abortion has become a convenience, an acceptable form of birth control.
This debate has illustrated the dilemma in which we find ourselves. The rights of women are being pitted against the lives of the unborn. Let us look at some figures. Each year in Canada approximately 65,000 unborn children are killed. In the United States since the Wade vs. Roe decision in 1973, over 20 million Americans have lost their lives without ever having seen the light of day. No atrocity of history can match these figures.
The violence which is abortion is a violence against the unborn and a violence against women. The very heart of this position is an understanding that women, men and children, including the unborn are equal.
American psychologist, Sidney Callahan states: "It is my personal conviction that all human beings are of equal intrinsic moral worth; that no human being is

Government Orders
morally inferior to another". This is also a basic tenet of our liberal democratic society.
From this moral premise it follows that those persons in a society endowed with power, ability and goods have moral obligations to protect and aid those who are in need, those who are vulnerable, and those who are dependent upon others.
The unborn child, being a dependent human being, relies on others in the human community. These others have a moral obligation to its protection and nurture. The woman who alone has the power to sustain life in her womb has a corresponding obligation to protect and nurture it. Our most fundamental right is the right to life, the right not to be killed. This intrinsic right to life is more basic than the right to self-determination or liberty. In fact, it is the right upon which all others depend.
This, I believe to be the bottom line in this entire debate. Abortions which serve social ends or are used for contraception or family planning negate the basic principle of the moral equality of all human beings. Therefore, if the basic issue of this debate is reduced to the mother's right to choose versus the child's right to life, there is no question, absolutely no question, the unborn child's right to life must prevail.
While being unequivocally opposed to abortion, I realize that being just anti-abortion does not make one fully pro-life. A new abortion law which would give full protection to the unborn should not stand by itself. It must be supported by policies and programs which would address the social and economic conditions that contribute to abortion.
In a full pro-life program, a thorough presentation of abortion alternatives must be presented. Abortion procedures, adoption procedures and incentives must be reconstructed to better serve the infant, the mother and the receiving family. For women the question becomes not only what is the national law, but in fact what is the legislation in each province.
There are already regions in this country where women do not have access to medical help in situations such as this. This will only be making it more difficult because not only do you have the moral question but you have the legal parameters which make many people afraid of getting involved with these situations.
Second, the administration of the criminal law generally speaking falls to the provincial government. The definition of what action should be taken and the definition of who should be prosecuted will end up falling in the Attorney General's office. Thus the two most important components of this piece of legislation, the definition of health which follows from the administration of health and the definition of an illegal activity, in fact fall within the parameters of the provincial governments.
For those reasons, instead of presenting us with a most progressive approach to a difficult problem, the government has in fact walked away from it entirely. It disappoints me greatly that we are going to be left with a criminal definition and no other suggestions.
Also, though the Minister of Health has intervened very briefly in this debate to indicate there will be new family legislation, I join my many colleagues to say that one of the sad things in this country is that once people are bom into it, in many circumstances, whether we are talking about reserves in northern Manitoba or low income families in downtown Winnipeg or elsewhere in this country, the plight of children weighs heavily upon all of us.
Although the Canadian government supports this universal declaration on the rights of children that is being discussed in the United Nations, in reality when it
November 27, 1989

comes to showing Canadians that their children will be looked after, that there will be nourishment, that there will be education, that there will be appropriate laws, that there will be supports for them, the Canadian government is totally absent.
In all particular efforts, whether we are talking about dealing with family law or family support systems for children the Criminal Code, this government has walked away from its responsibilities. In that respect the particular proposal to criminalize abortion should be rejected and the House of Commons should give every indication to the women of this country that as they make these difficult decisions, those are decisions that they make themselves, those are not decisions that we are going to impose upon them, that we respect their freedom and we respect their independence.

Mr. Speaker, I am speaking on this bill because this piece of legislation upsets me. I would much rather have spoken on a bill that talked about life, the right to life, this ultimate right which precedes all others. This bill deals with existence and non-existence, and for those like me who believe that life begins at conception, this bill is a matter of life and death.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, every one of us pursues freedom, all freedoms, freedom of expression, freedom to choose what we please, freedom to live our life as we see fit. But this pursuit of freedom should never lead us to refuse life and to make a judgement against life. I believe that if we took such a course, we would be mistaken.
The bill which the government has presented to us is an abdication of its responsibility to govern, to give Canadians direction, some clear indication, and I believe it also has a responsibility to protect life. As it is now written, this bill is an open door to abortion, it is abortion on demand, birth control via abortion. For me, this approach is completely unacceptable. I also find it unacceptable for this government to present us with such a vague and open bill that it will lead both supporters of the right to abortion and supporters of the right to life to vote against it for completely opposite reasons. Should
Government Orders
that happen, which seems quite likely, we would find ourselves with no law to protect and guarantee the foetus' right to life.
When he presented this bill to the House, the Minister of Justice told us that it was a compromise-the only compromise which the government could put forward. I would have hoped that if there had to be compromise, the government would have compromised on the side of life. I am very disappointed with this option which the government has chosen and also with the way it has chosen to proceed.
Very briefly, I can say I have no problem when people talk about protecting life, since in cases where the mother's life would have been at risk, no one would have denied the mother the same right to life.
I also have a problem with the various stages at which the bill will be considered. It is now being considered on second reading and will then go to committee. If I had any hope that the bill might be reported back with significant amendments, I would be inclined to support the bill on second reading. However, I am afraid the bill might come back from committee without amendments. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis) raised these doubts in my mind when he said the government could not accept any amendments and that the bill had to go ahead as tabled.
So you see the kind of dilemma I am facing. If I vote for the bill on second reading, the government may think it can go ahead and consider my vote as positive support for the bill. It may choose to go ahead without any amendments, and finally, the bill might not survive third reading, which brings us back to square one, and we would still have no legislation.
So I think it is unacceptable that we have no laws to protect this life, to give this right,-I should not say give, because it is not ours to give-to protect and secure the foetus' right to life.

In conclusion, I want to make very clear that I support the protection of life. I think the government should have come up with a bill that would have given this protection to the foetus and I will vote accordingly so that life is afforded all the protection we can give it.
