Mr. Speaker, everyone finds that they are in a unique position, a most difficult position in this debate. I rise as a member of the New Democratic Party and also as an ex-principal of a Catholic school for some 26 years. To suggest other than what I am about to suggest, I believe I would be labelled as a hypocrite. I am proud to be a member of my party, and I am also proud of my stance.
I would like to quote Father Bob Ogle who, on November 18, 1980, delivered a speech on abortion. He stated, as reported at page 4826 of Hansard:
The human rights which 1 support are, first, the right to be born; second, the right to adequate food, housing, medical care, and education; third, the right to live in, at least, frugal comfort within one's cultural tradition; fourth, freedom of conscience, worship expression, political participation and peaceful dissent; fifth, equal treatment in public, job markets, and courts, regardless of sex, age, ethnic origin, marital status, religious of political beliefs, social and economic status; sixth, the right to social assistance when age or other circumstances make self-support inadequate; and seventh, the right to die with dignity.
I am proud to espouse those same principles.
People asked me just one year ago how I could become a New Democrat and have an anti-abortionist stance. I am proud of both of my decisions. Over the past month I have undergone the most poignant, gut-wrenching, if you will, period of my life. I know that our party has a pro-choice stance but I believe that our party has the most pro-life philosophies and policies of any party available to the Canadian public.
I am going to digress, no doubt, from the context of my speech. I am going to thank my women colleagues in the New Democratic Party for empathizing with me at a most difficult time in my life. I have become very sensitive to what they believe in and I believe that they have shown empathy to me. Through this all, they have taught me a great deal. Once we have become sensitized to one another, the issue has not become any easier. In fact, it has become much more difficult. They have told me that we must continue to dialogue and we have continued to dialogue.
My party stands for choice. It was clear and it is clear that I have not agreed with the position. We, nevertheless, stand together against this legislation for different reasons. But even in this variance in opinion we agree
that the proposed legislation is nothing more than a sham, a feeble attempt at a compromise.
It is proffered that if you do not vote for this, you are not getting anything in its stead; this is the best you can expect. I believe that oftentimes in politics, compromise is important but on this issue I do not believe the compromise is acceptable.
In isolation the abortion issue cannot be addressed. In this legislation there is no mention of the rights of the foetus. There is no accompanying legislation, no mention of social spending, no mention of assistance in areas of obvious need, counselling, infrastructure, support systems, adoption; nothing to address the obvious significant demand for abortion. We must reduce this demand but we can only do it through legislation that helps, not hinders the poor, the homeless, the uncared for and the unloved.
We can be occupied with deficits but not preoccupied with them. We must be concerned with GST's and clawbacks, but not overly concerned. We must be concerned with foreign aid, but not overly concerned when our own suffer each and every day. We should not persecute those who make their choice, although different from ours, because it is not an acceptable way to act. We should not accuse others of being chauvinist or feminist because of the choices they have made. We must not pretend to not understand or appreciate the opposing viewpoints when we truly do understand and appreciate.
These are the letters that I have received in one week, I think because of my station in life prior to my position as a member of Parliament. I would like to say that I have read them all. It does not make the decision any easier. I will say that I am a little disappointed in some of my friends at home because some long-term associates greeted me with "Dear Mr. Butland, My future political decisions will be based on your vote". There were no P.S.'s saying "Hi Steve, how are you doing?", nothing personalized at all. They were generic letters from people that I knew and know and am very friendly with on a regular basis. I hope that they will not be affronted by what I have said but that we can continue to dialogue as well.
I have literally thousands of generic letters. I received one letter that touched me to the very core and I would
November 27, 1989

like to read just a few excerpts because I think this woman has put it more succinctly and more poignantly than any of the other thousands of letters I have received.
It reads: "I would like to address the issue of abortion and would appreciate your reading this letter. I was an unwanted child bom into an alcoholic home. I was severely abused; physically, sexually, emotionally and psychologically. I now cany the scars of this abuse. If abortion had been legal then I am sure I would not be writing this letter today. I have been in therapy for 13 years, have contemplated suicide many times and have had two emotional breakdowns. I wake up with the pain in the morning and I go to bed with it at night. My point to you, Sir, is not that I should not have been bom but, instead, that I had every right to be born and every right to walk this planet for the last number of years. My only mistake all those years was believing I did not have a right to the air that I breathe."
It really does get more and more poignant as it continues and I think that it is appropriate that I stop now.
I will be opposing this legislation because it does not take a stand on either side of an issue which demands a very definite stand.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening in this House to debate one of the most important issues facing our nation, Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion. I feel I must rise this evening and speak in this debate in order to put my opinions forward as unequivocally as possible. Tonight in this Chamber we are debating abortion but, more important, we are debating life.
The bill proposed by the Conservative government was presented as a bill that attempted to strike a compromise between the right of the woman to personal freedom, to personal choice, to personal privacy and, of course, the community's and the nation's interest in protecting the right to life of the unborn child.
Obviously the government thought that this bill represented a balanced approach. Well, it is not a balanced approach to the issue of life. Hon. members, everything I believe, everything that I hold dear, my social and cultural make-up, my personal beliefs as a human being, tells me that abortion is wrong. I feel within myself,
Government Orders
passionately, that abortion is against the natural order. It negates the essence of our being.
This bill does absolutely nothing to protect the life of the unborn child. It does not in any way answer the fundamental question, the question of life. It does not address the value and the dignity of human existence. This bill's definitions are unbelievably vague. The bill states that abortion is prohibited unless the mother's health is endangered, but how does the government define health? The definition is so broad and so vague that we are basically speaking about abortion on demand.
Who is this government trying to fool? This government, I believe, really needs to do some soul searching from within, it needs to look within itself and take a serious stand on this extremely important issue. I think this government has failed drastically with this bill. I particularly do not think that abortion on demand is the answer to building a caring, compassionate and humanitarian society, a responsible society.
There is no question in my mind that personal freedom, personal liberty, is one of the most fundamental characteristics of our state, of our nation. However, I must also say that the personal freedom of one individual should take into consideration the impact, the effects it has on other lives and one must always focus on the essence of human rights and human dignity. Nor does personal freedom give you a licence to destroy other life. Thus, tonight we have to debate the right of the mother versus the right of the unborn.
Tonight I am going to speak on behalf of those who cannot speak for themselves, the unborn children of our nation. As members of Parliament, we are all here today simply because our parents decided to allow us to live. Quite frankly, with all due respect to my mother, I do not think she had the right to decide whether I should continue to live or not.
All of the hon. members in this House I am sure are happy to be alive. If we can make this statement consciously and responsibly, then I do not understand how any of us can accept giving the responsibility and the right to anyone to decide on who will live and who will not. Abortion is a human issue that affects all of us. We never think of leaving an abandoned child to die. We take great pain in seeing children in poor countries dying of malnutrition and starvation. Our hearts go out to them. Why then do we allow ourselves and why do we

November 27, 1989
Government Orders
allow thousands of babies bom alive in late term abortions to die? How can we allow millions more to be destroyed in the womb and still do nothing about it?
I firmly and passionately believe that we owe the same responsibility to these unfortunates as we do to all other human beings. We certainly have the right and the obligation to initiate laws and to establish laws to protect all human life. We have it in our power to re-establish the value of human life and respect due to it.
We often hear this so-called right to choose argument. While often cited, I believe it is irrelevant to the issue. The issue is not the right of the mother to control her own body, but whether she has the right to decide the future of another human being who shares her body. The innocent baby is certainly denied the right to choose. No one has the right to take the life of another person at will. Not the doctor, not the mother. Absolutely no one.
If there is a cause to be concerned about the health of the mother, then as a society we must make all possible efforts to save, not just one life, but both.
We must remember that pregnancy is not an illness. It is a natural state, a beautiful gift of life that unfortunately many people are not able to experience. We must build a nation that welcomes childbirth rather than promote abortions.
As Parliamentarians, I think we must devote our attention toward building the type of socio-economic infrastructure that will give the unborn child a better chance to live. Today, with the introduction of this bill we have taken a serious step backwards. We should concentrate our energies on better education, more accessible social services such as day care, counselling, adequate housing for the disadvantaged, a social safety net that will mean that women of this nation, by giving birth to a
child are not signing their names on the poverty role of our nation. Unfortunately, in this country this is the reality. More attention should be placed on the identification of causes of abortion so that our social and economic structure can better address the needs of our people.
As a Member of Parliament, I have always believed that one of my important duties and obligations was to represent those Canadians who, through no fault of their own, could not help themselves, the disadvantaged. The unborn child is certainly disadvantaged. He cannot express his views. He cannot manifest his emotions or his feelings. He is helpless and weak. I cannot accept the law that will allow the continuous destruction of human life. We must help people at the most vulnerable point of their lives. We must have faith and endure to protect human life. Canadians must realize that caring for the unborn child is the cornerstone and the beginning of a caring nation, caring for our future and caring for our people.
I am sure that the residents of York North agree that all measures must be taken by this government to make sure that the life of the unborn child is protected. I will vote against this bill because it does not show any consideration for the life of the unborn child.
